explanation.summary: Pre-eclampsia is a multisystem hypertensive disorder of pregnancy after 20 weeks gestation. The SOMANZ 2014 definition is new-onset hypertension (systolic over 140 or diastolic over 90 on two readings 4 hours apart, or any reading above 160/110) plus one or more of: significant proteinuria (urinary protein-creatinine ratio over 30 mg/mmol), renal insufficiency (creatinine over 90 micromol/L), liver involvement (transaminases over twice ULN, severe RUQ or epigastric pain), neurological complications (eclampsia, altered mental status, severe headache, persistent visual disturbance, hyperreflexia with sustained clonus), haematological involvement (platelets under 100, DIC, haemolysis), or uteroplacental dysfunction (FGR, oligohydramnios, abnormal umbilical artery Doppler, abruption, stillbirth). Severe features mandate admission, antihypertensive control (labetalol, nifedipine, hydralazine), magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, and timing of birth balanced against gestation. Definitive cure is delivery of the placenta.
key_points: SOMANZ end-organ criteria: platelets <100 x10^9/L, creatinine >90 micromol/L, ALT/AST >2x ULN, pulmonary oedema, eclampsia/severe headache/visual symptoms/stroke
Uteroplacental dysfunction: fetal growth restriction, abnormal Dopplers, stillbirth
Significant proteinuria: PCR >=30 mg/mmol or 24-hour >=300 mg
Hyperuricaemia is associated but not a diagnostic criterion
explanation.pearls: Pre-eclampsia after 20 weeks no longer requires proteinuria - new hypertension plus any maternal end-organ dysfunction (platelets under 100, creatinine over 90, AST/ALT over 40, neurological features, pulmonary oedema) or uteroplacental dysfunction satisfies SOMANZ criteria (SOMANZ 2014).

sources.label: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.rationale: Hyperuricaemia is associated with pre-eclampsia and useful for prognosis but is NOT part of SOMANZ diagnostic criteria. Hyperuricaemia is correct as a supportive prognostic feature in established PET, not for diagnosis (SOMANZ 2014).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.rationale: Hyperreflexia is a clinical sign that raises suspicion of CNS involvement but is not a SOMANZ diagnostic criterion; the neurological criteria are eclampsia, persistent severe headache, visual scotomata, or stroke. Hyperreflexia would be correct as a magnesium-toxicity monitor, not as a PET diagnostic criterion (SOMANZ 2014).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.rationale: SOMANZ defines pre-eclampsia as new hypertension after 20 weeks with at least one maternal end-organ feature or uteroplacental dysfunction. Thrombocytopenia below 100 x10^9/L and transaminases more than twice the ULN are each independently diagnostic criteria (SOMANZ 2014; RANZCOG 2023). SOMANZ thrombocytopenia threshold is <100 x10^9/L; transaminase threshold is >2x ULN.
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.rationale: Epigastric/RUQ pain raises suspicion for hepatic capsular stretch but is not a stand-alone SOMANZ diagnostic criterion without biochemical confirmation of hepatic dysfunction. RUQ pain plus transaminitis >2x ULN would be diagnostic (SOMANZ 2014).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

options.rationale: Significant proteinuria by SOMANZ requires PCR >=30 mg/mmol or 24h urine protein >=300 mg; 18 mg/mmol is below threshold. PCR >=30 mg/mmol would be diagnostic (SOMANZ 2014).
source_refs: SOMANZ Guideline for the management of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Late-pregnancy thrombocytopenia with microangiopathic features spans pre-eclampsia/HELLP, acute fatty liver of pregnancy (AFLP), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome (aHUS) - each demands different management but shares early presentation. HELLP (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) typically appears in the third trimester with epigastric or RUQ pain and pre-eclamptic features; coagulation is initially preserved. AFLP presents with nausea, vomiting, hypoglycaemia, raised ammonia, coagulopathy and renal impairment; the Swansea criteria help diagnose. TTP shows ADAMTS13 activity under 10%, microangiopathy, thrombocytopenia, neurological features and fever, with normal coags - treatment is urgent plasma exchange plus caplacizumab. aHUS is complement-mediated, predominantly renal, and responds to eculizumab. Initial workup in any pregnant woman with thrombocytopenia and microangiopathy: FBC, blood film, LDH, haptoglobin, LFTs, coagulation, fibrinogen, glucose, ammonia, ADAMTS13. Delivery is mandatory for HELLP and AFLP regardless of gestation.
key_points: HELLP: Hb low, platelets <100, AST/ALT >70, LDH >600, INR normal, glucose normal
AFLP: hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, hyperammonaemia, AKI
TTP: ADAMTS13 <10%, severe thrombocytopenia, neuro features
HUS: AKI dominant, often post-diarrhoeal (STEC) or complement-mediated
Mississippi classification grades HELLP severity by platelet count
explanation.pearls: HELLP vs AFLP vs TTP discriminators within hours: HELLP has elevated LFTs with normal coags and glucose; AFLP has hypoglycaemia, coagulopathy, hyperammonaemia and creatinine; TTP has ADAMTS13 activity under 10% and prominent neurology. All three demand delivery and tertiary referral (SOMANZ; RANZCOG).

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice - HELLP, AFLP, TTP, HUS

options.rationale: HELLP is diagnosed by Haemolysis (anaemia, schistocytes, raised LDH, raised indirect bilirubin), Elevated Liver enzymes (ALT/AST >70 U/L typically) and Low Platelets (<100 x10^9/L), usually with normal coagulation and normal glucose. This patient has all three features with preserved fibrinogen, normal INR, normal glucose and ADAMTS13 >10%, distinguishing it from AFLP, TTP and HUS (RANZCOG 2023; SOMANZ 2014).

AFLP typically causes HYPOGLYCAEMIA, COAGULOPATHY (raised INR, low fibrinogen), HYPERAMMONAEMIA, and more pronounced hyperbilirubinaemia. This patient has normal glucose, INR, fibrinogen, and ammonia. AFLP is correct when Swansea criteria are met (RCOG; BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - HELLP, AFLP, TTP, HUS

options.rationale: TTP is defined by ADAMTS13 activity <10%, severe thrombocytopenia, MAHA, neurological features, and fever; ADAMTS13 of 65% effectively excludes TTP. MAHA with thrombocytopenia is not TTP by itself. TTP is correct only with ADAMTS13 <10% (BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - HELLP, AFLP, TTP, HUS

options.rationale: HUS is dominated by acute kidney injury with relatively preserved transaminases; this patient has normal creatinine and very high transaminases - opposite pattern. HUS and HELLP both show MAHA + thrombocytopenia, so the organ pattern separates them. HUS/aHUS is correct with renal-dominant injury (BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - HELLP, AFLP, TTP, HUS

options.rationale: ICP causes pruritus (often palms/soles) and isolated raised bile acids with modest transaminitis WITHOUT thrombocytopenia or haemolysis. Transaminitis alone does not make it ICP. ICP is correct with bile acids >19 micromol/L and pruritus, without HELLP features (RANZCOG ICP statement).

explanation.summary: Australia uses ADIPS 2014 (IADPSG-aligned) criteria: 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks for universal screening. Any one value at or above fasting 5.1, 1 h 10.0 or 2 h 8.5 mmol/L makes the diagnosis.
key_points: Universal OGTT at 24-28 weeks
Early OGTT in first or early second trimester if high risk (previous GDM, BMI >=30, age >=40, ethnicity, family hx, PCOS, prior macrosomia)
One abnormal value is enough
Repeat 75 g OGTT 6-12 weeks postpartum
explanation.pearls: Memorise 5.1 / 10.0 / 8.5 - they are the only three numbers you need for diagnosis in Australia.

options.rationale: ADIPS 2014 criteria: ANY of fasting >=5.1, 1 h >=10.0, 2 h >=8.5 mmol/L. Her fasting 5.3 meets the threshold; even though the 1 h and 2 h values are below cut-off, GDM is diagnosed. Initial management is multidisciplinary team referral with SMBG (RANZCOG; ADIPS).

ADIPS criteria require only ONE elevated value to diagnose GDM (IADPSG single-value rule); her fasting 5.3 already meets the threshold. Requiring multiple abnormal values reflects older WHO or two-step criteria. One-value rule is the Australian standard (ADIPS).
The Australian fasting cut-off is 5.1 mmol/L, not 5.5. 5.5 mmol/L threshold was used historically but Australia adopted the IADPSG/ADIPS 5.1 in 2014 (ADIPS).

Diabetes outside pregnancy uses fasting >=7.0; in pregnancy the GDM cut-off is 5.1. She has GDM, not overt T2DM. Overt diabetes in pregnancy is diagnosed only with fasting >=7.0, HbA1c >=6.5%, or random glucose >=11.1 with symptoms - thresholds for T2DM diagnosis (ADIPS).

She meets diagnostic criteria; deferral risks fetal complications (macrosomia, stillbirth, neonatal hypoglycaemia). Confirmed diagnostic results need action, not reassurance. Re-testing is correct only when initial OGTT is in borderline ambiguous range (very rare with the single-value rule) (ADIPS).

explanation.summary: Gestational diabetes mellitus affects around 15% of Australian pregnancies and is screened with a 75 g OGTT at 24-28 weeks (or earlier if risk factors). ADIPS diagnostic thresholds are fasting 5.1 or above, 1 hour 10.0 or above, 2 hour 8.5 or above. First-line management is dietitian-led medical nutrition therapy, blood glucose monitoring (fasting plus 1- or 2-hour postprandial), and 30 minutes of moderate exercise daily. Pharmacotherapy is initiated when more than 50% of fasting or postprandial readings exceed targets (fasting under 5.0, 1 hour under 7.4, 2 hour under 6.7) over 1-2 weeks. Insulin is matched to the glucose pattern: isolated fasting hyperglycaemia responds to bedtime isophane; isolated postprandial to prandial rapid-acting analogue; both elevated to basal-bolus regimen. Metformin is an option in women who decline or cannot tolerate insulin, with counselling that it crosses the placenta but has reassuring short-term safety data. Postnatal OGTT at 6 weeks identifies overt diabetes.
key_points: ADIPS targets: fasting <5.1, 1 h <7.4, 2 h <6.7 mmol/L
Isolated fasting hyperglycaemia: bedtime NPH first
Isolated postprandial: prandial rapid-acting analogue
Both: basal-bolus
Metformin: alternative or adjunct; crosses placenta; not for severe hyperglycaemia
SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists: contraindicated in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Match insulin to glucose pattern in GDM: isolated fasting hyperglycaemia gets bedtime isophane (NPH); isolated postprandial gets prandial rapid-acting (aspart or lispro); both elevated get basal-bolus. Metformin is an option after counselling on placental transfer (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

options.rationale: Full basal-bolus is reserved for patients with BOTH elevated fasting and postprandial values. This patient has isolated elevated fasting glucose only, so basal alone is sufficient. Basal-bolus is correct when both fasting and postprandial fail despite stepwise titration (ADIPS 2014; RANZCOG 2023).

Prandial insulin would not address the predominant fasting hyperglycaemia and would risk daytime hypoglycaemia. Prandial-only insulin is correct for isolated postprandial elevations with normal fasting (ADIPS 2014).

Fasting glucose remains above target despite four weeks of optimised lifestyle; pharmacotherapy is indicated to reduce risk of macrosomia and stillbirth. Continued lifestyle is correct only when targets are achieved (ADIPS 2014).
SGLT2 inhibitors are contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenicity concerns and lack of safety data (TGA category D). SGLT2i is never correct in current pregnancy management (TGA; AMH).

For isolated fasting hyperglycaemia in GDM, the ADIPS-recommended first-line pharmacotherapy is bedtime intermediate-acting (isophane/NPH) insulin titrated to achieve fasting glucose <5.1 mmol/L. Metformin is an acceptable alternative or adjunct in suitable patients but insulin is the established first-line agent (ADIPS 2014; RANZCOG 2023).

explanation.summary: First-line oral antihypertensives for non-severe hypertension in pregnancy in Australia: labetalol > nifedipine SR > methyldopa. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated. Treatment target BP 110-140 / 80-90 mmHg per SOMANZ.
key_points: Labetalol 100-400 mg BD-TDS (first-line)
Nifedipine SR 20-60 mg BD (second-line)
Methyldopa 250-500 mg TDS-QID (second/third-line)
ACE inhibitors and ARBs: contraindicated
Acute severe BP: IV labetalol or IV hydralazine or oral nifedipine SR
explanation.pearls: Avoid labetalol if the patient has asthma, heart block, or significant bradycardia; switch to nifedipine SR.

options.rationale: Labetalol is standard first-line in pregnancy hypertension, but in significant asthma (recent exacerbations on ICS-LABA) beta-blockade risks bronchospasm; SOMANZ and RANZCOG list significant asthma as a relative contraindication. Labetalol is correct in pregnancy hypertension without asthma or other beta-blocker contraindication (SOMANZ; RANZCOG).
In a woman with significant asthma where labetalol is unsafe, nifedipine (calcium channel blocker) is the preferred first-line alternative; both are SOMANZ-recommended options (SOMANZ; RANZCOG).

ACE inhibitors are CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy due to fetal renal failure, oligohydramnios, calvarial hypoplasia, and pulmonary hypoplasia. Enalapril is never correct in current pregnancy; pre-conception switch to pregnancy-safe agent is mandatory (SOMANZ; AMH).

Methyldopa is an acceptable second-line agent but is less effective (higher target BP achievement failure) and has higher rates of depression/sedation/postural hypotension. Nifedipine is preferred in this asthma context. Methyldopa is correct as alternative second-line when first-line agents fail (SOMANZ).

Oral hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and unpredictable response; IV hydralazine is used for severe acute hypertension but oral hydralazine is not first-line maintenance. Oral hydralazine is correct only as add-on in resistant pregnancy hypertension with specialist input (SOMANZ).

explanation.summary: Maternal toxoplasmosis seroconversion during pregnancy carries a transmission risk that rises with gestation (10% in first trimester, 30% in second, 60-70% in third) but disease severity in the fetus is inversely related to timing - earliest infections produce the most severe congenital toxoplasmosis (chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, intellectual disability), while third-trimester infections are usually asymptomatic at birth. Diagnosis is by maternal serology: IgM positive plus IgG positive with low avidity suggests recent infection (within 4 months). Spiramycin 1 g TDS started within 3 weeks of seroconversion reduces vertical transmission by about 50% without crossing the placenta significantly. Amniocentesis after 18 weeks (and at least 4 weeks after maternal seroconversion) with PCR confirms or excludes fetal infection. If confirmed, switch to sulfadiazine plus pyrimethamine plus folinic acid (to reduce marrow toxicity) for ongoing treatment until delivery. Serial fetal ultrasound surveillance for hydrocephalus and calcifications.
key_points: Spiramycin: first-line in pregnancy to prevent transmission (does not cross placenta well)
Sulfadiazine + pyrimethamine + folinic acid: for confirmed fetal infection from 14-18 weeks
Folinic acid (leucovorin) protects against pyrimethamine-induced bone marrow toxicity
Diagnose primary infection with low IgG avidity within 16-20 weeks of seroconversion
Vertical transmission risk: T1 ~10-15%, T2 ~30%, T3 ~60% - but severity decreases with gestation
Sources: cat faeces, raw/undercooked meat, unwashed produce, soil
explanation.pearls: Suspected maternal toxoplasmosis: start spiramycin 1 g TDS within 3 weeks of seroconversion to reduce vertical transmission by half; switch to sulfadiazine-pyrimethamine-folinic acid only when amniocentesis (after 18 weeks) confirms fetal infection (RANZCOG; eTG Antibiotic).

options.rationale: Spiramycin is the first-trimester treatment of choice as it concentrates in the placenta and reduces vertical transmission without causing fetal harm. If fetal infection is confirmed (positive amniotic fluid PCR after 18 weeks), therapy switches to sulfadiazine + pyrimethamine + folinic acid to treat established fetal infection (RANZCOG; BMJ Best Practice; RCOG). Spiramycin reduces vertical transmission; sulfadiazine-pyrimethamine-folinic acid is reserved for confirmed fetal infection by amniotic fluid PCR at >=18 weeks.

Pyrimethamine is a folate antagonist and is teratogenic in T1 (neural tube defects, oral clefts); it should be avoided before 14-18 weeks. Treatment of the fetus is reserved for confirmed fetal infection. Sulfadiazine-pyrimethamine-folinic acid is correct only after confirmed fetal infection on amniotic fluid PCR (BMJ Best Practice).

Co-trimoxazole has activity against Toxoplasma but is not standard first-line therapy in pregnancy; spiramycin is preferred to prevent transmission and is the WHO-endorsed agent for prevention. Co-trimoxazole is correct in some non-pregnancy contexts (HIV-positive patients on prophylaxis) (BMJ Best Practice).

Azithromycin has weak in vitro activity but is not a recommended first-line agent in pregnancy. Azithromycin is correct only as adjunct in some refractory toxoplasmic chorioretinitis regimens (BMJ Best Practice).

Maternal primary T1 infection carries low vertical transmission risk (~10-15%) although severe consequences if transmitted; treatment with spiramycin substantially reduces transmission. Termination is not default. ToP is correct only after confirmed severe fetal infection (multiple anomalies on US/MRI) with informed maternal choice (RCOG; BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Congenital CMV is the most common congenital infection and the leading non-genetic cause of childhood sensorineural hearing loss. Primary maternal infection transmits in 30-40% of cases; non-primary in 1-2%. Management includes serial fetal ultrasound, amniotic PCR after 21 weeks, and consideration of maternal high-dose valaciclovir.
key_points: Primary infection: 30-40% transmission; non-primary: 1-2%
Diagnose by IgG seroconversion or low IgG avidity + IgM positive
Amniotic PCR: after 21 weeks AND >=6 weeks post seroconversion
Fetal US findings: ventriculomegaly, periventricular calcifications, hyperechogenic bowel, IUGR, hepatosplenomegaly
Valaciclovir 8 g/day may reduce vertical transmission (RCT 2020)
No effective vaccine; childcare hand hygiene is key prevention
explanation.pearls: Maternal CMV is often clinically silent; hearing screening at birth is critical for affected neonates.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

options.rationale: Primary maternal CMV has SUBSTANTIALLY HIGHER vertical transmission rate (~30-40%) and higher severity than non-primary (~1-2%). Non-primary higher-risk reassurance is never correct; the framing should always be 'primary infection = highest risk' (RANZCOG; BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

options.rationale: IV ganciclovir is teratogenic in animal studies and is not routinely used in pregnancy; valaciclovir trials have shown some benefit. IV ganciclovir is correct for neonatal symptomatic congenital CMV, not maternal pregnancy (BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

options.rationale: Spiramycin has NO role in CMV management; it is specific to toxoplasmosis. Spiramycin is correct only for maternal toxoplasmosis prevention of vertical transmission (BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

options.rationale: Congenital CMV is the MOST COMMON congenital infection in developed countries (~0.5-1% of live births) and the leading non-genetic cause of sensorineural hearing loss. Serial fetal US plus amniotic PCR after 21 weeks is recommended. Reassurance without surveillance is never correct (RANZCOG).

This reflects the current RANZCOG/RCOG/BMJ Best Practice approach: confirm primary infection (low avidity, seroconversion), serial fetal ultrasound, amniotic PCR after 21 weeks and at least 6 weeks post-seroconversion to maximise sensitivity, and consider maternal high-dose valaciclovir 8 g/day which a randomised trial showed reduces vertical transmission (RANZCOG; BMJ Best Practice; Shahar-Nissan 2020). Surveillance includes brain biometry and growth; amniocentesis sensitivity rises after 21 weeks and 6 weeks post-seroconversion; high-dose valaciclovir is the only intervention with RCT-supported reduction in vertical transmission.
source_refs: BMJ Best Practice - CMV in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Acute asthma in pregnancy is treated identically to non-pregnant patients with the additional priority of avoiding maternal hypoxia. Continue ICS, give salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone for moderate/severe exacerbations, and supplemental oxygen.
key_points: Maintenance ICS: safe and essential in pregnancy
Salbutamol: safe; first-line bronchodilator
Oral prednisolone 37.5-50 mg daily for 5-10 days for exacerbation
Target SpO2 94-98% (or >=95% in pregnancy)
IV magnesium for severe refractory cases
Step up therapy if severity criteria escalate; involve obstetric medicine
explanation.pearls: Maternal asthma control is more important than any medication risk; uncontrolled asthma causes IUGR, preterm birth and pre-eclampsia.

sources.label: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

options.rationale: Oral prednisolone is safe in pregnancy and is essential for moderate/severe asthma exacerbation; withholding it risks maternal AND fetal hypoxia, which is FAR more harmful than transient corticosteroid exposure. Pregnancy is not a contraindication to systemic corticosteroids. Steroid withholding is essentially never correct (Therapeutic Guidelines; National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

options.rationale: This is the standard exacerbation algorithm. Salbutamol bronchodilation, oxygen to target SpO2 94-98% (95% to maintain fetal oxygenation), maintenance ICS continued, oral prednisolone 37.5-50 mg daily for short course are all safe and indicated. Maternal hypoxia harms the fetus far more than these medications (National Asthma Council; Therapeutic Guidelines; RANZCOG). ICS and oral prednisolone are safe in pregnancy and reassurance about safety is part of the management.
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

options.rationale: LTRAs (montelukast) are adjuncts, not first-line, and have NO role in acute exacerbation management. Montelukast is correct as adjunct maintenance in exercise-induced or aspirin-sensitive asthma (National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

options.rationale: IV magnesium is reserved for severe exacerbations refractory to initial bronchodilator and corticosteroid therapy. IV magnesium is correct after 1 hour of maximal nebulised bronchodilator + systemic steroid with inadequate response (National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

options.rationale: PEFR 60% of best with a recent severe exacerbation does not meet safe discharge criteria; she needs systemic corticosteroids, observation, and a written asthma action plan. Discharge is correct at PEFR >75% best with sustained response 1 hour after last salbutamol (National Asthma Council).
source_refs: National Asthma Council - Australian Asthma Handbook (Pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Pre-conception epilepsy care: switch from valproate to lamotrigine or levetiracetam (lowest teratogenicity), folate 5 mg daily, plan for AED level monitoring (lamotrigine clearance rises ~2-3 fold), continue therapy because uncontrolled seizures cause more fetal harm than well-chosen AEDs.
key_points: Major malformation rates: lamotrigine ~2.3%, levetiracetam ~2.4%, carbamazepine ~5%, phenytoin ~6%, topiramate ~4-9%, valproate ~10%
Valproate also causes 30-40% neurodevelopmental impairment
Folate 5 mg daily for AED users (vs 0.5 mg general population)
Lamotrigine levels fall in pregnancy; monitor and dose-adjust
Vitamin K 1 mg IM to neonate at birth (standard)
Breastfeeding is safe on most AEDs (lamotrigine, levetiracetam, carbamazepine, valproate)
explanation.pearls: Switch off valproate at least 3-6 months before conception, not once pregnancy is confirmed - by then the teratogenic window is open.

options.rationale: Valproate carries the highest major congenital malformation rate of all AEDs (~10%) plus 30-40% risk of neurodevelopmental impairment; contraindicated in women of childbearing potential unless all alternatives have failed. Folate dose for AED users is 5 mg, not 0.5 mg. Multiple errors. Continuing valproate is correct only after documented failure of all safer alternatives with informed consent (TGA; AMH; Therapeutic Guidelines).

Phenytoin causes fetal hydantoin syndrome (microcephaly, cleft lip/palate, hypoplastic distal phalanges) with major malformation rate ~5-6%, higher than lamotrigine/levetiracetam. Older antiepileptics are not the safer choice in pregnancy. Phenytoin is correct in some refractory epilepsy without safer alternatives, never as first-line pregnancy choice (Therapeutic Guidelines; AMH).

Lamotrigine and levetiracetam have the lowest major malformation rates (~2-3%, similar to background). Valproate (~10%) is avoided in women of childbearing potential. Folate 5 mg daily is recommended for women on AEDs. Lamotrigine clearance increases substantially in pregnancy, requiring level monitoring and dose adjustment (Therapeutic Guidelines - Neurology; AMH; RANZCOG; NICE). Switch should be 3-6 months pre-conception; lamotrigine levels fall markedly in pregnancy. Continued AED therapy is essential because uncontrolled seizures cause more fetal harm than well-chosen AEDs.

Polytherapy increases teratogenic risk in a dose-dependent fashion; valproate remains highly teratogenic at any dose. The goal is monotherapy with the safest agent. Valproate is switched, not dose-reduced. Polytherapy is correct only in refractory epilepsy on a single safer agent, not adding lamotrigine to valproate (Therapeutic Guidelines).

Stopping AEDs risks status epilepticus, maternal injury, hypoxia, and fetal loss; uncontrolled seizures cause more fetal harm than well-chosen AEDs. Cessation is appropriate only after 2 or more years seizure-free with neurology confirmation, not reflexively in pregnancy (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Graves in pregnancy: PTU in T1 (lower embryopathy risk), then carbimazole/methimazole in T2/T3 (lower hepatotoxicity risk). Radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated. TRAb positivity confers neonatal thyrotoxicosis risk; neonatal TFTs are mandatory.
key_points: T1: propylthiouracil (PTU)
T2-T3: carbimazole/methimazole (PTU = severe liver injury risk)
Conversion: 1 mg carbimazole ~ 10-20 mg PTU (use 10:1 conventionally)
Target: maternal fT4 at or just above upper limit of trimester-specific range
Radioactive iodine: contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation
TRAb positive: fetal/neonatal thyrotoxicosis risk - neonatal TFTs day 4-7
explanation.pearls: Methimazole/carbimazole embryopathy includes aplasia cutis and a distinctive choanal/oesophageal atresia phenotype; switch off it before or by 6-10 weeks gestation.

sources.label: Endocrine Society - Thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum
ATA Guidelines for thyroid disease in pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: Carbimazole/methimazole is associated with aplasia cutis and embryopathy in T1; PTU is preferred in T1 but switched back in T2-T3 due to PTU hepatotoxicity. Positive TRAb requires fetal surveillance for goitre/tachycardia and neonatal monitoring (RANZCOG; ATA; AMH).
source_refs: ATA Guidelines for thyroid disease in pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: Carbimazole in T1 risks teratogenicity (methimazole/carbimazole embryopathy: aplasia cutis, oesophageal/choanal atresia); positive TRAb crosses placenta with fetal goitre/tachycardia/hydrops risk requiring surveillance. PTU is preferred in the first trimester; carbimazole is reintroduced for T2-T3 after the T1 switch (RANZCOG).

Graves may improve in T2-T3 (immune modulation) but T1 has highest activity; abrupt cessation risks thyroid storm and miscarriage. Stopping antithyroid drugs is correct only when biochemically euthyroid for >=6 months and TRAb negative (RANZCOG).

Radioactive iodine is ABSOLUTELY contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal thyroid ablation, cretinism). RAI is correct only post-partum if breastfeeding ceased and 6-month conception avoidance is acceptable (RANZCOG; AMH).

PTU causes severe hepatotoxicity (FDA black box); it should be limited to T1 and switched back to carbimazole in T2-T3. PTU throughout is correct only in carbimazole hypersensitivity or thyroid storm (RANZCOG; AMH).

explanation.summary: Established hypothyroidism in pregnancy: increase levothyroxine ~25-30% on confirmation of pregnancy, monitor TSH every 4 weeks until 20 weeks then again in third trimester, target trimester-specific TSH (T1 <2.5; T2/T3 <3.0 mIU/L) within the local reference range.
key_points: Immediate ~25-30% dose increase (or 9 doses/week)
TSH every 4 weeks until 20 weeks, then once between 26-32 weeks
Trimester-specific upper limits: T1 ~2.5, T2-T3 ~3.0 mIU/L (use local ranges if available)
Take levothyroxine on empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before food and 4 hours apart from iron/calcium
Postpartum: revert to pre-pregnancy dose and recheck TSH at 6 weeks
Untreated overt hypothyroidism: miscarriage, preterm birth, neurodevelopmental delay
explanation.pearls: Tell women to add two extra tablets per week as soon as they get a positive pregnancy test (9 doses per week) - a practical way to deliver the ~28% increase without waiting for clinic review.

sources.label: Endocrine Society - Thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum
ATA Guidelines for thyroid disease in pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: Dose typically needs to INCREASE by 25-30% in early pregnancy due to increased thyroid hormone requirement; TSH should be checked every 4 weeks until mid-pregnancy. Trimester-specific upper TSH targets are LOWER than 4.0 (typically <2.5 T1, <3.0 T2-T3). Multiple errors. This regimen is correct only outside pregnancy (Endocrine Society; ATA).
source_refs: Endocrine Society - Thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum
ATA Guidelines for thyroid disease in pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: Although beta-hCG can transiently suppress TSH in T1, women with established hypothyroidism need a DOSE INCREASE of ~25-30%, not reduction, due to higher TBG and placental transfer. Physiological T1 TSH suppression does not apply to hypothyroid women on replacement. Dose reduction is essentially never correct in pregnancy (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society - Thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum

options.rationale: Stopping levothyroxine risks severe hypothyroidism, miscarriage, and impaired neurodevelopment; continue and increase dose. Pregnancy is not the time for a 'wash-out' assessment of endogenous function. Stopping levothyroxine is correct only with documented full thyroid recovery (e.g., transient post-partum thyroiditis resolved) (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society - Thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum

options.rationale: Endocrine Society/ATA/RANZCOG guidance: known hypothyroid women should immediately increase levothyroxine by ~25-30% on pregnancy confirmation, recheck TSH every 4 weeks until 20 weeks then at least once in T3, targeting trimester-specific TSH (T1 <2.5 mIU/L is the historical target; current ATA recommends using local trimester-specific reference ranges, with an upper limit typically <2.5-3.0 mIU/L). The 9-doses-per-week trick is a practical 28% increase (Endocrine Society 2007/2012; ATA 2017; RANZCOG). Trimester-specific TSH targets are typically <2.5 mIU/L T1, <3.0 mIU/L T2-T3, with lower bound ~0.1 mIU/L.
source_refs: Endocrine Society - Thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum
ATA Guidelines for thyroid disease in pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: Symptoms are unreliable in pregnancy (overlap with normal pregnancy symptoms - fatigue, weight gain, constipation); routine 4-weekly TSH monitoring until mid-pregnancy is required because of dynamic dose requirements. Symptom monitoring alone is correct only in stable euthyroid post-partum patients (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society - Thyroid in pregnancy and postpartum

explanation.summary: A high-risk combined first-trimester screen (commonly >=1 in 300) should trigger counselling about contingent NIPT or definitive diagnostic testing. CVS is available from about 10 weeks; amniocentesis from 15 weeks. NIPT is a screening test - positive results require diagnostic confirmation.
key_points: cFTS window: 11+0 to 13+6 weeks (CRL 45 to 84 mm)
High-risk threshold typically 1 in 300 in Australian labs
NT >=3.5 mm independently increases risk of aneuploidy AND congenital heart disease - fetal echo at 20 weeks
NIPT sensitivity ~99% for T21, ~97% for T18, lower for sex chromosome aneuploidies
Procedure-related miscarriage CVS/amnio ~0.1 to 0.2% in experienced units
explanation.pearls: Never report an NIPT positive result as diagnostic - always confirm with CVS or amniocentesis before any irreversible decision.

sources.label: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing
HGSA/RANZCOG Joint statement on prenatal screening

options.rationale: Risk of 1 in 80 is well above the high-risk threshold (commonly 1 in 300 in Australian labs) and NT >=3.0 mm independently warrants further evaluation. Low-risk reassurance is correct only with cFTS risk <1:1000 or NIPT low-probability result (RANZCOG Prenatal screening).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: cFTS is a single screening event; repeating it will not move risk meaningfully and delays definitive evaluation. Screening tests are not serial monitoring tools. Repeat cFTS is essentially never correct as a follow-up of high risk (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: Maternal age alone is no longer an indication for invasive diagnostic testing; risk is individualised by cFTS or NIPT. CVS-by-age was the pre-2000 practice and is now superseded (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: RANZCOG recommends that after a high-risk cFTS the woman is offered counselling about both contingent NIPT (high sensitivity for T21) and definitive diagnostic testing (CVS from about 10 weeks or amniocentesis from 15 weeks). NIPT remains a screening test - a positive must be confirmed diagnostically. Procedure-related miscarriage risk for CVS and amniocentesis is approximately 0.1 to 0.2% in experienced units (RANZCOG; HGSA).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing
HGSA/RANZCOG Joint statement on prenatal screening

options.rationale: Amniocentesis is not performed before 15 completed weeks because of higher procedure-related fetal loss and limb defect risk (Canadian Early Amniocentesis Trial showed talipes equinovarus excess at 11-12 weeks). CVS is the T1 diagnostic option. Amniocentesis is correct from 15 weeks (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

explanation.summary: A positive NIPT is a high-probability screening result that must be confirmed by diagnostic testing (CVS or amniocentesis) before any irreversible decision. Fetal fraction above 4% is technically adequate; the test still has false positives through confined placental mosaicism, vanishing twin and maternal causes.
key_points: NIPT sensitivity ~99% for T21, specificity ~99.9%; PPV varies with prior risk
Fetal fraction below 4% is a no-call/low-confidence result; 8.2% is adequate
Causes of false positive NIPT: confined placental mosaicism, vanishing twin, maternal CNV, rarely maternal malignancy
CVS 10 to 13+6 weeks; amniocentesis from 15 weeks
Procedure-related miscarriage 0.1 to 0.2% in experienced units
explanation.pearls: When telephoning a positive NIPT result, always say 'high-probability screening positive - we need a diagnostic test to confirm'. Never imply diagnosis.

sources.label: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing
HGSA/RANZCOG Joint statement on prenatal screening

options.rationale: Even at advanced maternal age, NIPT is a SCREENING test not diagnostic. False positives occur (confined placental mosaicism, vanishing twin, maternal mosaicism, maternal malignancy). Irreversible decisions should not be made on screening alone, since a high PPV is not 100% (RANZCOG; HGSA).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing
HGSA/RANZCOG Joint statement on prenatal screening

options.rationale: Amniocentesis before 15 completed weeks is associated with higher fetal loss and talipes (early amniocentesis); CVS is the correct first-trimester diagnostic test. Amniocentesis is correct after 15 weeks if she prefers to wait, with the trade-off of later decisional timing (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: Repeating NIPT does not resolve the screening-diagnostic distinction; the same biological mechanism producing the positive (e.g., CPM) will produce the same result. Diagnostic testing (karyotype on tissue) is required. Repeat NIPT is correct only with technical failure (low fetal fraction), not for confirming positive results (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: Normal NT and morphology scan reduce but do not exclude T21; up to 50% of T21 fetuses have normal NT and ultrasound is not diagnostic. Reassurance from normal scan is correct only with low-risk screening and no flagged findings (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: RANZCOG and HGSA both emphasise that a positive NIPT requires diagnostic confirmation by CVS or amniocentesis before any decisions about pregnancy continuation. PPV for T21 with high-probability NIPT is high in older women but not 100%, and false positives occur through placental mosaicism, vanishing twin, maternal copy number variants and rarely maternal malignancy. CVS from 10 to 13+6 weeks is the earliest diagnostic option (RANZCOG; HGSA).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing
HGSA/RANZCOG Joint statement on prenatal screening

explanation.summary: CVS (10 to 13+6 weeks) and amniocentesis (from 15 weeks) are the two diagnostic options for fetal chromosomal analysis. Procedure-related miscarriage risk is approximately 0.1 to 0.2% in experienced units for both. Early amniocentesis (before 15 weeks) is contraindicated due to higher fetal loss and talipes.
key_points: CVS window: 10 to 13+6 weeks, transabdominal preferred if placenta accessible
Amniocentesis from 15 weeks; never before 15 due to Canadian Early Amnio Trial findings
Procedure-related miscarriage 0.1 to 0.2% for either in experienced units
Anti-D 625 IU IM after any procedure in an RhD-negative woman
QF-PCR results in 24 to 48 hours for common aneuploidies; full karyotype 1 to 2 weeks; microarray 1 to 2 weeks
explanation.pearls: If the placenta is posterior and inaccessible at 11 to 13 weeks, wait two weeks for amniocentesis rather than attempting transcervical CVS routinely.

sources.label: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing
HGSA/RANZCOG Joint statement on prenatal screening

options.rationale: Transcervical CVS has slightly higher infection and miscarriage rates than transabdominal in most series and is used when placenta is posterior and inaccessible transabdominally. 2-3% overstates the risk in experienced units; modern figure is 0.1-0.2% (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: Amniocentesis before 15 weeks (early amniocentesis) is no longer offered because of higher fetal loss and talipes equinovarus per the Canadian Early Amniocentesis Trial. CVS is the correct T1 option. Early amniocentesis is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: NIPT is non-invasive but remains a SCREENING test; she has already had high-risk cFTS and explicitly wants a definitive answer. Offering only NIPT does not meet her stated need. NIPT is correct as contingent screen if she preferred to defer diagnostic testing (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: CVS is performed from 10 to 13+6 weeks (most commonly 11 to 13 weeks); transabdominal CVS is preferred when the placenta is accessible. Australian and international meta-analyses estimate procedure-related miscarriage in experienced units at 0.1 to 0.2%, similar to amniocentesis (RANZCOG; HGSA).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing
HGSA/RANZCOG Joint statement on prenatal screening

options.rationale: Morphology scan is a screening tool, not diagnostic for aneuploidy, and does not satisfy her wish for early definitive information; up to 50% of T21 fetuses have a normal morphology scan. Deferring to morphology-only would be correct only if she explicitly declined diagnostic testing (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

explanation.summary: Soft markers on the morphology scan (echogenic intracardiac focus, choroid plexus cyst, mild pyelectasis, single umbilical artery, short femur, echogenic bowel) carry small individual likelihood ratios for aneuploidy and must be interpreted against the prior screening risk, not in isolation. RANZCOG guidance is that an isolated soft marker in a woman with a low-risk cFTS or NIPT result does not change management and warrants reassurance rather than further invasive testing. The exception is echogenic bowel, which carries a stronger association with cystic fibrosis, congenital infection (CMV), and trisomy 21 and warrants serology, NIPT or amniocentesis. Multiple soft markers or any major structural anomaly mandate maternal fetal medicine referral. Detailed cardiac imaging is reserved for true structural anomalies, not for isolated EIF.
key_points: Soft markers: nuchal fold >=6 mm, echogenic bowel, short humerus/femur, EIF, pyelectasis >=4 mm, choroid plexus cyst
Isolated EIF likelihood ratio for T21 ~1.4 to 1.8
Nuchal fold >=6 mm has highest likelihood ratio (LR ~17 to 20)
Fetal echo if NT >=3.5 mm, diabetes, family history CHD, or structural cardiac concern
Soft markers do not require repeat scanning if isolated
explanation.pearls: Isolated echogenic intracardiac focus carries a likelihood ratio of about 1.4 for trisomy 21 - clinically meaningless in a woman whose cFTS or NIPT has already placed her risk well below 1 in 1000. The marker only counts when integrated with prior risk.

sources.label: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: NIPT can be offered if the woman wishes but is not indicated by isolated EIF in a woman with low-risk cFTS; residual probability of aneuploidy is too low for routine contingent screening to be cost-effective. NIPT is correct in higher-risk soft marker combinations or maternal request, not routine isolated EIF (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: Isolated EIF in a low-risk population carries a small likelihood ratio (1.4-1.8) that does not meaningfully change a prior risk of 1:4200; offering amniocentesis exposes the woman to procedure-related miscarriage risk EXCEEDING the residual aneuploidy probability. Low-yield soft markers do not justify invasive testing (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

options.rationale: Isolated EIF without other findings on high-quality four-chamber, outflow tract, and three-vessel views is not an indication for fetal echocardiography. Fetal echo is correct for diabetes, NT >=3.5 mm, family history of CHD, or other suspicious findings (RANZCOG; ASUM).

Isolated EIF is a static finding requiring no surveillance; repeat scanning is not recommended unless there are growth or other concerns. Serial scanning for benign findings generates anxiety without yield. Repeat scan is correct only with growth concerns or new symptoms (ASUM).

An isolated EIF in a woman with a low-risk first-trimester screen and no other soft markers does not meaningfully alter the prior risk of aneuploidy and is not an indication for diagnostic testing. RANZCOG and ASUM advise reassurance in this setting; the focus is most often a benign mineralisation in a papillary muscle (RANZCOG; ASUM).
source_refs: RANZCOG Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing

explanation.summary: Australian anti-D guidance (NBA) does not recommend anti-D for sensitising events before 12 completed weeks except CVS, ectopic, molar pregnancy or termination. From 12 weeks, give 625 IU IM after a sensitising event within 72 hours. Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 625 IU IM at both 28 and 34 weeks, and 625 IU IM after birth if the baby is RhD positive (Kleihauer if >20 weeks event to titrate).
key_points: Pre-12 week sensitising events: anti-D only for CVS, ectopic, molar, ToP
12 to 20 weeks: 625 IU IM after sensitising event (within 72 hours)
>20 weeks: 625 IU IM plus Kleihauer-Betke to quantify additional dose
Routine antenatal: 625 IU IM at 28 AND 34 weeks (two-dose Australian regimen)
Postnatal: 625 IU IM if baby RhD positive within 72 hours
explanation.pearls: Australian 625 IU IM is not interchangeable with the UK 1500 IU or 250 IU regimens - always cite the NBA guideline in Australian practice.

sources.label: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Australian NBA guideline states anti-D is not routinely indicated for a sensitising event before 12 completed weeks, EXCEPT for CVS, ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, or termination of pregnancy. Anti-D in T1 is correct for the specific exceptions only (NBA Anti-D guidelines).
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: 1500 IU is the UK single-dose antenatal regimen at 28 weeks; Australia uses TWO-dose 625 IU IM at 28 and 34 weeks, not single 1500 IU. 1500 IU single dose is correct only in UK practice (NBA).
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Two errors. (1) At 9 weeks for threatened miscarriage with no instrumentation, anti-D is not indicated at all under NBA guidance - first-trimester anti-D applies only to CVS, ectopic, molar pregnancy, or termination. (2) Kleihauer-Betke quantification is reserved for sensitising events from 20 weeks, since first-trimester fetal red-cell volume is too small to measure reliably. The 250 IU figure itself would be the correct AU pre-12-week dose if anti-D were indicated, but here it is not (NBA Anti-D Ig Guidelines).
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Per the National Blood Authority guidelines, sensitising events before 12 completed weeks (threatened or complete miscarriage with no instrumentation, minor uterine bleeding) do not require anti-D. Routine antenatal anti-D 625 IU IM is given at 28 and 34 weeks, and 625 IU IM is given for any sensitising event from 12 weeks onwards (with Kleihauer-Betke if >20 weeks to quantify additional dose) (NBA).
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Anti-D is given for sensitising events when they occur, not prophylactically deferred; routine antenatal prophylaxis begins at 28 weeks, not 12. Deferral is essentially never correct in anti-D management (NBA).
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Australia uses universal vaginal-rectal GBS screening at 35 to 37 weeks. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is given to GBS-positive women, prior GBS-affected baby, GBS bacteriuria in this pregnancy, intrapartum fever, preterm labour <37 weeks with unknown status, or ROM >=18 hours with unknown status.
key_points: First line: IV benzylpenicillin 3 g load then 1.8 g every 4 hours (or ampicillin 2 g load then 1 g every 4 hours)
Low-risk penicillin allergy: IV cefazolin 2 g load then 1 g every 8 hours
High-risk penicillin allergy with clindamycin-sensitive GBS: IV clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours
High-risk penicillin allergy with clindamycin-resistant GBS: IV vancomycin
Aim for >=4 hours of antibiotic before birth for adequate cord levels
explanation.pearls: Always check the GBS isolate sensitivities at the time of the positive swab - inducible clindamycin resistance is common and is the reason vancomycin is the safe fallback.

options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is first-line in non-allergic women but is contraindicated by her documented immediate hypersensitivity reaction (anaphylaxis-spectrum). Benzylpenicillin is correct in non-allergic GBS-positive women (RANZCOG GBS; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Cefazolin is the alternative in women with LOW-RISK penicillin allergy (non-anaphylactic, non-immediate). Her immediate hypersensitivity reaction with mucosal involvement is high-risk and cephalosporins are not recommended due to cross-reactivity risk. Cefazolin is correct only in low-risk allergy (rash without mucosal/anaphylaxis features) (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

For high-risk penicillin allergy with GBS resistant to clindamycin and erythromycin, IV vancomycin is the recommended intrapartum prophylaxis in Australia. Dosing is weight-based loading then maintenance, with at least 4 hours before birth ideally for adequate cord blood levels (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Clindamycin is an option in high-risk penicillin allergy only when GBS sensitivity to clindamycin is CONFIRMED on testing; her isolate is resistant. Sensitivity testing is required before clindamycin is used for GBS. Clindamycin is correct with documented sensitivity (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

Oral therapy does not achieve adequate cord blood levels for intrapartum prophylaxis, and her GBS isolate is resistant to erythromycin. Oral erythromycin has no role in intrapartum GBS prophylaxis (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Single-dose IM methotrexate (typically 50 mg/m2 in Australian units) is suitable for haemodynamically stable women with an unruptured tubal ectopic of <35 mm, no cardiac activity, beta-hCG <5000 IU/L, no contraindications and reliable follow-up. Failure or rising hCG triggers a second dose or surgery.
key_points: Methotrexate dose: 50 mg/m2 IM single dose, repeat at day 7 if <15% fall day 4 to 7
Eligibility: stable, unruptured, mass <35 mm, no FCA, hCG <5000, normal LFTs/FBC/UEC, no breastfeeding
Absolute contraindications: ruptured ectopic, haemodynamic instability, FCA, IUP coexists, blood dyscrasia, hepatic/renal disease, immunodeficiency, peptic ulcer disease, breastfeeding
Avoid pregnancy for 3 months after methotrexate; folate supplementation pre-conception
Surgery (laparoscopic salpingectomy) if unstable, ruptured, large mass, FCA, or contraindications to MTX
explanation.pearls: Always confirm reliable follow-up before MTX - missed day 4 and day 7 hCG checks is the commonest reason for treatment failure leading to rupture.

options.rationale: RANZCOG/RCOG eligibility criteria include adnexal mass <35 mm and absence of fetal cardiac activity; her mass is within range and there is no cardiac activity. This finding does NOT contraindicate methotrexate. Adnexal mass >=35 mm WOULD contraindicate methotrexate per most protocols (RANZCOG; RCOG).

Methotrexate eligibility usually requires beta-hCG <5000 IU/L (some units 1500-5000); 3800 is below threshold. hCG >5000 WOULD contraindicate single-dose MTX in favour of multi-dose or surgical management (RANZCOG; RCOG).

The presence of fetal cardiac activity within the ectopic is an explicit contraindication to single-dose methotrexate in both RANZCOG and RCOG guidance because failure rates are much higher; salpingectomy or salpingostomy is the recommended management. Other absolute contraindications are haemodynamic instability, ruptured ectopic, significant haemoperitoneum, intrauterine pregnancy, breastfeeding, immunodeficiency, active hepatic or renal disease, blood dyscrasia, and inability to comply with follow-up (RANZCOG; RCOG).

Mild pain in a stable patient with no peritonism is not a contraindication and is common in tubal ectopic; only acute severe pain or peritonism would mandate surgery. Severe abdominal pain with peritonism WOULD contraindicate MTX (RANZCOG).

Absolute hepatic contraindication to MTX is active or significant liver disease; an isolated transaminase rise less than 2x ULN with normal albumin/INR and no chronic liver disease is a relative caution rather than an absolute contraindication and would typically prompt closer monitoring rather than blocking single-dose MTX (RANZCOG Ectopic pregnancy; AMH Methotrexate monograph). Transaminases above approximately 2x ULN, hypoalbuminaemia, deranged INR or known chronic hepatitis would shift towards absolute contraindication.

explanation.summary: Pregnancy of unknown location is defined as a positive pregnancy test with no intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy on high-quality TV ultrasound. Management is risk-stratified by serial beta-hCG every 48 hours and rescanning once the hCG exceeds the discriminatory zone (approximately 1500 to 2000 IU/L on TV scan).
key_points: Discriminatory zone TV scan: 1500 to 2000 IU/L (some Australian units 1500)
Normal early IUP: hCG doubles every 48 to 72 hours
Failing PUL: >=50% fall in 48 hours
Suboptimal rise (<63% in 48 h) or plateau: high risk of ectopic
Safety net: PV bleeding, severe pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness - immediate review
explanation.pearls: Never treat a PUL with methotrexate based on a single hCG and an empty uterus; you must exclude a viable early IUP first via serial hCG and repeat imaging.

options.rationale: PUL with hCG below the transvaginal discriminatory zone (1500-2000 IU/L) and no ectopic seen on US is not yet diagnosed as ectopic; treating with MTX could terminate a viable early IUP. MTX is appropriate only with confirmed ectopic, or after a viable IUP has been confidently excluded with rising/plateauing hCG above the discriminatory zone (RANZCOG).

Diagnostic laparoscopy is reserved for haemodynamic instability, suspected rupture, or persistent diagnostic uncertainty after failed expectant management. Laparoscopy is correct in haemodynamic instability or after failed conservative management (RANZCOG).

Pregnancy of unknown location in a stable woman with hCG below the discriminatory zone is managed with serial 48-hour hCG and rescanning once the hCG exceeds the threshold. A normal early intrauterine pregnancy doubles hCG every 48 to 72 hours; a fall >=50% suggests failing pregnancy; a plateau or sub-optimal rise increases ectopic concern. Safety-netting and ready re-presentation are essential (RANZCOG; RCOG).

A high-quality scan has already been performed; immediate repeat scanning is low-yield. Waiting for hCG to cross the discriminatory zone is the standard approach. Repeat scan is correct only when there is concern about initial scan quality or new symptoms (RANZCOG).

Reassurance without exclusion of ectopic risks rupture; PUL must be followed up to a definitive diagnosis (IUP, failing PUL, or ectopic). Reassurance is correct only after IUP confirmed on follow-up scan (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Admission criteria for hyperemesis: severe PUQE-24, >5% weight loss, persistent vomiting despite oral antiemetics, ketonuria, dehydration with postural hypotension or tachycardia, electrolyte derangement (hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia), or inability to tolerate oral therapy. Treatment is IV rehydration with thiamine before dextrose, antiemetic ladder and electrolyte correction.
key_points: PUQE-24: 12+ = severe
Antiemetic ladder: pyridoxine-doxylamine -> metoclopramide / prochlorperazine -> ondansetron -> corticosteroids (refractory)
Thiamine 100 mg IV/IM daily BEFORE any dextrose (Wernicke prevention)
VTE prophylaxis on admission
Investigate for molar pregnancy, multiple pregnancy, thyroid storm if atypical features
explanation.pearls: Always check TFTs and exclude molar/multiple pregnancy in severe hyperemesis; suppressed TSH from beta-hCG cross-reactivity is common and rarely requires treatment.

sources.label: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

options.rationale: She meets admission criteria for hyperemesis gravidarum: severe PUQE, >5% weight loss, dehydration with postural hypotension, ketonuria, hypokalaemia and failed oral therapy. Treatment is IV rehydration (commonly normal saline with KCl), thiamine 100 mg IV/IM daily before any dextrose to prevent Wernicke's, a stepwise antiemetic (pyridoxine-doxylamine, metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, ondansetron), and serial electrolyte and weight monitoring (RANZCOG; SOMANZ Hyperemesis).
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

options.rationale: Severe PUQE, postural hypotension, hypokalaemia, ketonuria, and >5% weight loss are explicit admission indications. Outpatient antiemetics will fail. Outpatient management is correct in mild-moderate hyperemesis without dehydration or weight loss (RANZCOG; SOMANZ Hyperemesis).
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

options.rationale: TPN is reserved for women who fail standard rehydration and antiemetic regimens with persistent weight loss; it carries significant infection/thromboembolism risk (PICC complications). TPN is correct only after failure of standard escalation (RANZCOG; SOMANZ).

Dextrose-first rehydration without thiamine cover risks WERNICKE'S ENCEPHALOPATHY in hyperemesis - a critical preventable iatrogenic injury. Use saline; give thiamine BEFORE any dextrose. Giving glucose before thiamine is essentially never correct in malnourished/hyperemesis patients (RANZCOG; SOMANZ).
source_refs: RANZCOG Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

options.rationale: Termination is rarely indicated and only after exhausting medical management with the woman's informed wish; the great majority of hyperemesis resolves by 16-20 weeks. ToP is correct only after refractory disease with maternal informed decision (RANZCOG; SOMANZ).

explanation.summary: Hydatidiform mole is treated by suction curettage in theatre with histopathological confirmation. Beta-hCG surveillance follows: weekly until three consecutive negative samples, then monthly for 6 months (complete) or one month (partial). Reliable contraception is required throughout because pregnancy obscures the rising hCG signal of persistent GTN.
key_points: Complete mole: no fetus, 'snowstorm' USS, hCG often >100 000, 15 to 20% progress to GTN
Partial mole: fetus/fetal parts, triploid, 1 to 5% progress to GTN
Primary management: suction curettage in theatre with histology
Surveillance: weekly hCG until 3 consecutive negative weekly samples, then monthly 6 months (complete) or 1 month (partial)
Contraception throughout surveillance; avoid pregnancy until cleared
Refer to GTD multidisciplinary service if hCG plateaus, rises, or new metastatic features develop
explanation.pearls: Suspect mole in any first-trimester pregnancy with hyperemesis, early pre-eclampsia, hyperthyroidism, very high hCG, or uterus large for dates - get a TV scan.

options.rationale: Methotrexate is first-line for persistent gestational trophoblastic NEOPLASIA, not for primary evacuation of a hydatidiform mole. Surgical evacuation is the primary treatment. MTX is correct for persistent GTN after evacuation with rising hCG (RANZCOG GTD).

RANZCOG and the Australian/New Zealand Gestational Trophoblastic Disease group recommend suction curettage as the primary treatment for hydatidiform mole. Histopathology confirms complete (no fetus, diploid androgenetic) vs partial (fetus or fetal parts, triploid) mole. Surveillance: weekly beta-hCG until three consecutive negative weekly samples, then monthly for 6 months (complete mole) or until one month after normal hCG (partial). Reliable contraception is mandatory throughout because pregnancy obscures rising hCG that would indicate persistent GTN (RANZCOG GTD).

Molar pregnancies do not reliably resolve spontaneously; surgical evacuation with histological confirmation is required to confirm diagnosis and remove trophoblastic tissue. Expectant management is correct only for very small failed early pregnancies, not molar (RANZCOG GTD).

Hysterectomy is reserved for women who have completed their family AND have a complete mole, or for refractory disease; suction curettage is standard first-line for women wishing to preserve fertility. Hysterectomy is correct in completed family with high-risk complete mole or persistent disease (RANZCOG GTD).

Medical evacuation with uterotonics/prostaglandins is associated with HIGHER rates of incomplete evacuation, embolisation of trophoblastic tissue, and persistent GTN. Suction curettage is preferred; molar pregnancy is not managed like a missed miscarriage (RANZCOG GTD).

explanation.summary: Asymptomatic bacteriuria affects 2 to 10% of pregnancies and carries a 20 to 30% risk of progression to pyelonephritis if untreated, plus an increased risk of preterm birth and low birthweight. Treat with a short course of a culture-directed agent and confirm clearance with a test-of-cure MSU.
key_points: Significant bacteriuria: single MSU with pure growth >=10^8 CFU/L
Dipstick has poor sensitivity (~50%); MSU MCS at booking is the standard
First-line agents (AU): cefalexin, nitrofurantoin (not at term), amoxicillin
Avoid trimethoprim in first trimester (folate antagonist); avoid nitrofurantoin at term
Test of cure 1 week post-treatment; recurrence -> investigate and consider suppression
explanation.pearls: Always check the booking MSU result actively at the 12 to 16 week visit - it is the commonest treatable cause of preterm birth and pyelonephritis that gets missed by dipstick.

options.rationale: GBS bacteriuria at any colony count in pregnancy is significant: (1) treat antenatally (asymptomatic bacteriuria) AND (2) it is an indication for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis regardless of vaginal-anorectal swab result. Both steps are required (RANZCOG GBS; eTG).

Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy is treated regardless of dipstick (5-10% progress to pyelonephritis if untreated). GBS bacteriuria additionally mandates intrapartum prophylaxis. No treatment is correct only outside pregnancy with no symptoms (RANZCOG).

GBS bacteriuria is an INDEPENDENT indication for intrapartum GBS prophylaxis at delivery; antenatal treatment does not eliminate this need (the rectovaginal colonisation persists). Antenatal treatment and intrapartum prophylaxis are distinct interventions (RANZCOG GBS).
Pregnant ASB warrants prompt empirical treatment, not deferral; growth at 10^8 CFU/L is diagnostic. Repeat MSU is correct only for borderline results <10^5 CFU/mL or contamination concern (eTG).

Continuous suppression is reserved for recurrent UTI in pregnancy after multiple confirmed episodes, not single ASB. Nitrofurantoin is also avoided near term (haemolysis risk). Continuous suppression is correct after >=2 confirmed UTIs in pregnancy (eTG).

explanation.summary: Heterotopic pregnancy (intrauterine plus ectopic) is rare in spontaneous conception (~1 in 30 000) but much more common after assisted reproductive technology (~1 in 100 to 1 in 500). Methotrexate is contraindicated because it would terminate the IUP; laparoscopic surgery is the treatment of choice, taking care to minimise uterine manipulation and continue luteal support.
key_points: Heterotopic incidence: ~1 in 30 000 spontaneous; ~1 in 100 to 500 with ART
hCG trajectory is uninterpretable when an IUP is present
Methotrexate contraindicated when a viable IUP coexists - it would terminate the IUP
Surgical treatment: laparoscopic salpingectomy (or salpingostomy) with minimal uterine handling, continue luteal support
Anti-D 250 IU IM if RhD negative; this is a sensitising event regardless of gestation
Suspect heterotopic in any post-ART pregnancy with pain and adnexal findings even when an IUP is visible
explanation.pearls: Always image both adnexae in any pregnant ART patient with pelvic pain, even after confirming an intrauterine pregnancy - the IUP does not exclude a coexistent ectopic.

sources.label: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.rationale: Methotrexate is CONTRAINDICATED when a viable intrauterine pregnancy coexists with an ectopic (heterotopic) because it would terminate the IUP. MTX is correct only for isolated ectopic without coexistent IUP (RANZCOG; RCOG).

Heterotopic with 30 mm adnexal mass, increasing pain, dizziness, and free fluid carries high rupture risk; expectant management is not appropriate. The beta-hCG trajectory is uninterpretable because the IUP confounds it. Expectant management is correct only for small ectopic with falling hCG without IUP (RANZCOG).

Watchful waiting in a haemodynamically stable but symptomatic heterotopic with adnexal mass and free fluid is unsafe; rupture risk is high. Surgery should be planned rather than reactive. Watchful waiting is correct only in asymptomatic small heterotopic with no rupture features (RANZCOG).

KCl injection is used in interstitial or cornual ectopics where surgical access is hazardous, but not first-line for a tubal heterotopic with rupture risk and prior salpingectomy. KCl is correct in interstitial/cornual ectopics or cervical ectopics where surgery would cause major haemorrhage (RANZCOG).

Heterotopic pregnancy (coexistent IUP and ectopic, much more common after ART) requires surgical treatment of the ectopic component because methotrexate would terminate the IUP. Laparoscopic salpingectomy is preferred for a complete tubal ectopic, particularly with prior contralateral salpingectomy; care is taken to minimise uterine manipulation and continue luteal support to protect the IUP. Anti-D 250 IU IM is given if RhD negative as this is a sensitising event pre-12 weeks (RANZCOG; RCOG; NBA).
source_refs: NBA Guidelines on the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Safe DV enquiry requires the woman be alone, a validated framework be used, the disclosure be documented in a non-shared place, and immediate referral pathways be activated. Antenatal pregnancy is a peak-risk window for escalation (RANZCOG C-Obs 57; NSW Health DV Routine Screening).
key_points: Never enquire with the partner present (RANZCOG C-Obs 57)
Use validated tool: HARK, AAS, or abbreviated WAST (RANZCOG C-Obs 57)
Document outside shared/hand-held notes (NSW Health)
Warm referral to 1800RESPECT and on-site social worker (1800RESPECT)
Pregnancy is a peak risk window for first-time and escalation DV (RANZCOG C-Obs 57)
explanation.pearls: If the partner refuses to leave, use a urine sample request or imaging excuse to create a private window (NSW Health).

options.rationale: Asking in the presence of the suspected perpetrator places the woman at increased risk of escalation and produces unreliable answers. Partner-present enquiry is essentially never correct in IPV screening (RACGP IPV; WHO).
source_refs: RACGP: Abuse and violence - working with our patients

options.rationale: Routine antenatal IPV enquiry must occur in private without the partner; a face-saving clinical reason to separate them, in an environment with social-work backup, is the recommended approach (RACGP; WHO).
source_refs: RACGP: Abuse and violence - working with our patients

options.rationale: Antenatal enquiry is recommended specifically because pregnancy is a high-risk period for IPV escalation; deferring to postnatal misses the engagement window. Postnatal-only enquiry is correct only when antenatal opportunity is missed (RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP: Abuse and violence - working with our patients

options.rationale: Visible leaflets in shared records are unsafe if the partner reviews them; safe enquiry in private is recommended. Written information is correct only when given discreetly during private consultation, not via shared documents (RACGP).
source_refs: RACGP: Abuse and violence - working with our patients

options.rationale: Mandatory police reporting against the woman's wishes endangers her and damages the therapeutic alliance; she must consent to any external action. Police involvement is correct only with the woman's consent or where mandatory child-protection thresholds apply (RACGP; WHO).
source_refs: RACGP: Abuse and violence - working with our patients

explanation.summary: AMIHS / Birthing on Country / Bubup-Wilam type continuity-of-carer models combining midwife and Aboriginal Health Worker, with ACCHO linkage, have Australian evidence for improved antenatal attendance, reduced preterm birth, increased breastfeeding, and improved cultural safety (NSW Health AMIHS Evaluation; RANZCOG W-WH 22; NACCHO).
key_points: AMIHS = NSW model; analogous services exist in Vic (Koori Maternity), Qld (Birthing in Our Community)
Continuity-of-carer is the active ingredient (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
Aboriginal identity is not itself a risk factor (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
Closing the Gap target 2 measures healthy birthweight (Closing the Gap)
Offer choice; do not force into Aboriginal-specific service if the woman prefers standard care
explanation.pearls: Birthing on Country is a movement returning birthing services to community control; it is not a single model but a principle (NACCHO).

options.rationale: Birthing-on-Country and AMIHS-type continuity-of-carer models have evidence for improved engagement, reduced preterm birth and improved cultural safety for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women. Given her history of disengagement from non-culturally-safe services, this is the best option (RANZCOG; AHMAC Birthing on Country).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

options.rationale: Bolting on an AHW as a separate referral is less effective than an integrated model where AHW and midwife share continuity from start; cultural safety is not an add-on. Standard midwifery with AHW referral is correct only when AMIHS is unavailable (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

options.rationale: Generalising all Aboriginal pregnancies as high-risk is racist and contradicts evidence; risk should be individually assessed. Obstetrician-led care is correct based on individual clinical risk factors, not ethnicity (RANZCOG; AHMAC).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

options.rationale: GP shared care is a valid model but does not provide the integrated cultural and clinical continuity that AMIHS offers. GP shared care is correct in low-risk pregnancies where cultural safety is met by other means (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

options.rationale: Telehealth is an adjunct, not a substitute for face-to-face culturally safe care; removing in-person AHW/midwife contact reduces engagement. Telehealth is correct as supplement to face-to-face care, not replacement (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Care of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Women

explanation.summary: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease remain leading causes of maternal cardiac morbidity in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women in Australia, with incidence rates around 50-100 times non-Indigenous rates. Secondary prophylaxis with benzathine benzylpenicillin G (BPG) IM every 4 weeks continues throughout pregnancy and lactation at the standard adult dose (1.2 million units) - penicillin does not harm the fetus, and interruption is a recurring contributor to recurrence and worsening cardiac disease. Multidisciplinary cardiac-obstetric review is recommended for any woman with moderate or severe rheumatic heart disease, ideally pre-conception, then at booking, 28 weeks and 36 weeks, with planning for mode and timing of delivery, anticoagulation if AF or mechanical valve, and intrapartum endocarditis prophylaxis. Echocardiogram should be repeated antenatally to assess progression. Antibiotic prophylaxis for delivery is generally not required unless there is established endocarditis risk per RHDAustralia/Therapeutic Guidelines.
key_points: BPG is Pregnancy Category A and safe in lactation (AMH)
Cessation risks ARF recurrence and progressive valve damage (RHDAustralia)
Moderate/severe RHD requires combined obstetric-cardiac team (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
Echocardiography baseline + each trimester for moderate or severe disease (RHDAustralia)
Anaesthetic and intrapartum planning at 28-32 weeks (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
explanation.pearls: Benzathine benzylpenicillin G 4-weekly IM continues through pregnancy and lactation at the standard dose for any woman with established secondary prophylaxis for ARF/RHD - interruption is a recurring contributor to maternal cardiac morbidity (RHDAustralia Guideline; RANZCOG).

options.rationale: Benzathine benzylpenicillin does not cross the placenta in clinically meaningful amounts and is safe and recommended throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding; the dosing interval is unchanged. Multidisciplinary cardiac-obstetric review is required for any rheumatic heart disease in pregnancy (RHDAustralia Guideline; eTG Antibiotic; RANZCOG; NACCHO).

Oral prophylaxis has higher failure rates due to adherence and absorption; IM BPG is preferred. Oral PenV is correct only when IM cannot be tolerated and adherence is supervised (RHDAustralia Guideline).

Penicillin is safe across all trimesters; cessation risks ARF recurrence with permanent valve worsening. Cessation is essentially never correct in active RHD secondary prophylaxis (RHDAustralia Guideline; AMH).

Standard 4-weekly interval is retained for routine prophylaxis; 3-weekly is reserved for documented breakthrough ARF or selected high-risk situations per specialist advice, not pregnancy alone. 3-weekly is correct after documented breakthrough recurrence (RHDAustralia Guideline).
Macrolides are only used for documented penicillin allergy; pregnancy does not cause allergy. Azithromycin monthly is correct only in confirmed penicillin allergy (RHDAustralia Guideline).

explanation.summary: Severe MS decompensates with tachycardia and Valsalva. Acute management is rate control with beta-blocker, diuresis, oxygen, and planned assisted second stage to deliver vaginally under regional analgesia (RHDAustralia; RANZCOG W-WH 22; ESC 2018 Pregnancy CVD).
key_points: Diastolic filling time is the critical variable in MS (ESC 2018)
Beta-blocker rate control is first-line acute therapy (RHDAustralia)
Avoid fluid bolus; manage pulmonary congestion with diuresis (ESC 2018)
Assisted second stage (vacuum/forceps) to limit Valsalva (RANZCOG W-WH 22)
GA caesarean carries higher haemodynamic risk than well-conducted epidural (ESC 2018)
Continue endocarditis-prophylaxis consideration per RHDAustralia for high-risk lesions
explanation.pearls: Anaesthetic plan should be written and reviewed by 32 weeks for any severe valvular lesion in pregnancy (RANZCOG W-WH 22).

options.rationale: In severe MS the haemodynamic enemy is tachycardia (shortened diastole, raised LA pressure, pulmonary oedema). Lowering rate with beta-blockade and offloading with a loop diuretic is the cornerstone of acute management while planning an assisted second stage to limit Valsalva effort. Emergency caesarean and balloon valvuloplasty are only required if she fails to stabilise (RANZCOG; ESC Pregnancy Cardiovascular Disease Guideline).

Beta-agonist tocolysis causes tachycardia and pulmonary oedema in severe MS - contraindicated. Valvuloplasty is considered antenatally in refractory disease, not in established labour at term. Tocolysis is correct in preterm labour without severe MS (RHDAustralia; ESC 2018).

Fetus is reassuring and labour is progressing; GA carries high haemodynamic risk in severe MS. Vaginal birth with assisted second stage under regional anaesthesia is preferred. Emergency CS is correct with fetal distress or maternal cardiovascular collapse (RANZCOG W-WH 22; ESC 2018).

Fluid bolus in pulmonary congestion from severe MS worsens pulmonary oedema; preload must be preserved but not increased. Fluid bolus is correct only in clear hypovolaemia, never with pulmonary oedema (RHDAustralia; ESC 2018).

ECG shows sinus tachycardia, not AF; amiodarone is reserved for arrhythmia and carries fetal thyroid risk. Amiodarone is correct only in confirmed maternal arrhythmia refractory to safer agents (RHDAustralia; AMH).

explanation.summary: Victoria: TOP on-request to 24 weeks; after 24 weeks two doctors must reasonably believe it appropriate considering all relevant circumstances (Abortion Law Reform Act 2008). Late TOP for fetal anomaly is provided in tertiary services with feticide and IOL (RANZCOG; The Royal Women's).
key_points: Victoria: on-request to 24+0 (Abortion Law Reform Act 2008)
NSW: on-request to 22+0; after 22 weeks two specialists must agree (Abortion Law Reform Act 2019 NSW)
Qld: on-request to 22+0; after 22 weeks two doctors agree (Termination of Pregnancy Act 2018 Qld)
SA: on-request to 22+6; after 22+6 two doctors agree (Termination of Pregnancy Act 2021 SA)
WA: on-request to 23+0; after 23 weeks Ministerial panel of two specialists (Public Health Amendment Act 2023 WA)
Tasmania: on-request to 16+0; after 16 weeks two doctors agree (Reproductive Health Act 2013 Tas)
explanation.pearls: All states require conscientious objectors to refer to a non-objecting practitioner (RANZCOG TOP).

options.rationale: Victorian Act permits TOP on request up to 24 weeks; this is correct on the law, but BEST practice for advanced gestation with fetal anomaly is the two-doctor tertiary pathway (referral to a tertiary service). This option understates the appropriate referral pathway. On-request alone is correct for early gestations without anomaly (Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).
Victoria has no 20-week prohibition; TOP is on-request to 24 weeks and lawful after 24 weeks with two doctors. The 20-week limit applies in some other states (Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).

Under the Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008, TOP is lawful on request up to 24 weeks; after 24 weeks it requires two medical practitioners. At 23+1 weeks she is within the on-request limit. Standard practice for a confirmed major fetal anomaly at this gestation is referral to a tertiary service, which will offer feticide and induction of labour with multidisciplinary support (RANZCOG; Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).

Victoria does not require ethics committee approval; the framework is the Abortion Law Reform Act 2008 with practitioner-led decision making. Ethics committee approval was the pre-2008 NSW practice (Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).

No statutory list of qualifying anomalies; the test for TOP after 24 weeks is two-doctor reasonable belief considering all relevant circumstances. A statutory-list framework would be correct only in jurisdictions with such legislation (none in Australia) (Victorian Abortion Law Reform Act 2008).

explanation.summary: Septic incomplete abortion requires concurrent resuscitation, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, and surgical source control by evacuation of retained products. This is a gynaecological emergency (RANZCOG TOP; eTG Sepsis; ANZICS Sepsis).
