Tamoxifen causes subepithelial stromal change and cystic atrophy that thicken the endometrium on TVUS even in benign disease, making the standard >4 mm threshold less reliable; hysteroscopy with directed biopsy is the recommended investigation in any symptomatic tamoxifen user. Routine TVUS surveillance of asymptomatic tamoxifen users is NOT recommended in Australian guidance (RANZCOG; eviQ Endometrial cancer; eviQ Tamoxifen).

Repeat imaging delays diagnosis without changing the indication for histology in symptomatic tamoxifen user; TVUS findings are poorly specific. Repeat TVUS is correct only with technically inadequate initial scan (eviQ Endometrial cancer).

Standard >4 mm threshold cannot be applied to symptomatic tamoxifen users; any PMB on tamoxifen requires histological exclusion. Reassurance is correct only after histology excludes pathology (eviQ Tamoxifen).

Asymptomatic surveillance of tamoxifen users with TVUS is NOT recommended in Australian guidance; surveillance does not improve outcomes. Bleeding, not thickness, is the investigation trigger. TVUS surveillance is essentially never correct in asymptomatic tamoxifen users (eviQ Tamoxifen; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Workup of HMB follows PALM-COEIN. TVUS plus FBC/ferritin are universal. Endometrial sampling is indicated at age >=45, persistent intermenstrual bleeding, failed medical therapy, or risk factors for endometrial cancer (obesity, anovulation, tamoxifen, Lynch). TSH and coagulation screen are adjuncts based on history.
key_points: PALM (structural): Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia
COEIN (non-structural): Coagulopathy, Ovulatory, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified
FBC + ferritin in all; TSH if cycle change or clinical features; coags if bleeding history since menarche
Biopsy if age >=45 OR risk factor for endometrial cancer (obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch, unopposed oestrogen)
TVUS first-line imaging; saline-infusion sonohysterography or hysteroscopy for focal lesions
explanation.pearls: Obesity lowers the age threshold for endometrial sampling. Don't anchor on age 45 if other risk factors are present.

options.rationale: Random FSH/oestradiol in a 44-year-old with regular cycles is unhelpful; cycle regularity argues against anovulation. Hormonal testing is correct only with established cycle irregularity (RANZCOG HMB).

Inherited bleeding disorder screen is for HMB since menarche or personal/family bleeding cues; her 8-month history without bleeding red flags does not prioritise this. Coag/vWF panel is correct with bleeding history clues (RANZCOG HMB).

RANZCOG and NICE NG88 recommend endometrial sampling in women with HMB who are aged 45 or over OR who have risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia/cancer; obesity (BMI 34) is a major risk factor and TVUS alone is insufficient to exclude endometrial pathology in this setting (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

Hysteroscopy is appropriate where TVUS suggests focal pathology or sampling is unsuccessful, but TVUS remains first-line. Hysteroscopy-first is correct only with TVUS showing focal lesion (NICE NG88).
CA-125 is non-specific in premenopausal women and has no role in HMB workup. CA-125 is correct in suspected ovarian pathology (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: For fibroid-related HMB without significant cavity distortion: LNG-IUS first-line. Tranexamic acid and NSAIDs are useful adjuncts. GnRH analogues are short-term pre-surgical or perimenopausal bridging agents. Myomectomy preserves fertility; hysterectomy is definitive when family complete and other options failed.
key_points: LNG-IUS: first-line for HMB without cavity distortion (FIGO types 3-7 generally OK)
Submucosal fibroids (FIGO 0-2) distorting cavity: hysteroscopic myomectomy
GnRH agonist: short-term shrinkage pre-op or perimenopausal bridge
Uterine artery embolisation: alternative when fertility not desired
Myomectomy: preserves fertility; hysterectomy: definitive cure
explanation.pearls: Mirena requires a cavity that the device can sit in. A large submucosal fibroid distorting the cavity contraindicates Mirena and instead triggers hysteroscopic myomectomy.

options.rationale: GnRH analogues are used short-term (3-6 months) to shrink fibroids pre-surgery or to bridge perimenopause; not first-line ongoing therapy due to vasomotor symptoms and bone loss. GnRH is correct as bridge therapy, not chronic (RANZCOG).

The LNG-IUS is first-line medical therapy for HMB including fibroid-related HMB where the uterine cavity is not distorted by submucosal fibroids; it reduces blood loss by 70-95% and is acceptable for a woman who has completed her family (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).
TXA reduces blood loss by 40-50% but does not address bulk symptoms and is less effective than LNG-IUS overall. TXA is correct for acute heavy periods or as adjunct (NICE NG88).
NSAIDs reduce blood loss by ~25-30% and help dysmenorrhoea; useful adjuncts but not first-line for moderate-severe HMB with anaemia. NSAIDs are correct as adjunctive symptomatic therapy (NICE NG88).

Hysterectomy is definitive but should be reserved for failed/declined medical therapy; she has not yet trialled LARC. Hysterectomy is correct after failed conservative options or with patient preference (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Endometriosis affects about 1 in 9 Australian women and is consistently diagnosed late, with average symptom-to-diagnosis interval of 7-12 years. Cyclical pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, cyclical bowel or bladder symptoms, and subfertility are the core presentation. Examination may show tender nodularity of the uterosacral ligaments or a fixed retroverted uterus, but is often normal. Transvaginal ultrasound detects endometriomas and deep infiltrating disease in expert hands but is normal in superficial peritoneal disease - so a normal scan does not exclude endometriosis. Laparoscopy with histological confirmation is the gold standard but is not required to start empirical therapy. First-line medical management is NSAIDs plus continuous combined oral contraceptive (or POP or LNG-IUS), with 3-6 month review of symptom response. Second-line is GnRH agonist with add-back HRT, or dienogest. Laparoscopic excision is for confirmed disease, treatment-failure, infertility workup, or endometrioma over 3 cm.
key_points: Classic features: cyclical pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, dysuria
Empirical hormonal therapy precedes laparoscopy in straightforward presentations
TVUS first-line imaging; MRI for suspected deep disease
Laparoscopy: failed medical therapy, suspected deep disease, infertility, severe symptoms
Refer to gynaecologist if no response in 3-6 months or red flags
explanation.pearls: Endometriosis is a clinical diagnosis - TVUS is normal in superficial peritoneal disease, MRI and CA-125 add nothing to first-line management. Trial continuous COCP plus NSAID and review at 3-6 months; laparoscopy is for treatment failure or fertility concerns (RANZCOG; ESHRE).

options.rationale: RANZCOG and ESHRE endometriosis guidance support empirical hormonal therapy (continuous COCP or progestogen) as first-line in suspected endometriosis without requiring laparoscopic confirmation, especially if fertility is not imminently sought. Laparoscopy is reserved for refractory cases or fertility planning (RANZCOG; ESHRE 2022).

Empirical hormonal therapy is now preferred first-line over diagnostic laparoscopy for suspected endometriosis. Laparoscopy is correct after failed medical therapy or for surgical planning (ESHRE 2022; RANZCOG).
CA-125 has poor sensitivity and specificity for endometriosis. CA-125 is correct in suspected ovarian pathology, not endometriosis diagnosis (ESHRE 2022).
MRI is reserved for suspected deep infiltrating endometriosis with surgical planning, not primary diagnosis. MRI is correct for deep endometriosis surgical mapping (RANZCOG; ESHRE).
GnRH agonists are second/third line after COCP/progestogens due to bone density and menopausal symptoms. GnRH is correct after first-line hormonal failure (RANZCOG; ESHRE).

explanation.summary: POI: amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea >=4 months + FSH >25 IU/L on 2 readings 4+ weeks apart, in a woman aged under 40. Work-up: karyotype, fragile X premutation, adrenal (21-OH) and thyroid antibodies, baseline DXA. Treat with HRT until at least the average age of natural menopause (~51) for bone, CV and neurocognitive protection. Spontaneous pregnancy possible in ~5-10%; HRT is not a contraceptive.
key_points: Diagnosis: amenorrhoea >=4 months + 2 x FSH >25 IU/L, 4+ weeks apart, age <40
Causes: idiopathic, genetic (Turner, fragile X), autoimmune, iatrogenic (chemo/radiotherapy/surgery)
HRT (or COCP) until ~age 51
Discuss contraception separately - HRT not contraceptive
Refer for fertility counselling early
explanation.pearls: POI is not just early menopause - women may still ovulate intermittently and conceive; HRT does not prevent pregnancy.

options.rationale: POI diagnosis requires two FSH >25 IU/L at least 4 weeks apart; her first sample was 5 weeks prior, so confirmatory second now is appropriate. Reassurance with re-check at 6 months is correct only with isolated borderline FSH and no amenorrhoea (Australasian Menopause Society POI).
COCP can be used in POI but HRT provides more physiological replacement and better bone protection. COCP is correct when contraception desired alongside replacement (BMS).
Delaying oestrogen replacement until 40 risks cardiovascular, bone, and neurocognitive harm; replacement should commence at diagnosis. Defer HRT is essentially never correct in confirmed POI (ESHRE).
Adrenal autoimmune screen (21-hydroxylase antibodies) is part of POI workup but does not need to precede HRT commencement. Adrenal screen is correct concurrently, not before HRT (ESHRE).

POI confirmed by FSH >25 IU/L on two occasions at least 4 weeks apart with amenorrhoea >=4 months in a woman <40 mandates HRT until at least the average age of natural menopause to protect bone and cardiovascular health; concurrent work-up includes karyotype, fragile X premutation, adrenal antibodies, thyroid antibodies, and a fertility discussion (ESHRE 2016; Jean Hailes).

explanation.summary: Empirical outpatient PID regimen per Australian Therapeutic Guidelines: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM stat + doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg BD for 14 days. Take partner notification, STI screen, and HIV/hepatitis screening at presentation.
key_points: Ceftriaxone covers gonorrhoea
Doxycycline covers chlamydia and M. genitalium (test/retest if treatment failure)
Metronidazole covers anaerobes
Admit and treat IV if pregnant, severe, TOA, sepsis, or failed oral therapy
Partner notification and contact tracing essential
explanation.pearls: PID is a clinical diagnosis - don't wait for swab results before starting antibiotics.

options.rationale: Severe PID with tubo-ovarian abscess, systemic features (fever, tachycardia, vomiting) requires hospital admission and IV combination therapy. Drainage is added if there is no response in 48-72 hours or the abscess is large (RANZCOG PID; eTG).
Outpatient regimen is for mild-moderate PID without abscess or systemic features; her TOA, fever, tachycardia, vomiting require IV in hospital. Outpatient is correct in mild PID (RANZCOG PID; eTG).
Single-dose monotherapy is inadequate for any PID, let alone severe with TOA. Single-dose IM is essentially never sufficient in PID (eTG).
Surgery is reserved for diagnostic uncertainty, ruptured TOA, or failure of antibiotic therapy at 48-72 hours. Surgery is correct after antibiotic failure or rupture (RANZCOG).
Amoxicillin is not first-line PID therapy and does not cover gonorrhoea, anaerobes, or atypicals. Amoxicillin is correct in confirmed susceptible Listeria or strep infections, not PID (eTG).

explanation.summary: Postnatal contraception in breastfeeding women: progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, DMPA, LNG-IUS) are all safe at 6 weeks. Cu-IUD or LNG-IUS can be inserted from 4-6 weeks postpartum (or immediately postpartum within 48 h of birth). CHC is avoided <6 weeks (UKMEC 4) and category 2 between 6 weeks and 6 months while breastfeeding. LAM is ~98% effective only when ALL three criteria are met: <6 months, amenorrhoea, exclusive or near-exclusive breastfeeding.
key_points: POP can start day 21 postpartum without need to wait
IUD/IUS: insert immediately postpartum (within 48 h) or from 4-6 weeks
CHC: avoid <6 weeks if breastfeeding; from 6 weeks UKMEC 2; from 6 months UKMEC 1
DMPA: UKMEC 2 before 6 weeks if breastfeeding, then UKMEC 1
LAM strict criteria: amenorrhoea + exclusive BF + <6 months postpartum
explanation.pearls: Day 21 postpartum is the earliest fertility could return in non-breastfeeding women - that's why POP and CHC have day 21 as the earliest start if other criteria allow.

options.rationale: CHC is UKMEC 4 <6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding, UKMEC 2 from 6 weeks to 6 months. CHC is correct >6 months postpartum or not breastfeeding (FSRH UKMEC).
LAM requires all three: amenorrhoea, exclusive/near-exclusive breastfeeding, AND <6 months postpartum; reliability falls thereafter. LAM is correct when all three criteria met (FSRH UKMEC).

Intrauterine contraception (LNG-IUS or Cu-IUD) can be safely inserted from 4-6 weeks postpartum (UKMEC 1-2); progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, DMPA) are also suitable in breastfeeding women from any time postpartum (FSRH UKMEC; Family Planning Australia).
Etonogestrel implant does not adversely affect milk supply and can be inserted at any time postpartum. Implant delay is essentially never required (FSRH; WHO MEC).
DMPA is UKMEC 1 from 6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding (UKMEC 2 before). DMPA is correct from 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women (FSRH UKMEC).

explanation.summary: Under the NCSP: HPV 16/18 detected -> direct colposcopy regardless of LBC. Oncogenic HPV non-16/18 with negative or low-grade reflex LBC -> repeat HPV in 12 months (intermediate risk). Oncogenic HPV non-16/18 with possible high-grade or worse on LBC -> colposcopy. Persistent oncogenic HPV at 24 months -> colposcopy.
key_points: HPV 16/18 (any LBC): direct colposcopy
Other oncogenic HPV + negative/low-grade LBC: repeat HPV at 12 months
Other oncogenic HPV + possible high-grade or worse LBC: colposcopy
If 12-month repeat HPV negative -> return to 5-yearly screening
Self-collected vaginal swab is now universally available since July 2022
explanation.pearls: Reflex LBC is performed automatically by the lab if oncogenic HPV is detected; the practitioner does not need to order it separately.

options.rationale: Direct colposcopy is for HPV 16/18 regardless of cytology, or any oncogenic HPV with pHSIL/HSIL, or persistent HPV at 24 months. Direct colposcopy is correct in those higher-risk pathways (NCSP 2022).

Oncogenic non-16/18 HPV with reflex LBC negative or low-grade abnormality places the patient in the intermediate-risk group; repeat HPV at 12 months. If still HPV-positive then refer to colposcopy; if negative, return to 5-yearly screening (NCSP 2022).
5-yearly screening resumes only after HPV becomes negative; any oncogenic HPV detection triggers 12-month repeat or colposcopy. Routine 5-yearly is correct only with negative HPV (NCSP 2022).
6-month repeat is not NCSP-recommended; intermediate-risk repeat is at 12 months. 6-month repeat was the old pathway, now obsolete (NCSP 2022).
Treatment is based on histological diagnosis from colposcopy/biopsy, not on HPV status with negative cytology. LLETZ is correct after histology confirms high-grade dysplasia (NCSP 2022).

explanation.summary: TVUS endometrial thickness <=4 mm has a high negative predictive value (~99%) for endometrial cancer in PMB; sampling not mandatory if bleeding is a single episode. Thickness >=4 mm triggers Pipelle biopsy +/- hysteroscopy. Recurrent PMB warrants sampling regardless of TVUS. Risk factors: obesity, T2DM, nulliparity, late menopause, unopposed oestrogen, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome.
key_points: TVUS endometrial thickness >=4 mm -> Pipelle biopsy
Recurrent PMB -> sample regardless of TVUS thickness
Hysteroscopy if focal lesion, non-diagnostic Pipelle, or thickened endometrium
Risk factors: obesity, DM, PCOS, nulliparity, tamoxifen, Lynch, unopposed oestrogen
Approximately 10% of PMB has endometrial cancer
explanation.pearls: Any PMB warrants investigation. A thin endometrium does not equal a benign outcome if bleeding recurs.

options.rationale: Endometrial thickness <=4 mm has very low cancer risk and TVUS alone may be sufficient initial triage; sampling not mandatory below this cut-off. Mandatory sampling at <=2 mm is over-treatment (RANZCOG).

Although thin endometrium has high NPV, recurrent or persistent PMB requires sampling regardless of TVUS thickness. Reassurance without sampling is correct only for single PMB episode with thin endometrium and resolution (RCOG).
True but not directly relevant - she is not on tamoxifen (RANZCOG).

TVUS is appropriate first-line imaging; hysteroscopy is for thickened endometrium >=4 mm, recurrent PMB, or non-diagnostic Pipelle. Direct hysteroscopy is correct after TVUS shows thickened or focal endometrium (RCOG; RANZCOG).

The widely used 4 mm cut-off has a sensitivity of ~95% for endometrial carcinoma in postmenopausal bleeding; endometrial sampling is indicated above this threshold, with hysteroscopy +/- directed biopsy if focal pathology is suspected or Pipelle is non-diagnostic (RCOG Green-top 67; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: MHT principles: oestrogen alone if hysterectomy; combined (oestrogen + progestogen) if uterus intact. Cyclical progestogen for perimenopausal women still having periods; continuous combined for women >=12 months postmenopausal who want no bleed. Transdermal oestrogen preferred when VTE risk is elevated (prior VTE, obesity, age) - no first-pass hepatic effect. LNG-IUS is an effective progestogen for endometrial protection.
key_points: Uterus intact -> add progestogen (mandatory)
Hysterectomy -> oestrogen alone
Cyclical progestogen if still cycling; continuous if >12 months amenorrhoea
Transdermal oestrogen: no increased VTE risk; preferred if VTE risk factors
Absolute contraindications: current/recent breast cancer, oestrogen-dependent malignancy, undiagnosed PV bleeding, active VTE/PE, active liver disease, untreated endometrial hyperplasia
explanation.pearls: If a woman has a uterus and you forget the progestogen, you cause endometrial cancer. LNG-IUS plus transdermal oestrogen is an elegant solution in many women.

options.rationale: Cyclical progestogen produces monthly bleed and is preferred in perimenopausal women still cycling; this woman is >12 months postmenopausal preferring no-bleed. Cyclical regimen is correct in perimenopausal HRT (BMS; Jean Hailes).
Oral oestrogen increases VTE risk ~2-fold; transdermal at standard doses does not. Oral CEE is correct only in women without VTE risk factors (BMS; Jean Hailes).

Tibolone is reasonable for vasomotor and libido symptoms but increases stroke risk (especially age >60) and is not first-line in women with elevated stroke risk. Tibolone is correct in younger women without stroke risk factors (BMS).

Transdermal oestrogen avoids first-pass hepatic metabolism and does not increase VTE risk at standard doses, making it the preferred route in women with prior VTE, obesity or other VTE risk factors. The LNG-IUS provides effective endometrial protection in a no-bleed manner. Together this provides combined MHT for a woman with an intact uterus (BMS 2024; Jean Hailes).
Unopposed oestrogen in intact uterus causes endometrial hyperplasia/cancer; progestogen mandatory. Oestrogen-alone is correct only after hysterectomy (BMS; Jean Hailes).

explanation.summary: GSM (vaginal atrophy + urinary symptoms) responds well to low-dose vaginal oestrogen with minimal systemic absorption. In breast cancer survivors, local vaginal oestrogen is increasingly used after shared decision-making with the oncologist, especially in those not on aromatase inhibitors and with significant symptom burden. Non-hormonal moisturisers and lubricants are first-line; vaginal oestrogen is added when symptoms persist.
key_points: First-line: non-hormonal moisturisers (Replens) + lubricants
Second-line: low-dose vaginal oestriol cream or oestradiol pessary
Local vaginal oestrogen: minimal systemic absorption
In breast cancer survivors: shared decision with oncology; tamoxifen users generally acceptable; AI users more contentious
GSM also reduces recurrent UTIs in postmenopausal women
explanation.pearls: Recurrent UTIs in a postmenopausal woman are often a manifestation of GSM and respond to vaginal oestrogen better than to recurrent antibiotic courses.

sources.label: Jean Hailes: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.rationale: Low-dose vaginal oestrogen has minimal systemic absorption; recent observational data suggest no increased recurrence in non-AI users. Strict avoidance is correct only on aromatase inhibitor therapy or with patient/oncology preference (BMS; Jean Hailes).
source_refs: Jean Hailes: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.rationale: Systemic MHT is generally avoided in breast cancer survivors; local low-dose vaginal oestrogen is more appropriate and effective for GSM. Systemic MHT is correct only in selected refractory vasomotor symptoms with oncology consent (BMS; Jean Hailes).

Local vaginal oestrogen in a breast cancer survivor not on aromatase inhibitors is appropriate after shared decision-making with the oncology team; severe GSM significantly affects quality of life and the systemic absorption is minimal. Current evidence does not show increased recurrence risk for most survivors. She is on no current endocrine therapy (completed tamoxifen 12 months ago) (BMS 2024; Jean Hailes; NAMS 2020).
source_refs: Jean Hailes: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.rationale: Vaginal laser therapy lacks high-quality efficacy/safety evidence; TGA and international societies caution against use outside trials. Laser is correct only in clinical trial settings (TGA; NAMS).
source_refs: Jean Hailes: Genitourinary syndrome of menopause

options.rationale: Ospemifene is contraindicated in current/recent breast cancer due to oestrogen agonist effects on breast tissue. Ospemifene is correct in postmenopausal dyspareunia without breast cancer history (FDA labelling).

explanation.summary: Vulval lichen sclerosus is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis with a 4-5% lifetime risk of vulval squamous cell carcinoma (via differentiated VIN, typically HPV-negative). Management: potent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol 0.05% ointment) induction then maintenance, plus long-term clinician surveillance. Any persistent ulcer, hyperkeratotic plaque, induration or non-healing lesion warrants prompt biopsy. Self-management alone is inappropriate due to malignancy risk.
key_points: Clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment is the gold-standard topical therapy
Structured induction then maintenance (typically twice weekly long-term)
Lifetime vulval SCC risk ~4-5% via differentiated VIN (HPV-negative pathway)
Biopsy: persistent ulcer, hyperkeratotic plaque, induration, non-healing lesion
At least annual clinician review long-term, more frequent if uncontrolled or atypical features
Tacrolimus second-line; surgery reserved for adhesions/scarring or malignancy
explanation.pearls: Differentiated VIN looks innocuous and is easy to miss - any unhealed area in LS deserves a biopsy regardless of how unremarkable it appears.

sources.label: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

options.rationale: Unhealed, indurated, or hyperkeratotic lesion in longstanding lichen sclerosus must NOT be assumed steroid-responsive; biopsy required to exclude differentiated VIN/SCC. Steroid increase is correct only after biopsy excludes neoplasia (BSSVD).
source_refs: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

options.rationale: Topical tacrolimus is recognised second-line steroid-sparing agent, but priority here is biopsy of the suspicious lesion before changing therapy. Tacrolimus is correct after biopsy excludes neoplasia (BSSVD).

Lichen sclerosus carries 4-5% lifetime vulval SCC risk; long-term surveillance with prompt biopsy of suspicious lesions is recommended. Reassurance is essentially never correct in lichen sclerosus (BAD).
source_refs: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

options.rationale: Diagnostic biopsy precedes any wide excision; excisional treatment depends on histology. Wide excision is correct after histological confirmation of malignancy (BSSVD; RCOG).
source_refs: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

options.rationale: Persistent ulcer, hyperkeratotic plaque, induration, or non-healing lesion in established lichen sclerosus requires prompt biopsy to exclude differentiated VIN (the precursor most associated with LS-related vulval SCC, typically HPV-negative) and invasive SCC. Long-term annual surveillance is recommended due to ~4-5% lifetime risk of vulval SCC. Topical potent steroid (clobetasol) remains the cornerstone of medical management (BSSVD 2018; RCOG; Cancer Council).
source_refs: RCOG: The management of vulval skin disorders

explanation.summary: A FIGO pathological CTG without acute decompensation is managed with intrauterine resuscitation (stop oxytocin, left lateral, IV fluid, exclude hypotension, exclude tachysystole, consider tocolysis) and fetal scalp lactate sampling. Lactate >=4.8 mmol/L mandates delivery; 4.2-4.7 repeat in 30 minutes; <4.2 reassuring.
key_points: FIGO pathological = >=2 abnormal features OR sinusoidal OR prolonged bradycardia >5 min
Reduced variability + recurrent late decelerations = pathological
Intrauterine resuscitation mnemonic: SPOILT (Stop oxytocin, Position, Oxygen [no longer routinely recommended], IV fluid, Lower BP causes, Tocolysis)
Fetal scalp lactate cut-offs: <4.2 normal, 4.2-4.7 borderline, >=4.8 abnormal
Category 1 CS target decision-to-delivery 30 minutes
explanation.pearls: Reduced variability is the most predictive single feature of fetal acidosis. Recurrent late decelerations with a flat trace is the pattern that should provoke action even without bradycardia.

sources.label: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019
FIGO consensus guidelines on intrapartum fetal monitoring 2015

options.rationale: This CTG is FIGO pathological (recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability) but without a sustained bradycardia, so intrauterine resuscitation plus fetal scalp blood sampling for lactate is the appropriate next step before escalating to category 1 caesarean (RANZCOG IFSM 2019; FIGO 2015).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019
FIGO consensus guidelines on intrapartum fetal monitoring 2015

options.rationale: Recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability for 25 minutes is pathological; continuing oxytocin worsens fetal acidosis. Observation is correct only with normal/suspicious traces (RANZCOG IFSM 2019).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019

options.rationale: Category 1 CS is for acute decompensation (bradycardia, abruption, cord prolapse); pathological trace without acute decompensation warrants fetal scalp sampling first. Category 1 CS is correct with acute compromise (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019

options.rationale: Terbutaline tocolysis is indicated for tachysystole-related compromise; no tachysystole here. Terbutaline is correct in tachysystole-driven decelerations (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019

options.rationale: Membranes already ruptured and FSE without addressing the pathological pattern is insufficient. FSE alone is correct only with maternal-fetal CTG confusion needing direct trace (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Intrapartum Fetal Surveillance Clinical Guideline (IFSM) 2019

explanation.summary: Prolonged deceleration following an epidural top-up is most commonly due to maternal hypotension reducing uteroplacental perfusion. Manage with full left lateral position, IV crystalloid bolus 250-500 mL, and phenylephrine 50-100 microg IV bolus (first-line). If the deceleration does not resolve within 9 minutes, prepare for category 1 caesarean.
key_points: Phenylephrine first-line for neuraxial hypotension in obstetrics
Ephedrine causes more fetal acidaemia (crosses placenta, beta-agonist on fetal heart)
Metaraminol is an acceptable Australian alternative
Always exclude cord prolapse, abruption and uterine rupture as causes of prolonged deceleration
9-minute rule: prolonged deceleration not recovering requires immediate delivery decision
explanation.pearls: Treat the maternal BP first; the fetal heart rate almost always follows. If you are reaching for atropine for the baby, you have the wrong drug.

sources.label: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia
SOAP Consensus Statement on hypotension management 2018

options.rationale: Ephedrine is acceptable but contemporary obstetric anaesthesia favours phenylephrine because ephedrine crosses placenta and increases fetal acidaemia. Ephedrine is correct only when phenylephrine unavailable or maternal bradycardia (ANZCA).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia

options.rationale: Metaraminol is a reasonable alpha-agonist alternative commonly used in Australia, but phenylephrine has the strongest evidence base. Metaraminol is correct as second-line alpha-agonist (ANZCA).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia

options.rationale: Phenylephrine 50-100 microg IV bolus is the first-line vasopressor for neuraxial-induced maternal hypotension because it preserves uterine blood flow and reduces fetal acidaemia compared with ephedrine; combined with left uterine displacement and a fluid bolus this typically resolves the prolonged deceleration (ANZCA; SOAP consensus 2018).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia
SOAP Consensus Statement on hypotension management 2018

options.rationale: Adrenaline boluses are reserved for cardiac arrest or anaphylaxis; this is treatable neuraxial hypotension. Adrenaline is correct in cardiac arrest or anaphylaxis only (ANZCA).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia

options.rationale: Maternal HR is 102; atropine treats bradycardia not hypotension and would not correct uteroplacental hypoperfusion. Atropine is correct in bradycardia-driven hypotension only (ANZCA).
source_refs: ANZCA Professional Document PS - Obstetric Anaesthesia

explanation.summary: Primary dysfunctional labour in a nullipara at 6 cm with inadequate contractions and intact membranes is managed with oxytocin augmentation (after ARM if membranes intact). Start at 1-2 mU/min and double every 30 minutes to a usual maximum of 32 mU/min, titrated to 4-5 contractions per 10 minutes. Diagnose labour dystocia only after at least 4 hours of adequate contractions with no progress, then proceed to CS.
key_points: Active phase: >=6 cm with regular contractions (Zhang/ACOG)
Adequate progress nullipara: ~0.5-1 cm/h after 6 cm
Oxytocin start 1-2 mU/min, double every 30 min, max ~32 mU/min
Target: 4-5 contractions per 10 min, 45-60 s, moderate-strong
Diagnose dystocia after >=4 h adequate contractions without progress
explanation.pearls: Direct OP at 6 cm is a common cause of slow progress; many will rotate spontaneously with adequate contractions plus mobility/epidural.

sources.label: KEMH Clinical Guideline: Augmentation of labour
Royal Women's Hospital - Oxytocin in labour

options.rationale: Membranes are already ruptured and there is inadequate contraction frequency/strength causing slow progress in the active first stage. Oxytocin augmentation at 1-2 mU/min titrated every 30 minutes is the correct Australian protocol; faster titration risks hyperstimulation (RANZCOG; eTG).
Membranes already spontaneously ruptured; ARM not applicable. ARM is correct in intact membranes with poor progress (RANZCOG).

Failure to progress requires demonstration after adequate uterine activity (after oxytocin); proceeding to caesarean before oxytocin is premature. Cat 2 CS is correct after oxytocin trial fails (RANZCOG).

Starting at 6 mU/min risks hyperstimulation and fetal compromise; standard starts at 1-2 mU/min titrated every 30 minutes. High-dose start is correct only with maximum-dose review and continuous fetal monitoring in selected protocols (RANZCOG).

Pain relief is reasonable but does not address slow progress with inadequate contractions; delay risks fetal compromise. Epidural without augmentation is correct when contractions are adequate (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Cord prolapse with a non-imminent vaginal delivery requires manual elevation of the presenting part (or bladder filling with 500-700 mL warmed saline for transfer delay), knee-chest or exaggerated Sims position, stop oxytocin, consider tocolysis if hyperstimulation, and category 1 caesarean section with a 30-minute decision-to-delivery interval.
key_points: Diagnosis: pulsating cord palpated below the presenting part
Manual elevation preferred over cord replacement
Bladder filling 500-700 mL saline if transfer delay
Stop oxytocin; consider terbutaline 250 microg SC if hyperstimulation
Category 1 CS, decision-to-delivery target 30 min (RANZCOG/NICE)
Instrumental vaginal birth only if fully dilated AND station >=+2 AND operator confident
explanation.pearls: Keep the examiner's hand in the vagina elevating the presenting part during transfer; do not handle the cord more than necessary because handling causes vasospasm.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 50: Umbilical cord prolapse

options.rationale: Cord replacement is no longer recommended due to cord trauma and vasospasm; manual elevation of presenting part is preferred. Cord replacement is essentially obsolete (RANZCOG; RCOG Green-top).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top Guideline 50: Umbilical cord prolapse

options.rationale: Oxytocin must be STOPPED immediately to reduce contractions compressing cord; 5-minute observation is unsafe with prolonged deceleration. Continued oxytocin is essentially never correct in cord prolapse (RANZCOG).

Tocolysis with terbutaline may be considered for hyperstimulation or transfer delay, but ventouse at -2 station is contraindicated (station must be >=+2). Tocolysis + ventouse combination is never correct (RANZCOG).

At -2 station vaginal delivery is not imminent. Manual elevation of the presenting part off the cord (or bladder filling with 500-700 mL warmed saline if transfer delay) plus knee-chest/Sims position plus category 1 CS within 30 minutes is the standard pathway (RANZCOG; RCOG Green-top 50).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top Guideline 50: Umbilical cord prolapse

options.rationale: Fundal pressure contraindicated; head is at -2 station with vaginal delivery not feasible. Category 1 CS required. Pushing-fundal pressure is essentially never correct in cord prolapse (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: For mid-cavity or low-cavity OA position with maternal exhaustion and a suspicious (not pathological) CTG, non-rotational forceps have a higher success rate than ventouse and a lower neonatal cephalohaematoma rate, but a higher rate of maternal perineal trauma. Sequential instrument use is associated with higher neonatal morbidity and should be avoided. Document fetal station, position, caput/moulding, bladder, epidural, and consent prior to commencing.
key_points: Pre-instrumental checklist: full dilatation, ruptured membranes, head <=1/5 palpable abdominally, defined station, defined position, adequate analgesia, empty bladder, consent
Forceps: higher success rate, more maternal trauma
Ventouse: higher failure rate, more cephalohaematoma/subgaleal haemorrhage
Sequential use significantly increases neonatal morbidity
Failed instrumental: stop after 3 contractions with no descent or after 20 minutes total
explanation.pearls: Choose the instrument most likely to succeed first. If you would normally choose ventouse but conditions are marginal (exhaustion, suspicious CTG, OP), forceps usually has the better outcome.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top Guideline 26: Assisted Vaginal Birth

options.rationale: Position is direct OA, not transverse arrest; Kielland's restricted to experienced operators for rotational deliveries. Kielland's is correct in deep transverse arrest by experienced operators (RANZCOG; RCOG GTG).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top Guideline 26: Assisted Vaginal Birth

options.rationale: Direct OA at +1 station with maternal exhaustion and adequate epidural is suitable for low-cavity non-rotational forceps. Forceps have a lower failure rate than ventouse in maternal exhaustion and a suspicious (but not pathological) CTG (RANZCOG; RCOG GTG 26).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top Guideline 26: Assisted Vaginal Birth

options.rationale: Sequential instrument use significantly increases neonatal morbidity (ICH, subgaleal); generally avoided. Sequential is correct only when head on perineum and primary instrument fails (RCOG).

Ventouse has higher failure rate than forceps in maternal exhaustion and suspicious CTG, plus higher cephalohaematoma/subgaleal rates. Ventouse is correct in early descent and adequate maternal effort (RANZCOG).

At +1 station with 0/5 palpable abdominally and direct OA, trial of instrumental is appropriate. Category 2 CS is correct after failed instrumental or with malposition not amenable to instruments (RANZCOG; NICE).

explanation.summary: Categorisation of urgency for caesarean section (RANZCOG/NICE): Cat 1 - immediate threat (target 30 min decision-to-delivery); Cat 2 - maternal or fetal compromise, not immediately life-threatening (target 60-75 min); Cat 3 - early delivery needed but no compromise; Cat 4 - delivery timed to suit woman or staff.
key_points: Cat 1: 30 minutes (audit standard)
Cat 2: 60-75 minutes (audit standard)
30 minutes is an audit standard, not a strict outcome threshold
Common Cat 1 indications: cord prolapse, abruption, uterine rupture, scalp pH <7.20, prolonged bradycardia
explanation.pearls: Document time of decision, time of arrival in theatre, time of knife-to-skin, and time of delivery for every Cat 1 CS for departmental audit.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Categorisation of urgency for caesarean section

options.rationale: The Australian/NICE standard for category 1 caesarean is delivery as soon as possible, with a 30-minute auditable threshold; bypassing further bedside investigation is appropriate when uterine rupture is suspected, and parallel resuscitation and MTP activation are essential (RANZCOG; RCOG).

15 minutes is idealised target rarely achieved; audited standard is 30 minutes. MTP should be activated proactively given suspected rupture. 15-minute target is correct only in immediate intra-theatre rupture (RANZCOG).
60 minutes is threshold for category 2 CS; rupture is category 1 emergency. 60 minutes is correct for category 2 (RANZCOG).
Epidural availability does not change category-1 timing; target is 30 minutes. 75 minutes is essentially never appropriate in suspected rupture (RANZCOG).
TOLAC is abandoned the moment rupture is suspected, not after delivery; target is 30 minutes. 45 minutes is appropriate only in category 2 status (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with persistent neurological symptoms despite magnesium load requires (1) acute BP control to <160/110 with IV labetalol or oral nifedipine IR (first-line per SOMANZ), with hydralazine second-line, and (2) delivery after stabilisation (antenatal steroids if not given and time permits, but delivery should not be unduly delayed). Magnesium is for seizure prophylaxis, not BP control.
key_points: Severe HTN target: <160/110 within 30-60 minutes
SOMANZ first-line acute severe HTN: IV labetalol OR oral nifedipine IR
Hydralazine: second/third-line, more maternal hypotension
Magnesium: seizure prophylaxis only (4 g IV load, 1 g/h maintenance)
Persistent neurological symptoms despite magnesium = imminent eclampsia = deliver
Antenatal steroids 11.4 mg betamethasone IM x 2 doses 24 h apart if <34+6 weeks
explanation.pearls: Stabilise mother, then deliver. The cure for pre-eclampsia is delivery, and persistent neurological symptoms after a magnesium load are an indication that delivery cannot wait for the full steroid course.

options.rationale: Hydralazine is acceptable second- or third-line in Australian guidance, associated with more maternal hypotension and fetal distress than labetalol/nifedipine. Hydralazine is correct when labetalol/nifedipine fail or contraindicated (SOMANZ 2023).

Labetalol IV is first-line for acute severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia per SOMANZ 2023 (Australian guidance), with nifedipine immediate-release as an alternative first-line. Magnesium is for seizure prophylaxis and does not lower BP. Delivery is indicated after stabilisation given persistent neurological symptoms despite magnesium (SOMANZ).
Oral immediate-release nifedipine is acceptable first-line alternative to IV labetalol per SOMANZ, but carries overshoot hypotension risk. PO nifedipine is correct when IV access difficult (SOMANZ).
Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in pregnancy due to unpredictable absorption and severe overshoot hypotension. SL nifedipine is essentially never correct in pregnancy (SOMANZ).
Magnesium is for seizure prophylaxis only and does not lower BP. Increased Mg risks toxicity. Mg dose change is correct for breakthrough seizure or sub-therapeutic levels (SOMANZ).

explanation.summary: For a non-cephalic second twin after delivery of Twin 1, internal podalic version with breech extraction is the preferred approach by a skilled operator with a working epidural and a relaxed uterus. ECV is an alternative but has higher failure rates. Caesarean for the second twin is reserved for cord prolapse, fetal compromise unresponsive to manoeuvres, or operator inexperience.
key_points: Twin Birth Study (NEJM 2013): planned vaginal birth non-inferior to planned CS at >=32 weeks if Twin 1 cephalic
IPV preferred with intact membranes, relaxed uterus, working epidural
ECV alternative; higher failure rate
Always have theatre ready and the consultant available
Deliver Twin 2 within 30 minutes of Twin 1 to reduce abruption and cord prolapse risk
explanation.pearls: Do not break the membranes of Twin 2 until you have a cephalic or breech longitudinal lie. ROM with a transverse lie is a category 1 emergency.

sources.label: Twin Birth Study (Barrett et al. NEJM 2013)

options.rationale: ECV for second twin has lower success and higher failure than internal podalic version with breech extraction; with back inferior and relaxed uterus, internal podalic version is preferred. ECV is correct with back-up presentation and superior position (RANZCOG).
ARM with transverse lie is CONTRAINDICATED due to high cord prolapse risk; version must occur first. ARM-first in transverse lie is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).

Caesarean for second twin after vaginal birth of first is associated with higher maternal morbidity than internal podalic version with breech extraction in experienced hands. CS for twin 2 is correct only after failed manoeuvres (RANZCOG).

Delay risks cord prolapse on subsequent ROM, abruption from uterine retraction, and closing cervix; prompt management within 30 minutes is recommended. Waiting 60 minutes is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).

Transverse lie of the second twin with intact membranes, a relaxed uterus and a working epidural is the classic indication for internal podalic version with breech extraction by a skilled operator. This avoids caesarean for the second twin and outcomes are equivalent or better when performed by experienced operators (RANZCOG; ACOG).
source_refs: Twin Birth Study (Barrett et al. NEJM 2013)

explanation.summary: Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE) is a rare (~2-8 per 100,000 births) but devastating cause of maternal collapse. Mechanism: fetal amniotic constituents (squames, lanugo, vernix, trophoblast-derived tissue factor) breach the maternal venous compartment, triggering a biphasic insult - acute pulmonary vasoconstriction with right-heart failure producing hypoxia and hypotension, followed by a profound consumptive coagulopathy from tissue-factor-driven DIC and hyperfibrinolysis. The cluster of peripartum hypoxia, hypotension and DIC is therefore not coincidence; each element is a direct consequence of the same triggering embolic-immunological event. Diagnosis is clinical (Clark criteria); management is high-quality CPR with manual left uterine displacement (LUD), A-OK (atropine 1 mg, ondansetron 8 mg, ketorolac 30 mg IV per the AFE Foundation protocol), early massive transfusion protocol (1:1:1 RBC:FFP:platelets), and perimortem caesarean by 4 minutes if no ROSC.
key_points: Clark criteria (4 required): cardiovascular collapse OR hypotension+respiratory compromise, DIC, intrapartum or within 30 min of placental delivery, no fever
Manual left uterine displacement throughout CPR (not tilt)
Perimortem CS by 4 minutes (4-minute rule) if no ROSC and >=20 weeks
Massive transfusion protocol; expect early cryoprecipitate for low fibrinogen
Differential of obstetric collapse: AFE, PE, eclampsia, MI, anaphylaxis, LAST, intracranial bleed, hypovolaemia
explanation.pearls: If the mother collapses with the placenta still in the room and starts oozing from her IV site, do not wait for confirmation - call MET and run the AFE algorithm now.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy and the puerperium
Clark SL et al. Proposed diagnostic criteria for AFE 2016

options.rationale: Sudden peripartum collapse with hypoxia, hypotension and coagulopathy (PPH plus bleeding from puncture sites) is the classic Clark triad of AFE. PEA arrest within minutes of placental delivery in a multipara fits the AFE phenotype; management is high-quality CPR with left uterine displacement, A-OK protocol (atropine, ondansetron, ketorolac), early massive transfusion and cardiac arrest team activation (RANZCOG; AFE Foundation; Clark 2016).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy and the puerperium
Clark SL et al. Proposed diagnostic criteria for AFE 2016

options.rationale: Only 5 mL of 1% lidocaine (50 mg) was used, far below toxic threshold (3 mg/kg without adrenaline); LAST presents with seizures and arrhythmia. LAST is correct with confirmed high-dose LA exposure (ANZCA).

No history of hypertension, proteinuria, or seizures preceding collapse; presentation is hypoxic collapse with coagulopathy not seizure. Eclamptic seizure is correct with PE history and seizure activity (SOMANZ).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: PE is differential but does not classically cause early DIC and oozing from IV sites; AFE more consistent with full picture. PE is correct in unilateral chest pain or DVT history (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: ACS is possible but rare in a 36-year-old without risk factors and does not explain coagulopathy or temporal relationship with placental delivery. ACS is correct in older women with cardiac risk factors (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal collapse in pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: When the cervix remains unfavourable (Bishop <=6) after the maximum dose of prostaglandins, the next step is mechanical cervical ripening with a transcervical Foley catheter (or double balloon Cook catheter). This is comparable in efficacy to repeat prostaglandins with less tachysystole and is preferred for women with a previous CS. Caesarean for failed induction is reserved for women who fail mechanical ripening or who are not in active labour after ARM and oxytocin.
key_points: Bishop score: dilatation, length/effacement, station, position, consistency (max 13)
Bishop <=6 = unfavourable cervix; mechanical or pharmacological ripening required
Dinoprostone max 2 doses (Australian protocols)
Foley catheter 16 Fr with 30-60 mL balloon, leave 12-24 h or until expelled
Failed induction diagnosed only after ARM + adequate oxytocin trial without progress
explanation.pearls: Mechanical methods are particularly useful for women with a previous CS because they avoid the increased rupture risk of prostaglandins.

sources.label: KEMH Clinical Guideline: Induction of labour
Cochrane review: Mechanical methods for induction 2012

options.rationale: After failure of prostaglandins at maximum local dose with an unfavourable cervix, mechanical methods (Foley catheter or balloon) are the recommended next step. They are safe, effective and avoid hyperstimulation; ARM with oxytocin is inappropriate at Bishop 3 (RANZCOG IOL; NICE).
Local protocol permits maximum 2 doses dinoprostone in 24 hours; exceeding risks hyperstimulation. Third dose is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).
ARM at Bishop 3 with high station is technically difficult and carries cord prolapse risk; cervix must first be ripened. ARM is correct when Bishop favourable (RANZCOG).
Membrane sweep is for low-Bishop cervices >=1 cm dilated, but insufficient as single intervention after failed prostaglandins. Sweep is correct in latent labour with favourable cervix (RANZCOG).
Caesarean is for genuine failed induction after both pharmacological and mechanical methods; she has not failed mechanical. CS is correct after both methods exhausted (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Surgical escalation for intractable atonic PPH after failed medical and balloon therapy: (1) compression suture such as B-Lynch, (2) stepwise uterine devascularisation (uterine artery ligation, then ovarian artery ligation), (3) internal iliac artery ligation or interventional radiology embolisation, (4) peripartum hysterectomy as last resort. Hysterectomy is performed earlier if the patient is unstable, the uterus is severely damaged, or in placenta accreta spectrum.
key_points: Uterine-sparing options first unless contraindication
B-Lynch suture: vertical compression, leaves uterine cavity accessible
Stepwise uterine devascularisation: uterine arteries then ovarian arteries
Internal iliac (hypogastric) artery ligation: technically demanding
Peripartum hysterectomy: last resort, but do not delay if unstable
Always involve a senior obstetrician early; consider IR if available and patient stable enough
explanation.pearls: The clock matters: do not let pride in uterine-sparing surgery delay hysterectomy in an exsanguinating patient. The right operation is the one that stops the bleeding before the patient dies.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Postpartum haemorrhage clinical guideline

options.rationale: RANZCOG PPH algorithm: after failure of medical therapy and balloon tamponade, the recommended surgical sequence is conservative interventions (B-Lynch compression, uterine artery ligation) before hysterectomy. She has completed her family so hysterectomy is acceptable if conservative steps fail, but should not be the first surgical step (RANZCOG PPH).

Hysterectomy is last resort even with completed family; conservative surgical measures recommended first if stabilisable. Direct hysterectomy is correct in life-threatening haemorrhage when uterine-sparing measures cannot be performed safely (RANZCOG).
Haemodynamically unstable; transfer to IR outside theatre is unsafe. IR is correct in stable patients (RANZCOG).
Bakri has maximum fill ~500 mL; overinflation does not increase efficacy. Observation in shock is unsafe. Re-inflation is essentially never correct in failed Bakri (RANZCOG).

Internal iliac artery ligation is technically demanding, takes time, and reserved for after uterine artery ligation or by IR/vascular if available. Internal iliac is correct after B-Lynch and uterine artery ligation fail (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Active second stage delay thresholds: nullipara without epidural 2 h, with epidural 3 h; multipara without epidural 1 h, with epidural 2 h. The passive second stage (from full dilatation to active pushing) is allowed up to 2 h in nullipara, 1 h in multipara to allow descent.
key_points: Stage 1: latent (<4 cm) and active (4-10 cm); active progress benchmark ~0.5-1 cm/h in nullipara
Stage 2: passive (full dilatation to active pushing) + active (pushing)
Stage 3: delivery of baby to delivery of placenta; active management <=30 min
Epidural extends acceptable second stage duration by 1 h
Multiparas progress faster in all stages
explanation.pearls: If you cannot remember the four numbers, anchor on nullipara-no-epidural = 2 h and add 1 h for epidural, subtract 1 h for multipara.

sources.label: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017
KEMH Clinical Guidelines - Labour and Birth

options.rationale: Although 3 hours is the threshold, descent has stalled at 0 station with malposition, caput, and moulding; continued pushing risks fetal compromise. Continued pushing is correct only with ongoing descent (RANZCOG OVB).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: After 90 minutes of pushing with no descent below 0 station, malposition (OT), caput, moulding and inadequate contractions, an experienced obstetrician must assess for instrumental delivery (rotational) versus second-stage caesarean rather than continuing routine pushing (RANZCOG; NICE intrapartum).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: Rotational instrumental delivery requires experienced operator, often in theatre with trial-of-instrumental protocols; bypassing senior review is unsafe. Kielland's without senior review is essentially never correct (RANZCOG OVB).

Augmentation may be considered with descent and inadequate contractions, but with malposition at 0 station, caput, and moulding, oxytocin without resolution risks rupture. Augmentation is correct when descent + inadequate contractions (RANZCOG OVB).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: Passive observation is reasonable BEFORE active pushing begins but not after 90 minutes with stalled descent. Passive observation is correct only at 10 cm dilatation before pushing begins (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

explanation.summary: Bishop score guides IOL method: <=6 = unfavourable, ripening needed (Foley balloon or PGE2); >=7 = favourable, proceed to ARM and oxytocin. Mechanical Foley and prostaglandins are equivalent for vaginal delivery rates with less hyperstimulation with Foley.
key_points: Bishop components: Dilatation, Effacement (length), Consistency, Position, Station
Foley balloon: 30-60 mL, left in situ up to 24 h, no fetal monitoring needed during ripening (outpatient option in many AU units)
PGE2 gel/pessary (Cervidil/Prostin): inpatient with CTG, risk of hyperstimulation
Misoprostol 25-50 microg orally or vaginally for IOL
Previous CS: Foley preferred; PGE2 and misoprostol contraindicated (rupture risk)
explanation.pearls: If the cervix is closed and posterior, you cannot ARM. Ripen first. Bishop <=6 means ripen, >=7 means ARM/oxytocin.

options.rationale: ARM is not feasible with closed cervix at -3 station and unfavourable Bishop 3; ripening required first. ARM is correct with favourable Bishop and accessible cervix (RANZCOG IOL 2021).

A Bishop score of 3 indicates an unfavourable cervix and a mechanical Foley balloon is an appropriate first-line ripening agent, with comparable efficacy to prostaglandins but lower rates of hyperstimulation and CTG abnormalities. PGE2 is also acceptable; in this multipara with intact membranes Foley is widely preferred in Australian units to reduce hyperstimulation risk and allow outpatient ripening when local protocols permit (RANZCOG Induction of Labour 2021; Cochrane mechanical methods for IOL 2019; KEMH IOL guideline).
Oxytocin alone with unripe closed cervix is ineffective and associated with prolonged induction, exhaustion, and increased CS. Oxytocin is correct after ripening (RANZCOG IOL 2021).
Oral misoprostol IOL dosing is 25-50 microg every 2-4h; 200 microg is for PPH or TOP. 200 microg miso for IOL is essentially never correct (RANZCOG IOL).
Sweep alone unlikely to initiate labour with Bishop 3 at 41+2; post-dates beyond 41+0 warrants formal induction. Sweep is correct in earlier post-dates with favourable cervix (RANZCOG IOL).

explanation.summary: Australian practice offers IOL between 41+0 and 42+0 for low-risk women to reduce stillbirth and perinatal mortality. Other common indications: term PROM (after 18-24 h), GDM at 38-40 weeks depending on control, pre-eclampsia >=37 weeks, FGR with adverse surveillance, maternal request after 39+0.
key_points: Stillbirth risk: ~0.5/1000 at 40 weeks, ~1/1000 at 41 weeks, ~3/1000 at 42 weeks
SWEPIS 2019 stopped early for perinatal mortality benefit of IOL at 41+0
GDM diet-controlled: deliver by 40+6; on metformin/insulin: 38+0 to 39+6
PE >=37+0: deliver
PROM at term: IOL within 24 h reduces chorioamnionitis (Hannah TermPROM)
explanation.pearls: The reason 41+0 IOL exists is stillbirth, not convenience and not CS rates.

sources.label: Cochrane Induction of labour at or beyond 37 weeks 2020

options.rationale: Maternal age >=39-40 with multiple risk factors is used, but age alone is not strong stand-alone trigger at 39+0. Age alone is correct only with advanced age + other factors (RANZCOG; NICE).

Australian/RANZCOG guidance supports IOL between 39 and 40+6 weeks for diet-controlled GDM to reduce stillbirth and shoulder dystocia, particularly with BMI elevation and age. This is the strongest evidence-based reason at this gestation (RANZCOG; ADIPS).

Class I obesity without other risk factors does not by itself mandate induction before 39 weeks; supportive but not stand-alone. BMI 34 alone is correct only in research-grade evidence base (RANZCOG).
Unfavourable cervix does not preclude IOL; ripening precedes oxytocin. Bishop >=8 requirement is essentially never correct (RANZCOG IOL).
ARRIVE suggested small CS reduction in low-risk nulliparas, but not primary evidence base in this high-risk multipara. ARRIVE evidence is correct in low-risk nulliparas (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Late decelerations reflect uteroplacental insufficiency. Management: stop oxytocin, left lateral position, IV crystalloid bolus, correct maternal hypotension, exclude tachysystole (consider terbutaline if present), and perform fetal scalp blood sampling for lactate if the pattern persists.
key_points: Intrauterine resuscitation mnemonic: SPOILT (Stop oxytocin, Position, Oxygen no longer routinely recommended, IV fluid, Lower BP correct, Tocolysis if tachysystole)
Fetal scalp lactate: <4.2 normal, 4.2-4.7 borderline (repeat in 30 min), >=4.8 abnormal (deliver)
Reduced variability is the most predictive single feature of acidaemia
Tachysystole = >5 contractions in 10 minutes averaged over 30 min
Category 1 CS target decision-to-delivery 30 minutes
explanation.pearls: Late + flat = act. But act in the right order: resuscitate first, then sample, then deliver if not corrected.

sources.label: NSW Health Maternity - Fetal heart rate monitoring

options.rationale: Recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability are pathological; continuing oxytocin worsens acidaemia. Continued oxytocin is essentially never correct in pathological trace (RANZCOG IFSM 2019).

Category 1 CS is for acute decompensation (prolonged bradycardia, abruption, cord prolapse); pathological without acute decompensation warrants intrauterine resuscitation + scalp lactate first. Cat 1 is correct in acute compromise (RANZCOG IFSM 2019).
Increasing oxytocin in pathological trace is contraindicated and worsens uteroplacental hypoperfusion. Oxytocin increase is essentially never correct in pathological trace (RANZCOG IFSM 2019).

Recurrent late decelerations with reduced variability indicate uteroplacental insufficiency and warrant intrauterine resuscitation (stop oxytocin, left lateral position, IV fluid bolus, exclude hypotension and tachysystole) followed by fetal scalp blood sampling for lactate to guide ongoing management (RANZCOG IFSM 2019; FIGO Intrapartum Fetal Monitoring 2015; NSW Health Maternity).
source_refs: NSW Health Maternity - Fetal heart rate monitoring

options.rationale: Acute tocolysis is for tachysystole-related compromise; contractions are 5 in 10 (not tachysystolic >5/10/30min). Tocolysis is correct in tachysystolic patterns (RANZCOG IFSM 2019).

explanation.summary: Nuchal cord occurs in ~25% of deliveries. If loose: slip over head. If tight and cannot be slipped: somersault manoeuvre (flex head to maternal thigh, deliver body in forward roll, then unwind). Avoid routine clamp-and-cut before shoulder delivery.
key_points: Loose nuchal cord: slip over head, deliver normally
Tight nuchal cord: somersault manoeuvre preserves cord integrity
Clamp-and-cut before shoulder delivery is no longer recommended
If shoulder dystocia complicates and the cord has been cut, fetal hypovolaemia and HIE risk rise sharply
Nuchal cord is rarely the cause of poor neonatal outcome on its own
explanation.pearls: Somersault first, snip last. If you cut the cord and then meet a shoulder dystocia, the baby is on a clock without circulation.

sources.label: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017
KEMH Clinical Guidelines - Labour and Birth
Schorn MN, Blanco JD 2014 Somersault manoeuvre

options.rationale: Routine clamp-and-cut of tight nuchal cord before shoulder delivery is no longer recommended; converts contained circulation into acutely interrupted one if shoulder dystocia occurs. Clamp-and-cut is correct only as last resort with prolonged failure (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: Forceful traction risks brachial plexus injury and does not address the cord; controlled somersault is correct. Firm traction is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: Head is delivered; CS not feasible or indicated. Remaining task is to deliver body safely. Stop-pushing + CS is essentially never correct after head delivery (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: Cutting cord during shoulder dystocia is hazardous - removes fetoplacental reservoir while fetus wedged. Cord cutting during dystocia is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: When a nuchal cord is too tight to slip over the head, the somersault manoeuvre (flexing the fetal head towards the maternal thigh while the body delivers in a forward roll) keeps the cord intact and the fetoplacental circulation preserved, then the loop is unwound after delivery. This is preferred over clamp-and-cut, which risks fetal hypovolaemia and HIE if shoulder dystocia complicates delivery (RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017; Schorn and Blanco 2014).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017
Schorn MN, Blanco JD 2014 Somersault manoeuvre

explanation.summary: Episiotomy: not routine in spontaneous vaginal birth but indicated for operative vaginal delivery (particularly forceps), suspected imminent OASI, and some cases of shoulder dystocia. Mediolateral technique at 60 degrees from midline, cut at crowning, originating at the fourchette.
key_points: Mediolateral 60 degrees preferred over midline in Australia/UK
Midline episiotomy is standard in North America but has higher OASI rates
Cut at crowning, not before
Right-handed operators cut to the right; aim away from the anus
Episiotomy reduces OASI in forceps deliveries (NNT ~12 in nulliparas)
explanation.pearls: Sixty degrees to the side, at the fourchette, at crowning. Routine for forceps, considered for ventouse, never routine for spontaneous birth.

options.rationale: Mediolateral episiotomy at approximately 60 degrees from the midline at crowning is recommended for operative vaginal birth in Australia/UK practice to reduce obstetric anal sphincter injury (OASIS). Midline episiotomy is associated with markedly higher OASIS risk and should not be used (RANZCOG OVB; RCOG).

Midline episiotomy increases risk of third- and fourth-degree perineal tears, especially with forceps; mediolateral episiotomy is the Australian standard. Midline remains used in some US practices but is not Australian standard (RANZCOG OVB).
Recommended angle is 60 degrees from midline AT crowning; 30 degrees and pre-crowning is incorrect. 30 degrees pre-crowning is essentially never correct (RANZCOG OVB).

Routine episiotomy is not recommended for spontaneous birth, but selective mediolateral is recommended for forceps to reduce OASIS. Avoiding episiotomy in forceps is correct only in selected low-risk cases (RANZCOG OVB).
J-shaped episiotomy is not standard practice and risks OASIS extension before the curve. J-shape is essentially never correct (RANZCOG OVB).

explanation.summary: Sultan classification of perineal trauma: 1st - skin only; 2nd - perineal muscle; 3rd - anal sphincter (3a <50% EAS, 3b >50% EAS, 3c EAS+IAS); 4th - rectal mucosa. OASI repair: theatre, regional anaesthesia, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, end-to-end or overlap EAS repair (equivalent outcomes), separate IAS repair if torn, mucosal repair for 4th degree, laxatives 10-14 days, physiotherapy, follow-up 6-12 weeks.
key_points: 3a <50% EAS, 3b >50% EAS, 3c EAS + IAS torn, 4th involves rectal mucosa
Repair in theatre with good lighting and assistance
PR examination is mandatory after every vaginal delivery to exclude buttonhole tear
Single-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics at repair, then oral 5-7 days
Lactulose (not stool softener) to reduce wound dehiscence
Future deliveries: vaginal birth acceptable if asymptomatic; counsel about 5-7% recurrence
explanation.pearls: PR every birth. If you do not feel the sphincter, you cannot exclude OASI. The 50% rule separates 3a from 3b.

sources.label: RCOG Green-top 29 The Management of Third- and Fourth-degree Perineal Tears

options.rationale: Second-degree tears involve perineal muscle but NOT anal sphincter; EAS involvement makes this third-degree (OASI). 2nd-degree is correct without sphincter involvement (RANZCOG OASI 2020).
3a is <50% EAS thickness; this tear involves ~60% making it 3b. 3a is correct with <50% EAS (RANZCOG OASI 2020).
3c requires IAS involvement; IAS intact here. 3c is correct with EAS + IAS torn (RANZCOG OASI 2020).

Sultan classification: 3a <50% EAS thickness, 3b >50% EAS thickness, 3c EAS and internal anal sphincter torn, 4 includes rectal mucosa. With ~60% EAS thickness and intact IAS and mucosa, this is a 3b. Repair in theatre under regional or general anaesthesia with end-to-end or overlap technique for the EAS (equivalent outcomes), single-dose IV antibiotics, oral laxatives (lactulose for 10-14 days), pelvic floor physiotherapy, and 6-12 week follow-up (RANZCOG OASI 2020; RCOG Green-top 29 The Management of Third- and Fourth-degree Perineal Tears).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top 29 The Management of Third- and Fourth-degree Perineal Tears

options.rationale: 4th-degree extends through rectal mucosa; mucosa intact here. 4th-degree is correct with mucosa involvement (RANZCOG OASI 2020).

explanation.summary: Active management of third stage: 1) oxytocin 10 IU IM with anterior shoulder (or after birth); 2) controlled cord traction (Brandt-Andrews) with suprapubic counter-pressure; 3) uterine massage after placental delivery. Reduces PPH ~60%. Delayed cord clamping (1-3 min) is now incorporated.
key_points: Oxytocin 10 IU IM is first-line; carbetocin 100 microg IM/IV alternative
Ergometrine 500 microg IM avoided in hypertension/PE
Syntometrine (oxytocin 5 IU + ergometrine 500 microg) increases nausea/hypertension and is second-line
Delayed cord clamping 1-3 min unless asphyxia or maternal indication
Active management reduces PPH from ~13% to ~5% (Begley Cochrane 2019)
explanation.pearls: Three components: drug, traction, massage. Memorise the order; it is exam-favoured.

sources.label: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: Oxytocin 10 IU IM is the first-line uterotonic for active management of the third stage in Australian practice and is safe in hypertensive women. Ergometrine and Syntometrine are contraindicated in hypertension (RANZCOG; WHO).
Syntometrine contains ergometrine, CONTRAINDICATED in hypertension due to severe vasoconstriction and stroke risk. Syntometrine is correct in normotensive women (RANZCOG; eTG).
Ergometrine alone is contraindicated in hypertension. Ergometrine is correct in normotensive women (RANZCOG; eTG).
Misoprostol is second-line where oxytocin unavailable (home birth, resource-limited); oxytocin remains first-line in Australian hospitals. Misoprostol is correct as backup (RANZCOG; WHO).
Carbetocin is used selectively for elective CS in Australia, not routine vaginal birth. Carbetocin is correct in elective CS (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Retained placenta: >=30 min with active management or >=60 min with physiological management. Move to theatre for manual removal under regional or general anaesthesia. IV access, group and hold/crossmatch, IV antibiotics, oxytocin infusion. Suspect placenta accreta if removal is difficult or in women with previous CS, uterine surgery, or instrumentation. PPH and infection are the main complications.
key_points: Active management threshold: 30 min
Physiological management threshold: 60 min
Theatre, regional anaesthesia preferred, single-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotics
Oxytocin infusion during and after manual removal
Accreta risk: previous CS, D&C, myomectomy, placenta praevia - have escalation pathway ready
explanation.pearls: 30 minutes with active management means theatre, not another bedside pull. Always check for accreta clues in the history.

sources.label: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017
Royal Women's Hospital Retained Placenta guideline
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotics for obstetric procedures

options.rationale: Retained placenta at 30 minutes with active management is the trigger for definitive intervention. Continued expectant is correct only with physiological management and no bleeding (RANZCOG; NICE).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: Umbilical vein oxytocin has been studied but Cochrane and RANZCOG do not recommend as standard. UV oxytocin is correct only when manual removal cannot be arranged (Cochrane 2011; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: Ergometrine causes tetanic uterine contraction trapping rather than expelling placenta - contraindicated for retained placenta. Ergometrine is correct in atonic PPH, not retained placenta (RANZCOG; AMH).
Even with epidural, manual removal should occur in theatre due to haemorrhage, inversion, and accreta risks. Bedside manual is correct only in extreme emergency without theatre access (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017

options.rationale: Retained placenta with active management at >=30 minutes requires manual removal in theatre under regional (or general if regional not feasible) anaesthesia. Manage with IV access (two large-bore cannulae, FBC and crossmatch), single-dose IV broad-spectrum antibiotic prophylaxis (e.g. cefazolin and metronidazole or amoxicillin with clavulanic acid), oxytocin infusion during and after removal, and assessment for placenta accreta spectrum particularly with a history of uterine instrumentation (RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017; NICE NG235; Royal Women's Hospital Retained Placenta guideline).
source_refs: RANZCOG Provision of routine intrapartum care 2017
Royal Women's Hospital Retained Placenta guideline

explanation.summary: Pre-eclampsia at >=37+0 weeks: deliver. Route depends on Bishop and other obstetric factors. Antihypertensive target <140/90 (oral labetalol, nifedipine, methyldopa; IV hydralazine or labetalol for severe). MgSO4 for severe PE (4 g IV loading, 1 g/h infusion) for seizure prophylaxis. Continue antihypertensives postpartum and review at 6 weeks.
key_points: PE definition: new HTN >=20 wks plus one of proteinuria, AKI, hepatic, neurological, haematological, uteroplacental dysfunction
Severe features: BP >=160/110, platelets <100, creatinine >90, ALT >2x ULN, headache/visual/clonus, pulmonary oedema, FGR
Delivery: >=37+0 PE deliver; 34-37 expectant in selected cases with severe features under tertiary care; <34 expectant unless severe and uncontrolled
MgSO4: 4 g IV over 20 min then 1 g/h for 24 h post-birth or post-last seizure
Postpartum BP typically peaks day 3-5
explanation.pearls: 37+0 PE = deliver. MgSO4 is for severe, not all. Antihypertensive target is <140/90 antenatally and postnatally.

options.rationale: Pre-eclampsia diagnosed at or beyond 37+0 weeks is an indication for delivery in the same admission, not expectant to 39 weeks. Outpatient management is correct only in mild gestational hypertension without PE features (SOMANZ 2023; NICE NG133).

Pre-eclampsia at >=37+0 weeks is an indication for delivery (SOMANZ 2023; NICE NG133; HYPITAT trial 2009). With a Bishop score of 1 the route is induction of labour rather than caesarean unless other obstetric indications. Antihypertensive target is <140/90 (oral labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa). MgSO4 for seizure prophylaxis is indicated for severe pre-eclampsia (severe hypertension >=160/110, neurological features, severe biochemical features) rather than routine non-severe disease (SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy 2023; NICE NG133).

Bishop 1 does not mandate CS in non-severe PE with reassuring fetal status; ripening then induction is appropriate. Direct CS is correct with severe PE features or unfavourable fetal status (SOMANZ; RANZCOG).
Routine MgSO4 for all PE is not recommended in non-severe disease; reserved for severe PE or imminent eclampsia features. Routine MgSO4 is correct in severe PE only (SOMANZ).
Antenatal corticosteroids not indicated at 37+3 weeks; used between 24+0 and 34+6 weeks. Steroids are correct only in preterm gestation (RANZCOG corticosteroids).

explanation.summary: Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis: benzylpenicillin 3 g IV load then 1.8 g IV q4h until birth (first-line). Non-severe penicillin allergy: cefazolin 2 g IV load then 1 g IV q8h. Severe (anaphylactic) penicillin allergy: clindamycin 600 mg IV q8h if susceptible, vancomycin 20 mg/kg IV q8h if not. Adequate prophylaxis = >=4 h before birth.
key_points: Australian screening: vaginorectal swab at 35-37 weeks OR risk-based (preterm, prolonged ROM, intrapartum fever, previous infant with GBS disease, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy)
Severe allergy = anaphylaxis, angioedema, respiratory distress, hypotension; non-severe = rash without systemic features
Cefazolin is safe in non-severe penicillin allergy (cross-reactivity <2%)
Clindamycin resistance varies 13-20%; always check susceptibility
Adequate prophylaxis is >=4 h before birth
explanation.pearls: Allergy severity drives choice: non-severe = cefazolin, severe + susceptible = clindamycin, severe + resistant/unknown = vancomycin.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Group B Streptococcus

options.rationale: She has documented non-severe penicillin allergy; cefazolin is appropriate. BPG is correct in non-allergic women (Therapeutic Guidelines; RANZCOG).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Group B Streptococcus

options.rationale: Clindamycin is for severe (anaphylactic) penicillin allergy with documented isolate susceptibility; non-severe allergy uses cefazolin. Clindamycin is correct in severe allergy with susceptible isolate (Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Group B Streptococcus

options.rationale: Vancomycin is third-line, only with severe penicillin allergy and clindamycin resistance or unknown susceptibility. Vancomycin is correct only after first/second-line agents excluded (Therapeutic Guidelines; CDC).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Group B Streptococcus

options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines Australia and RANZCOG recommend cefazolin for women with non-severe (non-anaphylactic) penicillin allergy because cross-reactivity with first-generation cephalosporins is low (<2%). Loading dose 2 g IV with a maintenance dose of 1 g IV every 8 hours until delivery. Clindamycin is reserved for severe (anaphylactic) allergy with isolate susceptibility (Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic; RANZCOG Maternal Group B Streptococcus 2019; CDC GBS prevention 2019).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Group B Streptococcus

options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve reliable intrapartum levels for GBS prophylaxis; IV mandatory. Amoxicillin is also penicillin, contraindicated in allergy. Oral PCN-class is essentially never correct (Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic - Group B Streptococcus

explanation.summary: Term PROM: offer immediate IOL or expectant management up to ~24 h. The Hannah TermPROM trial showed equivalent perinatal outcomes between immediate IOL and expectant management, with lower chorioamnionitis and endometritis with immediate IOL. Avoid digital VE until necessary. Intrapartum GBS prophylaxis if GBS positive or ROM >18 h with unknown GBS, or other risk factors.
key_points: Confirm PROM: pool, ferning, IGFBP-1 or PAMG-1 if uncertain
Hannah TermPROM: immediate IOL reduces chorioamnionitis (4% vs 8.6%) and endometritis without increasing CS
Avoid digital VE until established labour or induction
GBS-negative + ROM <18 h + no fever = no antibiotics
GBS-positive = intrapartum prophylaxis as soon as labour or IOL begins
ROM >18 h with unknown GBS = treat as positive
explanation.pearls: PROM at term is a shared decision: immediate IOL versus brief expectant. Avoid digital exams; they buy infection without information.

sources.label: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: Australian practice for term PROM does not support prolonged outpatient management beyond 24 hours; chorio risk rises with time. Outpatient management beyond 24h is essentially never correct in term PROM (Hannah TermPROM 1996; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: The Hannah TermPROM trial (NEJM 1996) established that immediate IOL with oxytocin or expectant management for up to 96 hours have similar perinatal outcomes, but immediate IOL reduces chorioamnionitis and postpartum endometritis. Current Australian practice offers women either immediate IOL or expectant management with a clear plan to induce by approximately 24 hours from rupture, balancing maternal preference with infection risk. With negative GBS, intrapartum antibiotics are based on risk factors (ROM >18 h, intrapartum fever) rather than routine (Hannah ME et al NEJM 1996; RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes; NICE NG235). Per RANZCOG term PROM guidance: induction at any time after PROM is acceptable; expectant management up to 24 hours is reasonable; GBS prophylaxis triggered by ROM >18 hours or other risk factors.
source_refs: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics not indicated without clinical infection or risk factors. Antibiotics are correct with chorioamnionitis or ROM >18 hours with GBS-positive (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines).
