Digital VE after PROM should be deferred until labour is established or induction is planned; each exam increases infection risk. Digital VE is correct only when labour established (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

options.rationale: Patient preference matters; immediate ripening is one option but not the sole appropriate plan. Direct PGE2 is correct only with patient preference (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG Term Prelabour Rupture of Membranes

explanation.summary: Operative vaginal delivery prerequisites: full dilatation, ruptured membranes, head engaged (no abdominal palpable), station >=0 (preferably +1 or below), known position, adequate analgesia, empty bladder, consent, appropriate operator. Failure: no descent with three correct pulls, or non-completion after a reasonable trial. Failed forceps requires caesarean - do NOT switch instruments.
key_points: Forceps: better for OP/OT after rotation (Kielland) and where pulling is needed
Ventouse: better tolerated maternally, fewer perineal injuries, but higher failure rate, contraindicated <34 weeks and face presentation
Sequential instruments: significantly higher neonatal morbidity - avoid
Trial of instrumental in theatre when high failure risk (BMI >30, EFW >4 kg, OP/OT, mid-cavity, prolonged second stage)
Category 1 CS decision-to-delivery interval target 30 minutes
explanation.pearls: If forceps fails, the next stop is theatre, not the ventouse. The trolley is on standby for a reason.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Operative Vaginal Birth guideline

options.rationale: Repeated forceps after failure with three correct pulls is associated with significant maternal/neonatal trauma; transition to CS required. Repeat forceps is essentially never correct after three failed pulls (RANZCOG).
Sequential instrument use significantly increases neonatal morbidity (ICH, subgaleal); contraindicated except when head on perineum. Sequential is correct only with head on perineum (RANZCOG).

Failed forceps with pathological CTG mandates category 1 caesarean section. Sequential use of instruments is contraindicated due to combined neonatal trauma risk. The trial of instrumental should occur with theatre on standby precisely so this conversion can occur within minutes. The senior consultant should be present given the complexity (RANZCOG Instrumental Vaginal Birth 2016; RCOG Green-top 26 Operative Vaginal Birth; NICE NG235).

CTG is pathological and pushing without instrument has failed for >100 minutes; expediting delivery in theatre is required. Push-without-instrument is correct only with non-distressed fetus (RANZCOG).
Symphysiotomy is for shoulder dystocia or where CS is impossible (low-resource); not appropriate here. Symphysiotomy is correct in resource-limited settings without CS access (RANZCOG; WHO).

explanation.summary: Twin delivery: twin 1 cephalic and twin 2 cephalic = planned vaginal birth. Twin 1 cephalic, twin 2 non-cephalic = vaginal birth is appropriate where an experienced operator is available; CS only if both non-cephalic or if specific contraindications. After delivery of twin 1 with non-cephalic twin 2: internal podalic version + breech extraction (preferred) or ECV if back-superior. ARM of twin 2 only after presenting part engaged. Inter-twin interval should be minimised.
key_points: Twin Birth Study (Barrett NEJM 2013): planned vaginal birth equivalent to planned CS for selected DCDA/MCDA at 32+0 to 38+6 with twin 1 cephalic
Twin 2 non-cephalic: internal podalic version + breech extraction is preferred
ECV alternative for transverse twin 2 with back superior
Monoamniotic twins always CS (cord entanglement risk)
Inter-twin interval typically <30 min to minimise cervical closure and abruption risk
Combined vaginal-CS delivery worse than planned CS for both
explanation.pearls: Twin 1 cephalic + experienced operator = trial of vaginal birth even if twin 2 is breech or transverse. The non-cephalic second twin is not by itself a CS indication.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Twin Pregnancy guideline
Barrett JF et al NEJM 2013 (Twin Birth Study)
RCOG Green-top 51 Twin and Triplet Pregnancy
NICE NG137 Twin and triplet pregnancy

options.rationale: With twin 2 transverse after delivery of twin 1 and an experienced operator available, internal podalic version (operator inserts a hand through the cervix, identifies a fetal foot, brings it down through the introitus) followed by breech extraction is the preferred approach in Australia and is supported by the Twin Birth Study (Barrett JF et al NEJM 2013). External cephalic version is an alternative but has lower success after delivery of the first twin and risks fetal distress and abruption. Combined vaginal-CS delivery has worse outcomes than planned CS. The reassuring CTG provides a window for intervention, and internal podalic version with breech extraction is the most reliable mode in experienced hands. CS should be reserved for failed manoeuvres or non-reassuring CTG (RANZCOG Management of Twin Pregnancy 2022; RCOG Green-top 51 Twin and Triplet Pregnancy).
source_refs: Barrett JF et al NEJM 2013 (Twin Birth Study)
RCOG Green-top 51 Twin and Triplet Pregnancy

options.rationale: ECV has lower success rate than internal podalic version (~60% vs >90%); any delay risks cord prolapse, abruption, or cervical closure. ECV is correct in earlier antenatal management (RANZCOG).

Combined vaginal-CS delivery is associated with worse outcomes for both mother and twin 2 versus internal podalic version; reserve CS for failed manoeuvres. CS is correct after failed manoeuvres (RANZCOG).
source_refs: Barrett JF et al NEJM 2013 (Twin Birth Study)

options.rationale: Twin 2 transverse will not descend spontaneously; inter-twin interval should be as short as practical (commonly within 30 minutes). Waiting 60 minutes is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).
ARM with transverse lie is contraindicated due to high cord prolapse risk; version must occur first. ARM-first in transverse lie is essentially never correct (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Lactational mastitis with systemic features warrants oral antibiotics for 5-7 days plus effective milk removal. First-line is flucloxacillin; with immediate penicillin hypersensitivity the eTG alternative is clindamycin, which is breastfeeding-compatible (LactMed).
key_points: Most common pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus
Continue breastfeeding/expressing - drainage is therapeutic
Immediate (Type 1) penicillin allergy excludes cephalosporins as well
Clindamycin covers most CA-MRSA and concentrates in breast tissue
TMP-SMX avoided in mothers feeding infants <1 month (kernicterus risk)
explanation.pearls: If the mother fails to improve at 48 hours of appropriate antibiotics, image with ultrasound for abscess before broadening cover.

options.rationale: Flucloxacillin would be first-line but is contraindicated with immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin. Flucloxacillin is correct in non-allergic women (Therapeutic Guidelines).

Cephalosporins are avoided when penicillin reaction was immediate (Type 1) hypersensitivity with angioedema due to unpredictable cross-reactivity. Cefalexin is correct in non-immediate penicillin allergy (Therapeutic Guidelines).

Clindamycin is the eTG-recommended alternative for lactational mastitis in patients with immediate penicillin hypersensitivity; it covers S. aureus including most CA-MRSA, is compatible with breastfeeding per LactMed and concentrates well in breast tissue (Therapeutic Guidelines; LactMed).

Amoxicillin-clavulanate contains penicillin and is contraindicated in immediate hypersensitivity. Augmentin is correct in non-allergic women with suspected polymicrobial infection (Therapeutic Guidelines).
TMP-SMX is reserved for confirmed MRSA and avoided in mothers of infants <1 month due to theoretical kernicterus risk. TMP-SMX is correct in MRSA mastitis in older infants (Therapeutic Guidelines).

explanation.summary: The lactation inflammation spectrum runs from ductal narrowing/blocked duct (focal lump, no systemic features) through inflammatory mastitis (erythema, pain) to bacterial mastitis (systemic features) to abscess. Current evidence-based care de-emphasises deep massage and heat; the cornerstones are physiological feeding, lymphatic drainage and cold for symptom control.
key_points: Blocked duct: focal lump, no fever, no defined erythema
Inflammatory mastitis: erythema and pain, no systemic features
Bacterial mastitis: above plus fever/tachycardia, or non-resolution
Abscess: fluctuant collection on USS
Cold preferred over heat per ABM 2022 protocol
explanation.pearls: A long overnight feed gap is the classic precipitant of a blocked duct in an established 6-week breastfeeding dyad.

options.rationale: The Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine 2022 protocol describes this as ductal narrowing/inflammatory mastitis spectrum, not bacterial mastitis. Management is on-demand feeding, cold packs, NSAIDs, and AVOIDANCE of deep massage and pumping (both can worsen inflammation/oedema). Antibiotics are reserved for bacterial mastitis (RANZCOG; ABM 2022).

No fever, systemic symptoms, or defined erythema. Antibiotics are not indicated for inflammatory mastitis/ductal narrowing and may worsen dysbiosis. Flucloxacillin is correct in bacterial mastitis with fever/erythema (ABM 2022).
Aggressive massage worsens tissue oedema and risks abscess, and ABM 2022 specifically warns against it. Aggressive massage is essentially never correct (ABM 2022).
Cessation worsens engorgement and inflammatory cycle; on-demand feeding remains essential. Pump-and-dump is correct only with documented contraindications (ABM 2022).
No fluctuance, abscess features, or failure of conservative management; surgical referral premature. Surgical referral is correct after failed conservative management or abscess (ABM 2022).

explanation.summary: Lactational breast abscesses require source control. Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration with cultured aspirate is first-line for abscesses up to around 5 cm with intact skin and is repeated as needed; surgical drainage is reserved for larger, multiloculated, or skin-compromised collections.
key_points: Continue breastfeeding throughout treatment
USS-guided aspiration preserves duct anatomy
Send aspirate for culture to guide ongoing antibiotics
Surgical I&D for large, multiloculated, or skin-necrosed abscesses
Antibiotics alone are inadequate once a collection has formed
explanation.pearls: An apparently improving mastitis that develops a new fluctuant area at day 5 is an abscess until ultrasound proves otherwise.

options.rationale: Drained collection requires drainage to resolve; antibiotics alone are inadequate and risk chronicity/fistula. Antibiotics-alone is correct only in early cellulitic phase without collection (ABM).

For a lactational abscess under approximately 5 cm with intact non-necrotic skin, ultrasound-guided needle aspiration (often serial) with cultured aspirate and continued antibiotics is first-line; it preserves duct architecture, allows ongoing breastfeeding and avoids a surgical wound that complicates feeding (ABM; BMJ Best Practice).
Surgical I&D is reserved for very large abscesses, multiloculated, or thinned/necrotic skin; leaves wound that may interfere with feeding. I&D is correct for large/complex abscesses (ABM).
Cessation worsens milk stasis and slows resolution; current guidance is to continue feeding or express. Cessation is essentially never correct in mastitis/abscess (ABM).
Antibiotic broadening without drainage is inadequate; established collection needs source control. Clindamycin alone is correct only without abscess collection (ABM).

explanation.summary: Perceived low supply is far more common than true low supply. Assess transfer using objective markers (weight gain >20-30 g/day after nadir, regaining birthweight by 2 weeks, 6+ heavy wet nappies, mustard stools, audible swallowing) before introducing supplementation or galactagogues.
key_points: Expressed volume is a poor proxy for milk transfer
Cluster feeding and softer breasts are normal after 2-3 weeks
Confirm adequate output with weight + nappies + stools before intervening
Premature top-ups suppress supply (negative feedback)
Galactagogues are second-line after a structured assessment
explanation.pearls: Counsel that breasts feeling 'less full' often reflects normal calibration of supply to demand, not failing supply.

options.rationale: Supplementation without indication suppresses prolactin-driven supply and undermines breastfeeding; growth and output are normal. Formula top-ups are correct with documented poor growth/output (ABA; RANZCOG).

Soft breasts after the early hyperlactation phase, low expressed volumes (a poor proxy for transfer), and cluster-feeding behaviour are normal at 3 weeks. Adequate weight gain (>20-30 g/day after nadir), regaining birthweight by 2 weeks, and 6+ heavy wet nappies confirm adequate intake; perceived low supply without objective markers is the most common cause of unnecessary supplementation (ABA; RCH; ABM).

Galactagogues are considered only after structured assessment confirms inadequate supply, identifies reversible cause, and addresses technique. Domperidone is correct after structured supply assessment failure (ABM).

Test-weighing is anxiety-provoking, prone to error, and rarely changes management with reassuring growth/output. Test-weighing is correct only in specific research/clinical questions about transfer (ABA; ABM).
No clinical suspicion for Sheehan (no severe PPH, no other pituitary dysfunction); imaging not indicated. Pituitary MRI is correct in suspected Sheehan or other pituitary disease (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Frenotomy for ankyloglossia is indicated only when feeding is functionally impaired AND optimised positioning/attachment has not resolved the issue AND examination confirms restricted tongue function. RANZCOG and RCH caution against routine posterior tongue or lip tie release.
key_points: Frenotomy indicated only when function is impaired
Optimise positioning and attachment with IBCLC support first
RCT evidence supports anterior tongue-tie frenotomy when functionally significant
Posterior tongue tie and lip tie release evidence base is weak
Refer to an experienced clinician (paediatrician, ENT, paediatric dentist with training)
explanation.pearls: If the latch has been optimised across multiple reviews and the mother still has nipple trauma, look in the baby's mouth - not at the mother's technique.

sources.label: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

options.rationale: When ankyloglossia is associated with functionally significant feeding problems persisting despite optimised positioning and attachment (nipple trauma + impaired transfer + objective tongue-function deficit), frenotomy by an experienced clinician is appropriate and improves both maternal pain and infant transfer in RCT-level evidence (RANZCOG; RCH; ABM Protocol 11).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

options.rationale: Positioning already optimised with three lactation consultant reviews and infant growth faltering; further delay risks supply failure and breastfeeding cessation. Continued positioning is correct only with adequate transfer and growth (RCH; RANZCOG).

Mother wishes to continue and reversible structural cause identified; cessation not first-line when treatable lesion present. Formula transition is correct only after failed intervention or maternal preference (RCH; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

options.rationale: RANZCOG and RCH caution against indiscriminate posterior tongue tie or upper-lip tie release; evidence is weak and over-diagnosis documented. Posterior/lip-tie release is correct only with rigorous criteria and specialist assessment (RCH).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

options.rationale: Shields already failed and do not address underlying restriction; reliance can worsen transfer. Nipple shields are correct as short-term adjunct, not long-term solution (RCH).
source_refs: RCH Clinical Practice Guideline: Tongue tie

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE in a breastfeeding woman is treated with LMWH (preferred for ease and predictability) or warfarin; both are compatible with breastfeeding. DOACs are NOT recommended in lactation due to inadequate infant safety data.
key_points: LMWH: negligible oral bioavailability in infant - safe in lactation
Warfarin: high protein binding, undetectable in milk - safe in lactation
DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran): avoid in lactation
Acute PE/DVT requires therapeutic, not prophylactic, anticoagulation
Duration usually at least 3 months for provoked postpartum VTE
explanation.pearls: Tell the patient explicitly that LMWH and warfarin do not require pump-and-dump - common misconception that interrupts breastfeeding unnecessarily.

sources.label: RANZCOG: VTE in pregnancy and puerperium

options.rationale: Both LMWH (negligible oral bioavailability in the infant) and warfarin (high protein binding, undetectable in milk) are compatible with breastfeeding and are the RANZCOG-recommended options for postpartum VTE; DOACs are NOT recommended in lactation due to insufficient safety data (RANZCOG VTE; LactMed).
source_refs: RANZCOG: VTE in pregnancy and puerperium

options.rationale: DOACs not recommended in lactation; manufacturer data and LactMed advise against use. Apixaban is correct only outside breastfeeding (LactMed; AMH).
Rivaroxaban excreted into milk in animal studies; not recommended in lactation. Rivaroxaban is correct only outside breastfeeding (LactMed; AMH).

UFH is also compatible with breastfeeding but not preferred over LMWH for routine VTE outside renal failure or imminent procedure. UFH is correct in severe renal impairment or procedural bridging (AMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG: VTE in pregnancy and puerperium

options.rationale: Aspirin not adequate for acute PE or DVT; therapeutic anticoagulation required. Aspirin is correct for extended secondary prevention only after initial therapeutic period (RANZCOG; eTG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: VTE in pregnancy and puerperium

explanation.summary: Galactagogues are pharmacological agents used to augment milk supply when comprehensive non-pharmacological measures (positioning and attachment optimisation, frequent expressing, skin-to-skin contact, addressing maternal stress and fatigue) have failed. Domperidone (10 mg three times daily for 7-14 days) is the most evidenced agent in Australia, working as a peripheral dopamine antagonist that raises prolactin. Safety concerns centre on dose-dependent QTc prolongation and sudden cardiac death; the TGA contraindicates concurrent QT-prolonging drugs, baseline QTc 450 ms or more, significant electrolyte disturbance, and known cardiac conduction disease. ECG and electrolyte check before starting are standard practice. Metoclopramide is an alternative but carries tardive dyskinesia risk and is generally avoided. Fenugreek and other herbal galactagogues lack evidence and have no place as first-line therapy. Address any modifiable factors first: most low supply is from inadequate effective milk removal, not from intrinsic deficiency.
key_points: TGA dose ceiling: 10 mg TDS
Baseline ECG indicated before starting domperidone
Avoid with concurrent QT-prolonging drugs
Avoid with QTc >=450 ms or electrolyte derangement
Galactagogues are adjuncts, not replacements, for milk removal
explanation.pearls: Domperidone prolongs QTc dose-dependently and is contraindicated with concurrent QT-prolonging drugs (citalopram, escitalopram, ondansetron, clarithromycin, methadone, fluconazole) or baseline QTc 450 ms or more - check ECG before starting (TGA Safety Advisory).

options.rationale: TGA and ABM safety guidance contraindicate domperidone with concurrent QT-prolonging medication and QTc >=450 ms; citalopram is QT-prolonging. Domperidone is correct only with normal QTc and no QT drugs (TGA).

Domperidone is contraindicated when QTc is prolonged or when a patient is on concurrent QT-prolonging drugs (including citalopram); the safe step is to avoid it, address the modifiable risk (review citalopram) and continue evidence-based milk-removal optimisation (TGA; ABM).
TGA limits dosing to no more than 10 mg three times daily; cardiac risk dose-dependent. Plus active contraindications here. Higher dose is essentially never correct (TGA).

Metoclopramide has weaker galactagogue evidence and significant risks of extrapyramidal effects and depression with prolonged use. Metoclopramide is correct in short-term postpartum nausea, not long-term galactagogue (TGA).

Fenugreek has limited inconsistent evidence and is not a substitute for addressing milk removal or QT-drug review. Fenugreek is correct only as adjunctive lay-supported intervention, not medical recommendation (ABM).

explanation.summary: Pelvic organ prolapse is staged using the standardised POP-Q (Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification) system, which measures defined points along the anterior vaginal wall, posterior wall, and apex relative to the hymenal ring. Stage 0 means no descent; stage 1 means the leading edge sits more than 1 cm above the hymen; stage 2 within 1 cm of the hymen (above or below); stage 3 more than 1 cm beyond the hymen but not full eversion (which is stage 4). The dominant compartment - anterior (cystocele), posterior (rectocele), or apical (uterine or vault) - is named by the most dependent point at maximum Valsalva. Apical defects often coexist with anterior descent, so apical support (sacrohysteropexy, sacrocolpopexy or sacrospinous fixation) is integral to anterior repair. Conservative options (pessary, pelvic floor physiotherapy) are first-line; surgery is reserved for symptomatic patients after conservative trial.
key_points: Six points: Aa, Ba (anterior); Ap, Bp (posterior); C (cervix/cuff), D (posterior fornix if uterus present)
TVL, GH and PB are static landmarks
Most distal point sets the stage
Stage 4 requires near-complete eversion (TVL - 2 cm)
Vault prolapse = apical descent in a post-hysterectomy patient
explanation.pearls: POP-Q stages are anchored to the hymen: stage 1 leading edge over 1 cm above hymen, stage 2 within 1 cm, stage 3 over 1 cm beyond but not complete eversion, stage 4 essentially complete vault eversion. The most dependent point names the dominant compartment.

options.rationale: Most dependent point is C (cervix) at +3, not Ba; anterior wall at Ba +1 is stage 2 in isolation but dominant defect is apical. Stage 2 cystocele is correct with anterior dominant + apex above hymen (IUGA).

POP-Q staging uses the most dependent point: C at +3 (>1 cm beyond hymen but TVL is 9 cm so not complete eversion) is stage 3, with the apex (uterus) being the dominant compartment. Stage 4 would require complete eversion (most distal point at +/- TVL - 2 cm) (IUGA/ICS).
Stage 4 requires most distal point at TVL -2 cm or beyond (essentially complete eversion); cervix at +3 with TVL 9 cm does not meet criterion. Stage 4 is correct in complete vaginal eversion (IUGA).
Bp is -2, well above hymen; posterior compartment is not the dominant defect. Stage 3 posterior is correct with Bp beyond hymen (IUGA).
Stage 1 requires most distal point >1 cm ABOVE hymen; cervix at +3 well beyond that threshold. Stage 1 is correct with all points >1 cm above hymen (IUGA).

explanation.summary: Sacrocolpopexy (open or laparoscopic) with type 1 polypropylene mesh is the durability gold-standard for symptomatic vault prolapse where sexual function is to be preserved. Sacrospinous fixation is the principal native-tissue alternative. Colpocleisis is reserved for frail, non-sexually-active patients. Transvaginal mesh kits are not available in Australia since 2017.
key_points: TGA withdrew transvaginal mesh kits in 2017; sacrocolpopexy mesh is placed abdominally and remains available
Sacrocolpopexy preserves vaginal length and axis better than vaginal approaches
Sacrospinous fixation: native tissue, vaginal route, higher recurrence
Colpocleisis: obliterative, only for non-sexually-active
Conservative measures should be trialled first unless not feasible
explanation.pearls: The Australian Senate Inquiry into transvaginal mesh shaped the current TGA stance and is why the abdominal vs vaginal mesh distinction is essential to know.

sources.label: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Sacrocolpopexy (open or laparoscopic) using type 1 macroporous polypropylene mesh is the gold-standard procedure for symptomatic vault prolapse where coital function is to be preserved; it has the lowest recurrence rate and best preserves vaginal length; abdominal (non-vaginal) mesh placement is not subject to the TGA's transvaginal mesh restriction (RANZCOG; NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Transvaginal mesh kits withdrawn by TGA in Australia in 2017 due to harm signals; not available. TV mesh is essentially never correct in current Australian practice (TGA mesh statement).

Sacrospinous fixation is reasonable native-tissue alternative for poor abdominal surgical candidates but higher recurrence than sacrocolpopexy. SSLF is correct in patients unsuitable for abdominal surgery (RANZCOG).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Colpocleisis is obliterative procedure for older, frail, non-sexually-active women who accept loss of coital function; she remains sexually active. Colpocleisis is correct in elderly non-sexually-active women (RANZCOG).
Already failed conservative with recurrent pessary expulsion and ineffective PFMT; another pessary unlikely to succeed. Pessary is correct as initial trial or in patients declining surgery (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Overactive bladder in older Australians is initially managed with bladder retraining, scheduled voiding, fluid optimisation (cap caffeine and alcohol, avoid excessive evening fluids) and pelvic floor physiotherapy - typically delivered over 6-12 weeks before pharmacotherapy. Antimuscarinics (oxybutynin, solifenacin, darifenacin, tolterodine) carry a cumulative anticholinergic burden linked to cognitive decline, falls, constipation, dry mouth and acute urinary retention; oxybutynin IR has the worst CNS penetration. Mirabegron (beta-3 agonist) achieves comparable continence outcomes without anticholinergic effects but is contraindicated in uncontrolled severe hypertension - check BP at baseline and at 4 weeks. Always measure a post-void residual before any pharmacotherapy in older patients to exclude chronic retention masquerading as urge incontinence. Onabotulinum toxin A intradetrusor injection is the next step for refractory disease.
key_points: First-line: bladder training, PFMT, caffeine reduction, weight loss
Mirabegron: beta-3 agonist, no anticholinergic burden, check BP
Antimuscarinics rank by CNS burden: oxybutynin (worst) > tolterodine > solifenacin/darifenacin (lowest)
Desmopressin restricted in >65 (hyponatraemia)
Duloxetine is for stress UI, not urge UI
explanation.pearls: Anticholinergic burden compounds across medications in older adults - oxybutynin IR alone increases dementia risk after 3+ years of use; mirabegron (beta-3 agonist) is anticholinergic-free and the preferred second-line agent if uncontrolled HTN is excluded (eTG Urological; AMH).

sources.label: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Oxybutynin (especially IR) has highest CNS penetration; associated with cognitive decline in older adults. Listed as potentially inappropriate. Oxybutynin is correct only in younger patients without cognitive concern (Beers Criteria; STOPP).

Mirabegron is a beta-3 adrenergic agonist with no anticholinergic burden, making it preferred in older patients with cognitive impairment when conservative measures are inadequate, provided severe uncontrolled hypertension is excluded (NICE NG123; Continence Foundation Australia).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Solifenacin is more bladder-selective with lower CNS penetration than oxybutynin but still anticholinergic burden best avoided in cognitive impairment. Solifenacin is correct in moderate OAB without cognitive concern (Beers).
Duloxetine is used for stress UI; diary shows no stress component. Duloxetine is correct in stress-predominant or mixed UI (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Desmopressin restricted in older patients due to hyponatraemia risk; not first-line for OAB. Desmopressin is correct in younger patients with nocturnal polyuria and no hyponatraemia risk (Continence Foundation; AMH).

explanation.summary: Mixed UI is managed with a structured conservative bundle first (PFMT at least 3 months, bladder training, weight loss if BMI >30, caffeine and fluid optimisation, smoking cessation). When pharmacotherapy is needed, target the predominant symptom; urodynamics are reserved for selected indications.
key_points: Bladder diary identifies the predominant component
PFMT >=3 months helps both stress and urge
Weight loss of 5-10% halves leakage episodes
Pharmacotherapy targets predominant symptom (antimuscarinic/mirabegron for urge; duloxetine for stress)
Urodynamics not routine before conservative management
explanation.pearls: Treating the predominant component first often unmasks or relieves the secondary component without separate intervention.

sources.label: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: NICE and Continence Foundation Australia advise structured conservative therapy as initial management for mixed UI, with treatment then directed at the predominant symptom (urge here). PFMT helps both components, bladder training targets urge, and weight loss helps both; structured trial for at least 3 months before escalation (NICE NG123; Continence Foundation Australia).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Surgery not first-line for mixed UI; stress-incontinence surgery may worsen pre-existing urge symptoms. Plus she declines surgery. Surgery is correct after failed conservative + pharmacological management (RANZCOG; NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Combined pharmacotherapy from outset not recommended; conservative first-line with single-agent for predominant component. Combined therapy is correct after single-agent failure (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Urodynamics not required before conservative management of uncomplicated mixed UI; reserved for diagnostic uncertainty or pre-surgical planning. Urodynamics is correct pre-surgery (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Continence pessaries useful mainly for stress UI driven by hypermobility; topical oestrogen for urogenital atrophy; neither addresses mixed UI primarily. Pessary is correct in stress UI with hypermobility (Continence Foundation; NICE NG123).

explanation.summary: Continuous small-volume leakage with high PVR, palpable bladder, and rising creatinine with hydronephrosis is overflow incontinence from high-pressure chronic retention with post-obstructive AKI. Immediate bladder decompression with an indwelling catheter and urgent urology review is mandatory. Monitor for post-obstructive diuresis and hyperkalaemia.
key_points: Overflow UI: continuous leakage, high PVR, no urgency, often diabetic or neurogenic
High-pressure retention with hydronephrosis + rising creatinine = obstructive AKI
Decompress immediately with IDC
Stop all antimuscarinics
Watch for post-obstructive diuresis (replace half losses cautiously)
explanation.pearls: Any patient on antimuscarinics whose leakage gets worse should have a PVR scan before any further dose change - the most common missed cause of overflow incontinence is iatrogenic.

sources.label: NICE NG112 Lower urinary tract symptoms in men (decompression principles applicable)
NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: PVR 720 mL with new bilateral hydronephrosis and rising creatinine indicates high-pressure chronic retention with obstructive AKI - bladder decompression with an indwelling catheter and urgent urology review is the immediate priority; antimuscarinics worsen retention and must be stopped (NICE NG112; Continence Foundation Australia; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: NICE NG112 Lower urinary tract symptoms in men (decompression principles applicable)

options.rationale: Adding pharmacotherapy for assumed OAB ignores high-volume retention with renal compromise; risks worsening retention and renal injury. Mirabegron is correct in confirmed OAB without retention (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: She has OVERFLOW incontinence from chronic retention, not stress; sling will precipitate complete retention and worsen renal injury. Sling is correct in confirmed stress UI without retention (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Furosemide increases urine production into already obstructed bladder; worsens retention and AKI. Furosemide is correct in fluid overload only, never in obstructive uropathy (Therapeutic Guidelines).

Outpatient delay unsafe with post-obstructive AKI with bilateral hydronephrosis; immediate decompression required. Outpatient delay is essentially never correct in obstructive AKI (NICE; Continence Foundation).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

explanation.summary: Urodynamic studies are NOT required before a primary procedure for clinically straightforward stress urinary incontinence. They are indicated when: symptoms are mixed or urge-predominant, voiding dysfunction is suspected (high PVR, hesitancy), there is previous incontinence/pelvic surgery, concurrent prolapse repair is planned (occult SUI assessment), or there is neurogenic disease.
key_points: Pure, uncomplicated SUI -> no urodynamics needed before primary sling
Mixed UI with discordant findings -> urodynamics often helpful
Prior incontinence surgery -> urodynamics before redo
Neurogenic bladder -> urodynamics needed
Suspected occult SUI before prolapse surgery -> urodynamics
explanation.pearls: The single biggest indication people forget is concurrent prolapse repair, where reducing the prolapse can unmask stress incontinence.

sources.label: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: NICE NG123 advises against routine urodynamics before primary mid-urethral sling for clinically clear uncomplicated stress UI. Routine urodynamics-for-all is essentially never correct (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Her presentation is uncomplicated pure stress UI with normal PVR, no voiding symptoms, no prior surgery and no prolapse beyond the hymen; NICE NG123 and the Continence Foundation Australia consensus indicate urodynamics in this scenario do not change management (NICE; Continence Foundation Australia).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Failed primary procedure is one indication but not the only one; urodynamics may be appropriate before surgery in complicated cases. Failed-primary indication is correct but not exclusive (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: PVR is one input; symptom pattern, prior surgery, neurological history, and prolapse all guide decision. PVR-alone trigger is correct only as one of multiple criteria (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: Pharmacotherapy for urge UI does not require urodynamics; conservative measures and empirical trial first-line. Urodynamics for any pharmacotherapy is essentially never correct (NICE; Continence Foundation Australia).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

explanation.summary: Continuous painless urinary leakage after pelvic surgery is a vesicovaginal or ureterovaginal fistula until proven otherwise. The three-swab dye test (intravesical methylene blue plus tampons in upper, middle and lower vagina) localises the leak and distinguishes urethral, vesical and ureteric sources; cystoscopy and CT-IVU or CTU then characterise the defect for repair planning.
key_points: Continuous painless leakage post-pelvic surgery -> fistula until proven otherwise
Three-swab dye test: upper swab stained suggests ureterovaginal; mid/upper bladder; lower urethrovaginal
If dye test negative for vesical source, suspect ureterovaginal: oral phenazopyridine or IV indigo carmine plus CT-IVU
Cystoscopy maps the bladder defect for repair planning
Obstetric fistula remains the leading global cause; in high-income settings most fistulae are iatrogenic post-hysterectomy
explanation.pearls: If the upper vaginal tampon stains blue and the middle does not, suspect a ureterovaginal fistula and proceed to ureteric imaging.

sources.label: FIGO Global Competency-Based Fistula Surgery Training Manual
NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: The three-swab (tampon) test with intravesical dye distinguishes vesicovaginal from ureterovaginal and urethrovaginal fistulae and can identify a fistula site too small to see at speculum; it is a simple bedside test and is the standard first-line investigation alongside, or before, formal cystoscopy (RANZCOG; FIGO Fistula manual).
source_refs: FIGO Global Competency-Based Fistula Surgery Training Manual

options.rationale: Urinalysis clear and clinical picture not UTI; antibiotics will not address fistula. Antibiotics are correct in UTI, not fistula (Therapeutic Guidelines).
Urodynamics characterise bladder/sphincter function and not used to diagnose fistula. Urodynamics is correct in functional incontinence workup (NICE NG123).
source_refs: NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse

options.rationale: MRI may help anatomical mapping for surgical planning of complex fistulae but not first step; dye testing plus cystoscopy is standard. MRI is correct in complex fistula surgical planning (RANZCOG).

Continuous painless leakage after pelvic surgery with bladder dissection is fistula until proven otherwise; physiotherapy delays diagnosis. PT is correct in functional UI without fistula features (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Vulvar HSIL (uVIN) is HPV-driven and managed with one of: imiquimod (anatomy-sparing first line for selected lesions), wide local excision, or laser ablation. Differentiated VIN (dVIN), associated with lichen sclerosus and HPV-independent, has higher cancer risk and is managed with surgical excision (not imiquimod). Any non-responding or atypical area requires re-biopsy.
key_points: Vulvar HSIL = uVIN, HPV-driven, p16-positive, multifocal more common, lower per-lesion cancer risk
Differentiated VIN = dVIN, HPV-independent, p16-negative, on background of LS, HIGHER cancer risk, surgical excision
Imiquimod: anatomy-sparing for uVIN; ~50-80% clearance
Wide local excision: definitive histology, suitable for unifocal or suspicious lesions
Long-term surveillance after any treatment because of recurrence and dysplasia elsewhere
explanation.pearls: A non-healing or hyperkeratotic vulval lesion in a woman with long-standing lichen sclerosus should make you think dVIN/SCC, not uVIN - excise, do not topical-treat.

options.rationale: For non-invasive, HPV-driven vulvar HSIL (uVIN) in unifocal or limited multifocal lesions where anatomy preservation matters, topical imiquimod is RANZCOG/BSSVD-recommended first-line, with documented clinical clearance in ~50-80% and a re-biopsy threshold for any persistent lesion to exclude occult invasion (RANZCOG; BSSVD).
HSIL/uVIN carries ~5-10% progression risk to invasive SCC if untreated; active management required. Watchful waiting is essentially never correct in HSIL/uVIN (RANZCOG; BSSVD).
Radical vulvectomy + lymphadenectomy reserved for invasive vulvar carcinoma, not preinvasive HSIL. Radical surgery is correct for invasive disease only (RANZCOG).

Potent topical steroids are for inflammatory dermatoses (lichen sclerosus, lichen planus), not HSIL/uVIN; do not treat preinvasive dysplasia. Topical steroid is correct in inflammatory vulval dermatoses (BSSVD).

5-FU largely supplanted by imiquimod due to high rates of vulval chemical burn and lower tolerability; indefinite application not recommended. 5-FU is correct in specific resistant cases under specialist care (BSSVD).

explanation.summary: Primary Bartholin abscess is managed with a fistulising drainage procedure - Word catheter insertion is the office/ED first-line; marsupialisation is the operating theatre equivalent. Simple I&D recurs frequently and gland excision is reserved for recurrent failure. Antibiotics are adjunctive only if cellulitis, systemic features, immunosuppression or pregnancy.
key_points: Word catheter: local anaesthetic, low morbidity, in situ 4-6 weeks
Marsupialisation: equivalent recurrence, requires GA
Simple I&D: highest recurrence
Antibiotics adjunctive only with cellulitis, systemic features or immunosuppression
In women aged 40+ with a Bartholin mass, consider biopsy to exclude carcinoma
explanation.pearls: A new Bartholin mass in a postmenopausal woman is carcinoma until biopsy proves otherwise - very different from the under-40 abscess pathway.

options.rationale: Simple I&D + packing has high recurrence rates (this is third recurrence); definitive procedure now needed. Simple I&D is correct for first acute presentation (RANZCOG; eTG).

After recurrent Bartholin abscesses at the same site despite Word catheter or I&D, marsupialisation provides definitive long-term drainage with lower recurrence than I&D and is preferred over excision (which is reserved for failed marsupialisation or suspicion of malignancy) (RANZCOG; eTG).

Word catheter is acceptable first-line for primary or single recurrence; with three recurrences at same site, more definitive marsupialisation indicated. Word catheter is correct for first/second presentation (RANZCOG).
Abscess requires drainage; antibiotics alone do not resolve. Antibiotics reserved for surrounding cellulitis or sepsis. Antibiotics are correct as adjunct to drainage (eTG; RANZCOG).
Excision reserved for failed marsupialisation or suspected malignancy (usually women >40); higher morbidity. Excision is correct after failed marsupialisation (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: All women on any antiepileptic drug should receive folic acid 5 mg daily preconceptionally and through the first trimester, irrespective of the specific agent. The dose change should be made before conception because neural tube closure occurs by 28 days post-conception (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
key_points: High-dose folate (5 mg) is also recommended for diabetes, previous NTD-affected pregnancy, BMI >30 kg/m2 and some haemoglobinopathies
Lamotrigine is one of the safer antiepileptics in pregnancy but does not exempt the patient from the 5 mg recommendation
Start folate at least 1 month (ideally 3 months) preconception and continue until 12 weeks gestation
Do not stop antiepileptic therapy in a stable patient without specialist input
explanation.pearls: If a woman taking any antiepileptic asks about pregnancy, the answer to folate is almost always 5 mg, not 400 micrograms.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Pre-pregnancy counselling and routine antenatal assessment
Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology - epilepsy and pregnancy

options.rationale: Continuing valproate is wrong because it is highly teratogenic (NTD, cardiac, craniofacial, cognitive impairment) and is contraindicated in women of reproductive age unless a TGA Pregnancy Prevention Program is in place AND no alternative controls seizures; folate alone does not mitigate the teratogenic risk. Would be acceptable only when every alternative antiepileptic has failed and PPP criteria are fully met, never as routine preconception advice (RANZCOG; TGA valproate PPP; AMH).

Valproate must be avoided in pregnancy where possible. Neurology should switch to lamotrigine or levetiracetam, conception is deferred until seizure-free on the new agent, and folic acid 5 mg daily is started preconception until 12 weeks (RANZCOG; AMH; TGA valproate PPP).

Abrupt cessation is wrong because antiepileptic withdrawal risks status epilepticus, which carries higher maternal and fetal mortality than the drug itself; antiepileptics should not be stopped without neurology input. Would be correct only inside a supervised neurology switch with overlap onto a safer agent, not as standalone advice (RANZCOG; AMH).

Adding lamotrigine on top of valproate is wrong because polytherapy multiplies teratogenic risk rather than reducing it, and valproate must be removed entirely whenever possible. Would be correct only as a transient bridge during a planned cross-titration off valproate under neurology, not as a maintenance plan for pregnancy (RANZCOG; AMH).

Folic acid 400 mcg is wrong because women on antiepileptics require the high-dose 5 mg regimen preconception until 12 weeks, and even adequate folate does not neutralise valproate teratogenicity. Would be correct as the dose for a low-risk woman not on antiepileptics; here both the dose and the drug choice need to change (RANZCOG; AMH).

explanation.summary: Asthma affects about 12% of pregnant Australian women and tends to worsen in around a third, improve in a third and stay stable in a third. The dominant clinical risk is preventer non-adherence driven by misplaced concern about fetal harm. All inhaled corticosteroids are pregnancy category A or B3 and continued at the pre-pregnancy dose minimum; budesonide has the largest safety dataset and is preferred when starting therapy de novo. Stepped-up therapy follows the Australian Asthma Handbook: low-dose ICS, then ICS-LABA combination (budesonide-formoterol or fluticasone-salmeterol), then specialist input for biologics or oral steroids. Salbutamol PRN is safe in pregnancy. Acute exacerbations are managed exactly as in non-pregnant adults: oxygen to keep SpO2 over 94%, back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium, systemic prednisolone 37.5-50 mg, IV magnesium sulfate, and continuous fetal monitoring once viable.
key_points: Uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous to the fetus than asthma medication
Budesonide has the most extensive pregnancy safety data among ICS
Use a written asthma action plan and review every 4-6 weeks in pregnancy
Influenza vaccine is recommended for all pregnant women with asthma
explanation.pearls: Budesonide is the inhaled corticosteroid with the most pregnancy safety data; uncontrolled maternal asthma trebles the risk of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth and SGA, far outweighing any theoretical risk of preventer therapy (National Asthma Council Australia).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - asthma in pregnancy

options.rationale: Continuing the same ICS dose is wrong because deteriorating control (reliever more than twice weekly, nocturnal symptoms, falling FEV1) defines uncontrolled asthma, which is more dangerous in pregnancy than dose escalation. Would be correct only if control were stable and symptoms minimal, which is not the case here (RANZCOG; TSANZ; Australian Asthma Handbook).

Uncontrolled asthma is more dangerous to the pregnancy than inhaled corticosteroids. The Australian Asthma Handbook recommends standard step-up of inhaled therapy in pregnancy, including ICS-LABA combinations. Stopping ICS should be avoided (RANZCOG; TSANZ).

Stopping ICS is wrong because pregnancy is the exact setting where the Australian Asthma Handbook insists ICS be continued; cessation is associated with exacerbations, pre-eclampsia, prematurity and low birth weight. Would never be correct as a planned change in pregnancy (TSANZ; Australian Asthma Handbook).

Oral prednisolone as maintenance is wrong because oral corticosteroids are reserved for exacerbations, not chronic baseline therapy, due to maternal glycaemic, hypertensive and bone effects; the step-up ladder goes through inhaled ICS-LABA first. Would be correct only if she had severe steroid-dependent asthma already on optimised inhaled therapy (TSANZ; Australian Asthma Handbook).

Montelukast monotherapy is wrong because leukotriene receptor antagonists are an add-on, not a substitute for ICS, in the GINA/TSANZ pathway. Would be correct as a continuation if she was already on montelukast preconception with good control, not as a first-line switch (TSANZ; Australian Asthma Handbook).

explanation.summary: Acute severe asthma in pregnancy is one of the most common medical emergencies in obstetric practice and carries higher maternal and fetal mortality than non-pregnant asthma if undertreated. Pharmacological management is identical to non-pregnant adults: continuous high-flow oxygen titrated to SpO2 above 94%, back-to-back nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with ipratropium bromide 500 micrograms every 20 minutes, systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 37.5-50 mg or IV hydrocortisone 100 mg if oral not tolerated), then IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes if no response. Salbutamol IV, aminophylline, and intubation follow if needed. Pregnancy-specific points include early continuous fetal monitoring once viable, left lateral position to reduce aortocaval compression, and a low threshold for tertiary transfer. A normal or rising PaCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic indicates fatigue and impending respiratory failure - not improvement - and is an indication for urgent intensivist involvement. Document and continue preventer therapy during admission; discharge planning includes inhaler technique review and written action plan.
key_points: A normalising PaCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic is a red flag for tiring, not improvement
Position left lateral from 20 weeks to relieve aortocaval compression
Continuous CTG once viable; involve obstetrics and ICU early
Document discussion about steroids for fetal lung maturation if preterm delivery considered
explanation.pearls: Acute severe asthma in pregnancy is treated identically to non-pregnant adults: oxygen for SpO2 above 94%, back-to-back salbutamol with ipratropium, early systemic prednisolone or hydrocortisone, then IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes if not improving. A 'normal' PaCO2 in a tachypnoeic asthmatic signals fatigue, not improvement (National Asthma Council).

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - acute severe asthma

options.rationale: Oral montelukast loading is wrong because LTRAs have no acute bronchodilator effect and onset is hours to days; they are chronic add-on agents, not rescue therapy. Would be correct only as part of chronic step-up after discharge, not in acute severe asthma (National Asthma Council Australia).

IV aminophylline is wrong because of its narrow therapeutic window, arrhythmogenic risk and lack of mortality benefit over magnesium; current Australian practice reserves it for refractory cases after IV magnesium has failed. Would be correct only when IV magnesium has been given and the patient is still deteriorating in ICU, not as the next step (Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - acute severe asthma

options.rationale: IM adrenaline is wrong because it is anaphylaxis therapy, and in pregnancy uteroplacental vasoconstriction is a specific concern; the diagnosis here is severe asthma, not anaphylaxis. Would be correct only if anaphylaxis were the actual mechanism (ASCIA; National Asthma Council Australia).

Emergency caesarean is wrong because delivery is not a treatment for maternal asthma and the fetus is currently reassured; surgery and intubation would worsen bronchospasm. Would be correct only if maternal arrest were imminent or peri-mortem caesarean criteria were met, not at this stage (RANZCOG; Royal Women's Hospital).

Severe acute asthma not responding to back-to-back bronchodilators and IV corticosteroid warrants IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes; this is recommended in Australian asthma-in-pregnancy guidance and a normalising PaCO2 with rising lactate signals impending respiratory failure (Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory; National Asthma Council Australia).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory - acute severe asthma

explanation.summary: Women with treated hypothyroidism should empirically increase their levothyroxine by about 20-30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed, before booking bloods are back, because thyroid binding globulin rises rapidly under oestrogen stimulation. Target TSH is <2.5 mIU/L in the first trimester (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
key_points: Practical method: take two extra tablets per week or move up to next available strength
Recheck TSH 4 weeks after dose change and every trimester
Maintain iodine 150 micrograms daily across all pregnant women
Avoid liothyronine in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Empirical dose-up first, bloods later. Waiting for the lab risks first-trimester hypothyroxinaemia.

sources.label: NHMRC: Iodine supplementation in pregnancy and lactation
Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Maintaining 100 mcg is wrong because thyroid hormone requirements rise 25-50% in the first trimester driven by hCG-stimulated TBG; delay risks maternal hypothyroidism with neurodevelopmental impact on the fetus, and the Endocrine Society recommends an empirical bump on confirmation of pregnancy. Would be correct only if pre-pregnancy TSH was already optimised at the lower end and a recheck-only strategy was agreed, which is not standard (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Stopping iodine is wrong because NHMRC recommends 150 mcg iodine for all Australian pregnant and lactating women regardless of thyroxine status; iodine supports placental and fetal thyroid synthesis, while levothyroxine replaces maternal hormone. Would never be correct in an Australian antenatal context (NHMRC).
source_refs: NHMRC: Iodine supplementation in pregnancy and lactation

options.rationale: Doubling to 200 mcg is wrong because the evidence-based empirical increment is 20-30% (typically two extra tablets per week); doubling risks iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis with atrial fibrillation and growth restriction. Would be correct only in newly diagnosed overt hypothyroidism with very high TSH at booking, not for stable preconception disease (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Switching to liothyronine is wrong because T3 crosses the placenta poorly and the fetus depends on maternal T4 for cerebral development; combination or T3-only therapy is explicitly discouraged in pregnancy. Would be correct only in extremely rare specialist scenarios, never in routine antenatal care (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).

Australian and international guidance recommends a 20-30% empirical dose increase on confirmation of pregnancy in known hypothyroid women, typically achieved by taking two extra tablets per week or rounding up to the next strength, with TSH rechecked 4 weeks later (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

explanation.summary: First-trimester carbimazole exposure causes a recognisable embryopathy. Australian practice is to use propylthiouracil through organogenesis (typically up to about 16 weeks) and then switch back to carbimazole because of cumulative PTU hepatotoxicity. TRAb should be measured in the third trimester to predict neonatal thyroid disease (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
key_points: Carbimazole embryopathy: aplasia cutis, choanal/oesophageal atresia, omphalocele
PTU rare but serious hepatotoxicity - hence switch back at ~16 weeks
Target free T4 at the upper limit of the trimester-specific reference range
Check TRAb in the third trimester; high titres warn of fetal/neonatal Graves
explanation.pearls: First trimester = PTU. Second trimester onward = carbimazole. Always raise TRAb in the third trimester.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Continuing carbimazole in the first trimester is wrong because it is associated with embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal and oesophageal atresia, omphalocoele) during organogenesis; the standard approach is PTU until 16 weeks then switch back. Would be correct only after the first trimester is complete, not from 6 weeks (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Radioactive iodine ablation is wrong because it is an absolute contraindication in pregnancy due to fetal thyroid ablation and teratogenic radiation exposure. Would be correct only postpartum after cessation of breastfeeding with appropriate isolation precautions (Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Stopping all antithyroid drug is wrong because biochemically active Graves disease with raised TRAb risks maternal thyroid storm, fetal goitre and fetal tachycardia; pregnancy itself is not remission. Would be correct only if she were in true biochemical remission with negative TRAb and stable off therapy preconception (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Australian and international guidance is to use propylthiouracil during the first trimester to avoid carbimazole embryopathy, then switch back to carbimazole from around 16 weeks to reduce ongoing risk of PTU hepatotoxicity (RANZCOG; Endocrine Society; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Thyroid disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Adding propranolol while continuing carbimazole is wrong because beta blockade addresses adrenergic symptoms (which she does not have) without removing the teratogenic exposure during organogenesis. Would be appropriate as a short-term adjunct in symptomatic thyrotoxicosis or thyroid storm, not as a strategy to neutralise carbimazole risk (Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies cross the placenta and may cause neonatal lupus syndromes, with congenital heart block as the most feared. Serial fetal echocardiography between 16 and 28 weeks is the surveillance standard. Hydroxychloroquine should be continued throughout pregnancy (RANZCOG; EULAR).
key_points: Risk of congenital heart block ~2% in anti-Ro positive first pregnancies, ~15-20% recurrence
Hydroxychloroquine reduces recurrence of neonatal lupus and SLE flares
Aspirin 100-150 mg daily from before 16 weeks for pre-eclampsia prophylaxis in SLE
Plan delivery and neonatology input if any conduction abnormality detected
explanation.pearls: Anti-Ro changes the fetal cardiology pathway, not the rheumatology drug list. Keep the hydroxychloroquine.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Vic: SLE in pregnancy
EULAR recommendations: management of family planning and pregnancy in SLE

options.rationale: Anti-Ro and anti-La cross the placenta and can cause neonatal lupus, of which congenital complete heart block is the most serious feature. Australian and EULAR guidance is to perform serial fetal echocardiography (typically weekly to fortnightly) between 16 and 26-28 weeks in anti-Ro positive women (RANZCOG; Royal Women's Hospital Vic; EULAR SLE pregnancy guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Vic: SLE in pregnancy
EULAR recommendations: management of family planning and pregnancy in SLE

options.rationale: Stopping hydroxychloroquine is wrong because HCQ is the one drug we deliberately keep going through pregnancy in SLE: it reduces flares, reduces recurrence of congenital heart block in subsequent pregnancies, and may reduce pre-eclampsia. Would be correct only if she developed retinopathy or another HCQ-specific adverse effect, not because of the pregnancy itself (EULAR SLE pregnancy guidelines; RANZCOG).
source_refs: EULAR recommendations: management of family planning and pregnancy in SLE
RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Empirical IVIG is wrong because trials have failed to show that IVIG prevents first-occurrence congenital heart block; the established strategy is fetal echo surveillance with prompt intervention if first-degree block emerges. Would be considered only as research therapy or in selected high-risk recurrence cases at specialist discretion, not as routine primary prevention (EULAR).
source_refs: EULAR recommendations: management of family planning and pregnancy in SLE

options.rationale: Stopping aspirin is wrong because SLE carries a high pre-eclampsia risk and SOMANZ recommends low-dose aspirin from before 16 weeks for this exact indication; anti-Ro status does not change bleeding risk meaningfully. Would be correct only with active bleeding or genuine aspirin allergy (SOMANZ; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Empirical LMWH is wrong because thromboprophylaxis is reserved for antiphospholipid syndrome, prior VTE or otherwise high VTE risk; SLE alone with negative APL antibodies does not meet RCOG thromboprophylaxis criteria. Would be correct in coexisting APS, not in isolated SLE (RCOG; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Connective tissue disease in pregnancy

explanation.summary: In women with sustained HIV viral suppression (<50 copies/mL) at 36 weeks on combination ART, vaginal birth is recommended unless an obstetric reason exists for caesarean. Vertical transmission rates with suppressed viraemia are well under 1% and equivalent across delivery modes (ASHM; BHIVA).
key_points: Check viral load at 36 weeks to plan mode of delivery
Detectable VL >=50 copies/mL near term: elective caesarean at 38-39 weeks
VL >=400 copies/mL or unknown: intrapartum IV zidovudine plus elective caesarean
Continue ART through labour; avoid invasive fetal monitoring (FSE) and prolonged ROM
explanation.pearls: Suppressed viral load is the key determinant. Vaginal birth is not contraindicated by HIV status alone.

options.rationale: Routine elective caesarean is wrong because the ASHM/BHIVA threshold for offering caesarean is viral load at or above 50 copies/mL (or unknown) near term; with sustained suppression, vaginal birth has equivalent transmission risk and lower maternal morbidity. Would be correct only with detectable or undocumented viral load close to delivery (ASHM; BHIVA).

Australian and international guidance is that elective caesarean is not required if the viral load is suppressed (<50 copies/mL) near term; vaginal birth has similar or lower morbidity with comparable vertical transmission risk on suppressive ART (ASHM; RANZCOG; BHIVA pregnancy guidelines).

Stopping ART is wrong because viral rebound after cessation is rapid and would directly increase vertical transmission risk in late pregnancy and labour; ART is not optional once viral load is suppressed. Would never be correct in pregnancy (ASHM).

Elective caesarean plus IV zidovudine is wrong because intrapartum IV zidovudine is reserved for viral load at or above 400 copies/mL or unknown status; layering caesarean plus IV zidovudine on a virologically suppressed woman adds morbidity without benefit. Would be correct only if her viral load were not suppressed (BHIVA).

Induction at 37 weeks is wrong because there is no evidence early induction reduces vertical transmission in suppressed women; obstetric indications drive timing of birth, and iatrogenic prematurity carries neonatal morbidity. Would be correct only for standard obstetric reasons, not as HIV-specific intervention (ASHM; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Australian practice for infants born to HIV-positive mothers includes exclusive formula feeding plus a short course of infant zidovudine when the mother is virologically suppressed at term. The combination drives vertical transmission rates to well under 1% (ASHM; RANZCOG).
key_points: Formula provides nutritional equivalence in a high resource setting
Low risk infant prophylaxis: zidovudine 2-4 weeks
High risk: triple ART (e.g. zidovudine + lamivudine + nevirapine) for 6 weeks plus specialist input
Test infant with HIV NAT at birth, 6 weeks and 12 weeks; HIV antibody at 18 months
explanation.pearls: Formula + a short zidovudine course is the default. Breastfeeding is not recommended in Australia even with suppression.

options.rationale: Triple infant ART is wrong because high-risk neonatal regimens (zidovudine plus lamivudine plus nevirapine or raltegravir) are reserved for infants of mothers with detectable VL near term, late diagnosis or seroconversion in pregnancy; this infant is low risk. Would be correct only if maternal viral load were not suppressed at delivery (BHIVA).

Exclusive breastfeeding is wrong because Australian ASHM guidance recommends formula feeding in high resource settings: residual transmission risk is not zero even on ART, and formula is safe and accessible. Would be the WHO recommendation in resource-limited settings where replacement feeding is not AFASS, not in Australia (ASHM; WHO).

In high resource settings such as Australia, exclusive formula feeding is recommended because formula is safe, accessible and eliminates postnatal transmission risk; an infant born to a virologically suppressed mother receives 2-4 weeks of oral zidovudine as low-risk infant prophylaxis (ASHM; RANZCOG; BHIVA).

Mixed feeding is wrong because it is the highest-risk feeding pattern: HIV exposure from breast milk combined with mucosal disruption from formula. Would never be correct for HIV-exposed infants (WHO; ASHM).

No infant prophylaxis is wrong because all HIV-exposed infants receive at least short-course zidovudine even with suppressed maternal VL to cover residual transmission risk. Would be correct only if HIV status had been completely excluded antenatally, not after confirmed maternal HIV (ASHM; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Women with HBV DNA above 200,000 IU/mL should commence tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg daily from about 28 weeks to reduce residual vertical transmission. The infant additionally receives HBIG and the hepatitis B vaccine birth dose within 12 hours of birth, with completion of the vaccine schedule (ASHM; GESA; Australian Immunisation Handbook).
key_points: Treatment threshold for antiviral in pregnancy: HBV DNA > 200,000 IU/mL or > 5.3 log10
Tenofovir disoproxil is preferred over entecavir in pregnancy
Infant receives HBIG + first vaccine dose within 12 hours of birth in Australia
Breastfeeding is safe once infant has received immunoprophylaxis
explanation.pearls: High HBV DNA in pregnancy means tenofovir for the mother and HBIG plus birth-dose vaccine for the baby.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Chronic hepatitis B recommendations
EASL Clinical Practice Guideline: Hepatitis B

options.rationale: Maternal HBIG is wrong because passive immunoglobulin given to the mother does not reduce viral load and HBIG has no role in maternal antenatal prevention; HBIG belongs to the infant within 12 hours of birth. Would be correct only for non-immune individuals after high-risk exposure, not as antenatal prophylaxis (Australian Immunisation Handbook).

Entecavir is wrong because Australian guidance prefers tenofovir disoproxil in pregnancy due to a much larger safety dataset; entecavir is Pregnancy Category B3 with limited human data. Would be correct only in tenofovir intolerance or resistance, not first-line (ASHM; GESA).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Chronic hepatitis B recommendations

options.rationale: Australian and international guidance recommends maternal tenofovir disoproxil from approximately 28 weeks gestation for women with HBV DNA above 200,000 IU/mL (or HBeAg positive with high VL) because this substantially reduces the residual vertical transmission risk that remains despite infant immunoprophylaxis (ASHM; Gastroenterological Society of Australia; AASLD/EASL).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Chronic hepatitis B recommendations
EASL Clinical Practice Guideline: Hepatitis B

options.rationale: Elective caesarean is wrong because mode of delivery does not change HBV transmission when infant HBIG plus birth-dose vaccine are given; caesarean does not act as a viral barrier for HBV the way it can for HIV. Would be appropriate only for standard obstetric indications (ASHM; RANZCOG).

Advising against breastfeeding is wrong because HBIG plus birth-dose vaccine makes breastfeeding safe even with high maternal DNA; the Australian Immunisation Handbook explicitly endorses breastfeeding in HBV-positive women. Would be correct only with cracked nipples and uncovered infant (Australian Immunisation Handbook; ASHM).

explanation.summary: Direct-acting antivirals for hepatitis C are deferred until after pregnancy in current Australian practice. Vertical transmission is approximately 5-6% and is not reduced by elective caesarean; breastfeeding is safe except when nipples are cracked or bleeding (ASHM; GESA).
key_points: Treat HCV postpartum, ideally before any subsequent pregnancy
No role for routine elective caesarean section for HCV alone
Infant follow-up: HCV PCR at 2 and 6 months or antibody from 18 months
Higher transmission with HIV co-infection - test for both at booking
explanation.pearls: HCV currently waits. The biggest risk factor for vertical transmission you can act on antenatally is HIV co-infection.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Hepatitis C consensus statement

options.rationale: Direct-acting antivirals are not yet routinely recommended in pregnancy in Australia outside trial settings; treatment is deferred to postpartum. Breastfeeding is encouraged in HCV-positive women unless nipples are cracked or bleeding (ASHM; GESA; Australian Breastfeeding Association).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Hepatitis C consensus statement

options.rationale: Starting DAA at 12 weeks is wrong because sofosbuvir/velpatasvir is not yet recommended outside research protocols in Australian pregnancy due to limited pharmacokinetic and safety data; deferring to postpartum is standard. Would be correct only within a registered trial, not as routine care (ASHM; GESA).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): Hepatitis C consensus statement

options.rationale: Elective caesarean is wrong because HCV vertical transmission is not reduced by caesarean delivery; intrapartum factors (prolonged ROM, fetal scalp electrodes) matter more than mode of birth. Would be appropriate only for standard obstetric indications (ASHM; RANZCOG).

Advising against breastfeeding is wrong because HCV is not transmitted through intact lactation; ASHM and ABA explicitly recommend breastfeeding, pausing feeding from a side with cracked or bleeding nipples. Would be correct only with active nipple trauma on the involved side (ASHM; Australian Breastfeeding Association).

Neonatal anti-HCV at 48 hours is wrong because passively acquired maternal antibody persists in the infant for up to 18 months, making early antibody testing uninformative; HCV PCR at 2 and 6 months or antibody after 18 months is the recommended schedule. Would be correct only for documenting transient maternal antibody, not for diagnosing infant infection (ASHM).

explanation.summary: In ITP in late pregnancy the team should target platelets above 50 x10^9/L for vaginal birth, above 70-80 x10^9/L for epidural and above 80 x10^9/L for caesarean section. Oral prednisolone is first line with IVIG used for steroid failure or rapid response need (RANZCOG; ASH 2019; KEMH).
key_points: First line: oral prednisolone 20-30 mg daily aiming for response in 1-2 weeks
Second line: IVIG 1 g/kg for faster onset close to delivery
Avoid scalp electrodes, fetal blood sampling, vacuum and difficult forceps in neonates at risk of thrombocytopenia
Check neonatal platelet count - mother's count does not predict baby's
explanation.pearls: Memorise 50/80: 50 for vaginal birth, 80 for epidural/caesarean. Prednisolone first, IVIG if you are running out of time.

options.rationale: Doing nothing is wrong because >50 x10^9/L is the threshold for vaginal birth without instrumentation, not for neuraxial anaesthesia, which requires >70-80 x10^9/L per ASH 2019 and Australian practice. Would be correct only if she planned vaginal birth without epidural and no operative interventions (ASH 2019; KEMH).

Australian and international guidance aims for platelets above 80 x10^9/L for neuraxial anaesthesia and above 50 x10^9/L for vaginal delivery in ITP; first-line therapy is oral prednisolone, escalating to IVIG if response is inadequate or delivery is imminent (RANZCOG; ASH ITP guideline; KEMH).

Pre-emptive platelet transfusion is wrong because platelet survival is short in ITP due to antibody-mediated destruction, so transfusion does not provide durable counts; it is reserved for active bleeding or imminent surgery. Would be correct only at the time of caesarean or with bleeding, not as antenatal optimisation (ASH 2019).

Eltrombopag is wrong because TPO receptor agonists are second/third-line in ITP and have limited pregnancy safety data; first-line in pregnancy is prednisolone with IVIG as second-line. Would be correct only in refractory ITP after corticosteroids and IVIG have failed (Therapeutic Guidelines; ASH 2019).

Discussing splenectomy is wrong because splenectomy does not address delivery-time platelet optimisation in the current pregnancy; it is also factually misleading - splenectomy remains an option for selected refractory chronic ITP. Would be a postpartum discussion only after standard therapies fail (ASH 2019).

explanation.summary: Most IBD medications including 5-ASAs, thiopurines and anti-TNF biologics are continued in pregnancy because relapse worsens maternal and fetal outcomes more than the drug. Methotrexate and mycophenolate are absolutely contraindicated and must be stopped well in advance of conception (GESA; ECCO).
key_points: Azathioprine: continue; check TPMT once; routine monitoring of bloods
Anti-TNF (infliximab, adalimumab): continue; consider holding final dose if active disease is well controlled to limit transplacental transfer late in pregnancy
Avoid live vaccines in the infant for 6 months after intrauterine biologic exposure (e.g. rotavirus, BCG)
Methotrexate teratogenicity: aim 3-6 months washout in both partners
explanation.pearls: The general rule: most IBD drugs continue. The exceptions are methotrexate and mycophenolate, both teratogenic.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): IBD in pregnancy

options.rationale: Stopping azathioprine and switching to budesonide is wrong because thiopurines maintain remission whereas budesonide is induction therapy with limited long-term maintenance efficacy; flares in pregnancy harm the fetus more than the drug. Would be correct only if she were intolerant of azathioprine and seeking short-term flare control, not as preconception maintenance (GESA; ECCO).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): IBD in pregnancy

options.rationale: Thiopurines and most anti-TNF agents are continued through pregnancy because flare risk outweighs medication risk and both are considered low risk; methotrexate is teratogenic and must be stopped for 3-6 months preconception in both partners (GESA; ECCO IBD pregnancy consensus; Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): IBD in pregnancy

options.rationale: Stopping adalimumab at conception is wrong because anti-TNF agents are continued at least through to 24-30 weeks (often to delivery, depending on the specific biologic) because flare risk outweighs theoretical immunogenicity. Would be correct only if she were in deep remission with biomarker confirmation and accepted flare risk, and even then most guidelines do not endorse cessation (GESA; ECCO).
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia (GESA): IBD in pregnancy

options.rationale: Restarting methotrexate is wrong because methotrexate is teratogenic (folate antagonism, NTDs, craniofacial anomalies) and is contraindicated through pregnancy and the 3-6 month preconception window for both partners. Would never be correct during conception attempts or pregnancy (Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

Switching to mycophenolate is wrong because MMF is teratogenic (EMFO syndrome - cleft lip/palate, microtia, cardiac, oesophageal) and explicitly contraindicated in pregnancy; pregnancy prevention is required during MMF use. Would be correct only outside pregnancy planning, never as preconception maintenance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

explanation.summary: Preconception care in pre-existing type 1 diabetes targets HbA1c below 6.5% where safely achievable, folic acid 5 mg daily, retinal and renal review, and review of all non-insulin medications. Achieving these targets substantially reduces congenital anomaly and miscarriage rates (ADIPS; RANZCOG).
key_points: Target HbA1c <6.5% (or <7.0% if hypoglycaemia limits)
Folic acid 5 mg daily for diabetes is one of the standard 5 mg indications
Stop teratogenic agents preconception: ACE-i/ARB, statin, SGLT2i
Retinal screening before pregnancy and at least once per trimester
explanation.pearls: T1DM preconception target HbA1c is <6.5% and folate is 5 mg, not 400 micrograms.

sources.label: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes management in pregnancy

options.rationale: Substituting metformin for insulin is wrong because metformin does not provide adequate glycaemic control in type 1 diabetes and does not address the absolute insulin deficiency; pre-existing T1DM requires intensive insulin therapy. Would be appropriate only as an adjunct in type 2 diabetes or PCOS, not as substitution in T1DM (ADIPS).

Reassuring about HbA1c 8.4% is wrong because this level corresponds to substantially elevated rates of major congenital anomaly, miscarriage and stillbirth; ADIPS targets <6.5% (or <7.0% if hypoglycaemia limits) before conception attempts. Would be correct only if no further optimisation were achievable and she had been counselled on residual risk, which is not the case here (ADIPS).

ADIPS, RANZCOG and the Australian Diabetes Society recommend HbA1c below 6.5% (48 mmol/mol) preconception when achievable without significant hypoglycaemia, plus folic acid 5 mg daily for at least 1-3 months before conception in pre-existing diabetes (ADIPS; RANZCOG; Australian Diabetes Society pre-existing diabetes guideline).
source_refs: Australian Diabetes Society: Diabetes management in pregnancy

options.rationale: Advising against pregnancy is wrong because background retinopathy is not a contraindication; pregnancy is permitted with optimised glycaemia and antenatal ophthalmology surveillance every trimester.
