Would be correct only for severe untreated proliferative retinopathy or advanced cardiac/renal complications (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

SGLT2 inhibitors are wrong because they precipitate euglycaemic DKA in T1DM, are contraindicated in pregnancy and have no role in preconception glycaemic intensification. Would never be correct in T1DM preconception planning (Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Intrapartum care of T1DM uses a variable rate IV insulin infusion with hourly capillary glucose monitoring, targeting 4-7 mmol/L to reduce neonatal hypoglycaemia. After delivery of the placenta insulin requirements fall sharply and infusion rates must be halved or stopped to avoid maternal hypoglycaemia (ADIPS; RANZCOG).
key_points: Target intrapartum CBG 4-7 mmol/L
Hourly CBG, ketone check if CBG >12 or symptoms
Halve infusion or revert to subcut basal/bolus after placenta delivered
Neonatal CBG checks per local pathway (e.g. before second feed, then 3-4 hourly)
explanation.pearls: 4 to 7 in labour, halve the insulin after the placenta.

options.rationale: Continuing the pump with 4-hourly checks is wrong because intrapartum T1DM needs hourly capillary glucose to stay in the narrow 4-7 mmol/L band; pumps may continue only with strict hourly monitoring and a written failure protocol. Would be correct only with hourly testing and explicit pump-continuation protocol, not 4-hourly (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

Australian and international guidance is to target intrapartum capillary glucose 4-7 mmol/L, monitored hourly, using a variable rate intravenous insulin infusion with dextrose where needed; this reduces neonatal hypoglycaemia (ADIPS; RANZCOG; NICE Diabetes in Pregnancy).
Stopping all insulin is wrong because basal insulin withdrawal in T1DM precipitates DKA within hours. Would never be correct in T1DM intrapartum (Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

Higher targets are wrong because intrapartum maternal hyperglycaemia drives fetal hyperinsulinism and neonatal hypoglycaemia after cord clamp; 4-7 mmol/L is the established target. Would be correct only as a transient ceiling during hypoglycaemia recovery, not as a deliberate target (ADIPS).

Single long-acting glargine bolus is wrong because long-acting analogues are not titratable and cannot match the rapid changes in insulin requirement during labour and immediately postpartum; variable rate IV insulin is preferred. Would be correct only as an outpatient regimen, not in active labour (ADIPS).

explanation.summary: Anticoagulation in mechanical heart valves in pregnancy balances maternal valve thrombosis (best minimised with warfarin) and fetal embryopathy/bleeding (worse with warfarin). A common sequenced strategy is LMWH in the first trimester (especially if warfarin dose >5 mg), warfarin in mid-pregnancy, and LMWH again from 36 weeks for safe peridelivery management (ESC 2018; RANZCOG).
key_points: Daily warfarin dose <5 mg: lower embryopathy risk so warfarin throughout is more acceptable
Therapeutic LMWH requires anti-Xa monitoring (peak 4 hours post dose)
Plan delivery on LMWH; convert to IV unfractionated heparin 36 hours before and stop 4-6 hours before neuraxial
Restart anticoagulation 6-12 hours after vaginal birth or 12-24 hours after caesarean if no bleeding
explanation.pearls: Mechanical valves are anticoagulation jigsaws: never stop entirely, plan the trimester swaps in advance.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - anticoagulation in pregnancy
ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: LMWH throughout is wrong because mechanical mitral valve thrombosis rates are higher on LMWH-only regimens than on warfarin-containing strategies despite anti-Xa monitoring; ESC reserves this approach for women who decline warfarin after structured counselling. Would be correct only as a patient-preference option after counselling, not as default (ESC 2018).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Warfarin throughout is wrong because it carries warfarin embryopathy risk between 6 and 12 weeks (nasal hypoplasia, chondrodysplasia punctata) and fetal intracranial haemorrhage at delivery; pure-warfarin strategy is acceptable only when daily warfarin dose is low (<5 mg) with explicit counselling. Would be correct only when warfarin dose is <5 mg/day and the woman accepts fetal risk after counselling, not as default for high-dose warfarin requirements (ESC 2018).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: ESC and RANZCOG guidance recommend dose-adjusted LMWH (with anti-Xa monitoring) in the first trimester to avoid warfarin embryopathy when the daily warfarin dose is moderate to high, warfarin in the second and early third trimester for stable INR and lowest thrombotic risk on the valve, then LMWH again from 36 weeks to allow safe neuraxial anaesthesia and delivery (ESC 2018 Cardiovascular Disease in Pregnancy; RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular - anticoagulation in pregnancy

options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is wrong because DOACs are contraindicated in pregnancy and ineffective at preventing mechanical valve thrombosis (RE-ALIGN trial showed harm with dabigatran). Would never be correct in mechanical valves, pregnant or not (ESC 2018; AMH).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

options.rationale: Stopping anticoagulation in the first trimester is wrong because mechanical mitral valves have very high thrombotic risk and require uninterrupted anticoagulation; periods without anticoagulant cause valve thrombosis and maternal death. (ESC 2018).
source_refs: ESC Guideline 2018: Cardiovascular disease in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE risk assessment uses cumulative risk factors. Emergency caesarean alone earns prophylaxis for at least 10 days; combined with BMI >=30, age >=35 and parity >=3 the indication is robust. Standard agent is prophylactic-dose LMWH starting 6-12 hours after delivery if no bleeding (RCOG; RANZCOG; KEMH).
key_points: Score in late pregnancy and again postnatally; rescore if status changes
Standard prophylactic enoxaparin dose 40 mg daily for weight 50-90 kg; weight-band adjust outside this range
Continue 10 days postpartum at minimum; 6 weeks if previous VTE, persistent risk factors or thrombophilia
LMWH compatible with breastfeeding
explanation.pearls: Emergency caesarean plus any second risk factor almost always equals 10 days of enoxaparin.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium
KEMH: VTE prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium
RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Apixaban is wrong because DOACs are not recommended for postpartum thromboprophylaxis in Australia, partly due to limited lactation data and partly because LMWH has stronger evidence; non-pregnant orthopaedic practice does not transfer. Would be correct only outside the postpartum/breastfeeding context (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Mechanical prophylaxis alone is wrong because emergency caesarean plus multiple risk factors crosses the threshold for pharmacological prophylaxis; stockings are an adjunct, not a substitute. Would be correct only when LMWH is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding) (RCOG Green-top 37a).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Therapeutic-dose LMWH is wrong because therapeutic dosing is for confirmed VTE or very-high-risk prophylaxis (recent VTE, APS with prior thrombosis); the bleeding risk is unjustified for prophylactic indications. Would be correct only if she had had a recent VTE or thrombotic APS (RCOG Green-top 37a).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Emergency caesarean plus age >=35 plus BMI >=30 plus parity >=3 each adds points on Australian and RCOG postnatal VTE risk scoring; this combination indicates pharmacological prophylaxis for at least 10 days postpartum. Enoxaparin 40 mg daily is appropriate at her weight (RCOG Green-top 37a; RANZCOG; KEMH).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium
RANZCOG: Venous thromboembolism in pregnancy and the puerperium
KEMH: VTE prophylaxis in pregnancy and the puerperium

options.rationale: Aspirin is wrong because aspirin lacks evidence for postnatal VTE prevention in this risk profile and is not recommended by RCOG Green-top 37a; LMWH is the agent of choice. Would be correct only as pre-eclampsia prophylaxis, not VTE (RCOG Green-top 37a).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top 37a: Thrombosis and embolism during pregnancy and the puerperium

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is suggested by pruritus without rash, deranged transaminases and a raised total bile acid; bile acid level guides delivery timing. UDCA improves maternal pruritus and is standard of care. Delivery at 37-38+6 weeks is appropriate for bile acids 40-99 micromol/L; consider earlier delivery for >=100 micromol/L (RANZCOG; RCOG ICP 2022).
key_points: Stillbirth risk relates predominantly to peak bile acid concentration
UDCA 10-15 mg/kg/day in divided doses, typically 500 mg BD
Bile acids 40-99 micromol/L: deliver 37-38+6 weeks; >=100 micromol/L: consider 35-36 weeks
ICP usually resolves within days of delivery; consider recurrence in future pregnancies
explanation.pearls: UDCA helps the itch and bile acid level drives the calendar.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Vic: Obstetric cholestasis
RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

options.rationale: Ursodeoxycholic acid relieves maternal symptoms and is the recommended pharmacological treatment for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. For moderate disease (bile acids 40-99 micromol/L) Australian and RCOG guidance recommends planning delivery at 37-38+6 weeks to reduce stillbirth risk (RANZCOG; RCOG Green-top 43 ICP 2022; Royal Women's Hospital Vic).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022
Royal Women's Hospital Vic: Obstetric cholestasis

options.rationale: Emollients alone with 39-40 week delivery is wrong because emollients are purely symptomatic and do not address the underlying cholestasis; the stillbirth curve at bile acids 56 micromol/L rises substantially after 38 weeks, making term expectancy unsafe. Would be correct only for mild ICP (bile acids <40 micromol/L) where 39-40 week delivery is acceptable (RCOG ICP 2022).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

options.rationale: Colestyramine plus immediate delivery is wrong because colestyramine has fallen out of first-line use due to fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption (including vitamin K) and immediate delivery at 35+2 is reserved for severe disease at bile acids >=100 micromol/L. Would be correct only at severe-disease thresholds, not at 56 micromol/L (RCOG ICP 2022; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

options.rationale: Dexamethasone is wrong because corticosteroids are not effective primary treatment for ICP; UDCA is the established pharmacological agent. Would be correct only for antenatal lung maturation if early preterm delivery were planned, not as ICP therapy (RCOG ICP 2022).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

options.rationale: Antihistamines plus 40-week expectancy is wrong because chlorphenamine only modestly improves itch and does not change bile acid kinetics or stillbirth risk; delivery to 40 weeks at this bile acid level exceeds the safety window. Would be correct only for benign pruritus of pregnancy without raised bile acids (RCOG ICP 2022).
source_refs: RCOG Green-top: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy 2022

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a hepatic synthetic failure syndrome of the third trimester. Distinguishing features versus HELLP include hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, encephalopathy and a coagulopathy that exceeds what platelet count alone would explain. Definitive treatment for both is prompt delivery with maternal stabilisation (Swansea criteria; RANZCOG).
key_points: Swansea criteria: vomiting, abdominal pain, polydipsia/polyuria, encephalopathy, bilirubin, hypoglycaemia, urate, leucocytosis, ascites/bright liver, transaminitis, ammonia, AKI, coagulopathy, microvesicular steatosis (>=6 of 14)
Maternal stabilisation focuses on glucose, coagulopathy reversal and timely delivery
Consider LCHAD deficiency screening in the infant after maternal AFLP
Multidisciplinary management with hepatology and intensive care
explanation.pearls: Hypoglycaemia and hyperammonaemia in a third-trimester woman = think AFLP, not HELLP.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Vic: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Swansea criteria (Knight et al.) for acute fatty liver of pregnancy

options.rationale: Hypertension and proteinuria is wrong because it is more characteristic of HELLP (which sits on the pre-eclampsia spectrum) than AFLP, where blood pressure is often only modestly elevated and proteinuria less prominent. Would point to HELLP/pre-eclampsia rather than AFLP (RANZCOG).

RUQ pain with transaminases >500 is wrong because both AFLP and HELLP can present with this picture; it is shared rather than discriminating. Would be neutral, not diagnostic, between the two (Swansea criteria).
source_refs: Swansea criteria (Knight et al.) for acute fatty liver of pregnancy

options.rationale: Platelets <100 is wrong because it is part of HELLP criteria and can occur in AFLP from synthetic failure too; in AFLP the platelet drop is usually modest relative to the coagulopathy. It is a HELLP criterion rather than a feature that separates AFLP from HELLP (RANZCOG).

Hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia and a coagulopathy (low fibrinogen, raised INR) that is disproportionate to the relatively modest thrombocytopenia are highly suggestive of acute fatty liver of pregnancy, reflecting hepatic synthetic failure rather than microangiopathic haemolysis (Swansea criteria; RANZCOG; Royal Women's Hospital Vic).
source_refs: Swansea criteria (Knight et al.) for acute fatty liver of pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Vic: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

options.rationale: Hyperuricaemia is wrong because raised urate is a classic pre-eclampsia/HELLP marker (placental ischaemia, reduced renal clearance) and is not specific to AFLP. Would point to HELLP/pre-eclampsia (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: TTTS complicates around 10 to 15 percent of MCDA pregnancies and is diagnosed by discordant amniotic fluid (DVP under 2 and over 8 cm) before 20 weeks. Fetoscopic laser ablation of placental anastomoses is first-line.
key_points: Fortnightly TVS and US from 16 weeks for MCDA (RANZCOG)
Quintero staging: I fluid only; II absent bladder donor; III abnormal Dopplers; IV hydrops; V demise
Laser ablation reduces perinatal death and neurological injury vs amnioreduction
explanation.pearls: DVP, not AFI, is the standard discordance measure in twins.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy
NICE NG137: Twin and triplet pregnancy

options.rationale: She has stage I/II TTTS (Quintero stage II given absent donor bladder, with oligohydramnios <2 cm vs polyhydramnios >8 cm; normal Dopplers excluding stage III; no hydrops). Fetoscopic laser ablation between 16-26 weeks gives the best dual-survival outcome and is recommended over amnioreduction (RANZCOG twins; ISUOG).

Reassurance and fortnightly surveillance is wrong because untreated Quintero stage II TTTS has high perinatal mortality. Would be correct only for Stage I with stable Dopplers under close specialist review, not Stage II (RANZCOG).

Amnioreduction is wrong because the Eurofetus and subsequent trials showed fetoscopic laser ablation gives superior dual-survival and lower neurological morbidity than amnioreduction in stage II-IV TTTS at 16-26 weeks. Would be acceptable only if laser is unavailable, the woman declines transfer, or gestation is outside the laser window (RANZCOG; ISUOG).

Antenatal corticosteroids and delivery at 19+5 is wrong because 19+5 weeks is pre-viable; delivery would result in dual neonatal loss. Would be correct only at periviable gestations after 24 weeks with stage III-IV TTTS refractory to laser (RANZCOG).

Cord occlusion of the donor is wrong because selective reduction by cord occlusion is reserved for Stage IV-V or when laser has failed/is not feasible (e.g. severe hydrops in one twin, anterior placenta with poor access); at Stage II laser is first line. Would be correct only as salvage therapy when laser is unsuitable (RANZCOG; ISUOG).

explanation.summary: sIUGR in MCDA twins is classified by UA Doppler: Type I positive EDF, Type II persistent AEDF or REDF, Type III intermittent AEDF. Type III carries a particular risk of unexpected single-twin demise.
key_points: Definition: EFW under 10th centile in one twin or inter-twin discordance over 25% (ISUOG)
MCDA Type III: large arterio-arterial anastomoses cause unpredictable shunt reversal
Plan delivery 32 to 34 weeks with corticosteroids per RANZCOG
explanation.pearls: Co-twin demise risk and neurological injury risk rise sharply in MCDA Type III sIUGR.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Type I labelling is wrong because Gratacos Type I has persistently positive UA end-diastolic flow with a favourable prognosis; intermittent absent end-diastolic flow defines Type III. Would be correct only if UA Dopplers remained continuously positive (Gratacos sIUGR classification).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Type II labelling is wrong because Type II shows persistently absent or reversed UA flow with progressive deterioration and earlier delivery (often 28-30 weeks); the intermittent pattern here is Type III. Would be correct only if AEDF or REDF were persistent across studies (Gratacos sIUGR classification).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Intermittent AEDF in the smaller MCDA twin defines Type III, which carries unpredictable risk of sudden co-twin demise from large anastomoses; close surveillance and planned preterm delivery are recommended.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Reassuring as benign discordance is wrong because EFW below the 10th centile in either twin combined with greater than 25% discordance meets the consensus definition of sIUGR; this is not physiological variation. Would be correct only if both twins were AGA with milder discordance, not here (ISUOG).

TTTS labelling is wrong because TTTS requires discordant fluid (DVP <2 cm in one and >8 cm in the other); fluid is normal in both sacs, so the pathology is sIUGR not TTTS. Would be correct only if oligohydramnios-polyhydramnios were present (RANZCOG; ISUOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Anti-D immunoglobulin prophylaxis prevents alloimmunisation that would cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in subsequent pregnancies. The Australian National Blood Authority dose schedule is 250 IU before 12 weeks for sensitising events (miscarriage, ectopic, CVS, termination), then 625 IU IM from 13 weeks onward for any sensitising event (vanishing twin, antepartum bleed, ECV, abdominal trauma, amniocentesis). Routine antenatal prophylaxis is 625 IU at 28 and 34 weeks. After birth, a Kleihauer-Betke quantifies feto-maternal haemorrhage and any volume above 4 mL warrants additional anti-D 125 IU per 1 mL FMH. Vanishing twin in a DCDA pregnancy has a generally good prognosis for the survivor; in monochorionic pregnancies, single intrauterine death triggers urgent referral for assessment of the co-twin given shared circulation and risk of co-twin death or neurological injury.
key_points: DCDA vanishing twin in T1: routine antenatal care, no specific intervention
MC vanishing twin: risk of neurological injury or co-twin demise via shared anastomoses
Anti-D only if Rh-negative per NBA guidance
explanation.pearls: In any RhD-negative woman, single first-trimester sensitising events under 12 weeks (chorionic villus sampling, ectopic, termination, vanishing twin) require 250 IU anti-D; from 13 weeks onward, the dose is 625 IU IM (NBA Anti-D Guidelines).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy
RANZCOG: Prenatal screening and diagnostic testing for genetic conditions

options.rationale: Early vanishing twin (before 14 weeks) confers minimal increased risk to the surviving co-twin. As she is now 13+0 with a sensitising event, anti-D 625 IU IM is required (NBA gives 625 IU from 13 weeks). DCDA surveillance continues 4-weekly from 24 weeks (NBA; RANZCOG).

Anti-D 250 IU is wrong because the NBA dose increases to 625 IU IM from 13+0 weeks for sensitising events; 250 IU is the pre-12-week dose. Would be correct only before 13 weeks, not at exactly 13+0 (National Blood Authority Anti-D guidelines).

Withholding anti-D until 28 weeks is wrong because sensitising events require anti-D within 72 hours regardless of negative antibody screen or upcoming routine prophylaxis; waiting risks sensitisation. Would be correct only for a non-sensitising event with no bleeding (National Blood Authority).

Surgical evacuation is wrong because vanishing twins resorb naturally and instrumentation risks loss of the surviving twin from membrane disruption or infection. Would be correct only if there were septic retained products threatening the surviving pregnancy, which is not described (RANZCOG).

Serial coagulation studies for DIC is wrong because maternal DIC risk applies to single-twin demise after viability (typically >=20 weeks) with prolonged in-utero retention; first-trimester vanishing twin does not generate the necessary thromboplastin load. Would be correct only for second/third-trimester co-twin demise (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: MCMA twins share a single amniotic sac with high cord entanglement risk. Inpatient surveillance from around 26 weeks and planned caesarean at 32+0 to 34+0 after corticosteroids is the Australian standard.
key_points: MCMA delivery: planned caesarean 32+0 to 34+0 (RANZCOG, KEMH)
Inpatient daily CTG often offered from 26 to 28 weeks
Cord entanglement risk underlies the early delivery decision
explanation.pearls: MCMA is rare (around 1 percent of MC twins) but high-risk; centralise care.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: MCMA twins are recommended to deliver by planned caesarean at 32+0 to 34+0 weeks due to risk of cord entanglement and intrauterine death rising sharply after 32 weeks (RANZCOG, KEMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: 36+0 to 36+6 is wrong because that is the MCDA window; in MCMA, cord entanglement risk rises after 32 weeks and waiting to 36 is unsafe. Would be correct for MCDA, not MCMA (RANZCOG; KEMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Vaginal birth with CTG is wrong because cord entanglement in a shared sac makes labour intrinsically high-risk regardless of presentation. Would never be correct in MCMA, even with cephalic-cephalic presentation (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Aiming for 37+0 vaginally is wrong because it stacks the worst of both errors: extending well past the MCMA safety window plus exposing twins to labour-related entanglement risk. Would never be correct in MCMA (RANZCOG; KEMH).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Immediate caesarean at 31+4 is wrong because without a deterioration trigger (abnormal CTG, sIUGR progression, TTTS), birth at 31+4 imposes prematurity morbidity that the 32-34 week window is designed to avoid. Would be correct only with evidence of fetal compromise or maternal indication (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

explanation.summary: Tocolysis aims to delay birth for 48 hours to allow corticosteroid effect and in-utero transfer. In Australia, nifedipine (off-label) is the first-line tocolytic per RANZCOG, including in women on antihypertensives, provided maternal BP is monitored closely and dosing held for hypotension. Indometacin is an alternative under 32 weeks. Atosiban (oxytocin-receptor antagonist) is used in some overseas settings but is not routinely available in Australia.
key_points: First-line tocolytic in Australia: nifedipine (RANZCOG, eTG; off-label)
Indometacin: alternative under ~32 weeks; ductal constriction and oligohydramnios above 32 weeks
Atosiban: NOT routinely available in Australia (not PBS-listed)
Beta-agonists no longer used; magnesium sulfate is for neuroprotection, not tocolysis
explanation.pearls: In Australia, when antihypertensives are co-prescribed, nifedipine is still first-line for tocolysis - the management is dose vigilance and BP monitoring, not a switch to atosiban (which is not stocked here). Tocolysis is only justified when corticosteroids or transfer will meaningfully change neonatal outcome.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
Cochrane: Magnesium for preventing preterm birth

options.rationale: Nifedipine (off-label) is the RANZCOG first-line tocolytic in Australia. Concurrent labetalol and mild aortic stenosis are cautions rather than absolute contraindications: nifedipine is given with close maternal BP monitoring and withheld if systolic <90 mmHg, with cardiology input. There is no PBS-listed parenteral alternative routinely available in Australia (RANZCOG; Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetric).

Atosiban is an oxytocin-receptor antagonist used in some European jurisdictions but is NOT routinely available in Australia (not PBS-listed and not stocked by Australian maternity services). It cannot be selected as the practical first-line tocolytic here. Nifedipine is the Australian first-line per RANZCOG (RANZCOG: Tocolysis).

Indometacin is an acceptable alternative under 32 weeks but carries fetal renal and ductal risks with prolonged use, and is reserved for cases where nifedipine is contraindicated. Nifedipine, with careful BP monitoring, remains the first-line choice (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetric).

Magnesium sulfate is ineffective as a tocolytic and is instead reserved for fetal neuroprotection at <30 weeks. Would be correct only as neuroprotection (the question separately requires this), not tocolysis (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
Cochrane: Magnesium for preventing preterm birth

options.rationale: Beta-agonists are no longer recommended in Australia for tocolysis (maternal tachycardia, pulmonary oedema, hyperglycaemia, hypokalaemia) and are particularly hazardous in maternal cardiac disease. Would never be first-line in current Australian guidance (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetric).

explanation.summary: Indometacin (a non-selective COX inhibitor) is a reasonable tocolytic before about 32 weeks where prostaglandin-driven ductal patency is less mature and the latency benefit may outweigh harms. Past 32 weeks the fetal ductus becomes increasingly sensitive to prostaglandin inhibition: constriction can produce right-heart strain and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, and reduced fetal renal blood flow drives oligohydramnios within days. RANZCOG and KEMH guidance therefore use nifedipine (off-label) as the third-trimester tocolytic of choice in Australia. Atosiban (oxytocin-receptor antagonist) is used in some European jurisdictions but is not routinely available in Australia. Tocolysis at any gestation is for buying 48 hours to complete antenatal steroids, in-utero transfer, or both - not for prolonging pregnancy indefinitely.
key_points: Indometacin upper limit ~32 weeks (RANZCOG, eTG)
Nifedipine is the Australian first-line tocolytic 32+ weeks
Fetal renal and ductal effects are dose- and duration-dependent
explanation.pearls: After 32+0 weeks, indometacin closes the fetal ductus arteriosus within 24-48 hours of starting and shrinks amniotic fluid through reduced fetal urine output; nifedipine is the preferred tocolytic in the third trimester (RANZCOG; KEMH).

options.rationale: Indometacin is generally avoided from around 32 weeks because of dose-dependent fetal ductal constriction and oligohydramnios; nifedipine is preferred at 33+1 per RANZCOG.

Pulmonary oedema is wrong because that adverse profile belongs to beta-agonists (and prolonged combination tocolysis), not indometacin; the question targets indometacin-specific harm at 33+1. Would point to salbutamol concerns instead (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetric).

Maternal hypotension is wrong because vasodilator hypotension is a calcium channel blocker (nifedipine) effect, not an indometacin effect; indometacin acts on prostaglandin synthesis. Would describe nifedipine, not indometacin (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics).

Prior preterm birth as absolute contraindication is wrong because prior preterm birth is the indication for treatment, not a contraindication; gestational age and renal/GI status are the relevant flags. Would never be a valid contraindication (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics).

Reduced steroid efficacy is wrong because there is no evidence indometacin attenuates betamethasone lung maturation effect; the late-gestation concern is fetal ductus and oligohydramnios. Would not be a recognised concern (Therapeutic Guidelines: Obstetrics).

explanation.summary: Antenatal corticosteroids reduce neonatal respiratory distress syndrome, intraventricular haemorrhage, necrotising enterocolitis and perinatal death when given to women at risk of preterm birth within 7 days at gestations between 23+0 and 34+6. The Australian standard is betamethasone 11.4 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart (or dexamethasone 12 mg IM two doses 24 hours apart). Maximum benefit is seen 24 hours after the second dose and persists for about 7 days. A single rescue dose is given when the original course was more than 7 days previously, birth is anticipated within the next 7 days, and gestation is still under 34+0. Repeated full courses are not recommended because of evidence of reduced birth weight and head circumference. Late preterm (34+0 to 36+6) steroids reduce respiratory morbidity but increase neonatal hypoglycaemia; offer with shared decision-making in selected high-risk cases. Document time of every dose contemporaneously to inform later rescue decisions.
key_points: Rescue: single dose, not a repeat full course (RANZCOG)
Eligibility: prior course >7 days ago, gestation <34+0, birth likely within 7 days
Multiple repeats associated with lower birthweight
explanation.pearls: A single rescue dose of antenatal betamethasone 11.4 mg IM is given when the original course was more than 7 days ago, birth is anticipated within the next 7 days, and gestation is under 34+0 (ACTORDS; RANZCOG).

options.rationale: RANZCOG supports a single rescue dose when the initial course was given over 7 days ago, gestation is under 34+0, and birth is anticipated within the next 7 days.

Full repeat course is wrong because Australian guidance favours a single rescue dose rather than a full repeat; multiple repeat courses are associated with reduced birth weight and head circumference. Would be correct only in some international protocols, not RANZCOG (RANZCOG).

Withholding steroids entirely is wrong because evidence (ACTORDS, MACS analyses) shows a rescue dose provides meaningful neonatal benefit when the prior course was over 7 days ago and birth is now imminent. Would be correct only if the original course were within the past 7 days (RANZCOG).

Dexamethasone 6 mg single dose is wrong because Australian dexamethasone dose is 12 mg per dose, and the preferred rescue agent is betamethasone 11.4 mg IM; the dose stated is half-strength. Would never match Australian rescue dosing (RANZCOG).
Withholding until >5 cm is wrong because steroid fetal benefit takes hours to develop; steroid timing depends on anticipated birth, not on labour progress. (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Antenatal magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is one of the largest preterm-birth interventions to reach Australian practice. RANZCOG recommends magnesium when birth is anticipated within 24 hours at less than 30 weeks gestation, with at least 4 hours of infusion ideally achieved before delivery. The protocol is a 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes followed by 1 g/hour maintenance, continued until birth or 24 hours, whichever is sooner. Maternal monitoring is hourly: respiratory rate, deep tendon reflexes, urine output, BP. Toxicity (loss of reflexes, respiratory depression, ECG changes) is reversed with 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate IV. Magnesium is not given for tocolysis or general neuroprotection beyond 30 weeks; if maternal or fetal compromise demands urgent delivery, magnesium must not delay birth.
key_points: Window: <30 weeks Australian standard; some centres <32 weeks (RANZCOG)
Loading dose 4 g IV over 20 to 30 minutes then 1 g/hour infusion
Monitor reflexes, RR, urine output, magnesium level if prolonged
explanation.pearls: IV magnesium sulfate (4 g loading over 20 minutes, then 1 g/hour maintenance) given within 4 hours of preterm birth before 30 weeks reduces cerebral palsy by about 30% (number needed to treat about 60); the protective effect is gestation-dependent (RANZCOG; PReCISE).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
Cochrane: Magnesium for neuroprotection of the preterm fetus

options.rationale: RANZCOG and SOMANZ recommend antenatal MgSO4 for neuroprotection at gestations under 30 weeks when birth is anticipated within 24 hours; ideally given at least 4 hours pre-birth.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

options.rationale: Saying MgSO4 is only for pre-eclampsia is wrong because the fetal neuroprotection role is established independently (ACTOMgSO4, Cochrane meta-analysis NNT ~50 to prevent CP at very preterm gestations). Would be correct only if neuroprotection benefit had not been demonstrated, which is now well established (RANZCOG; SOMANZ).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
Cochrane: Magnesium for neuroprotection of the preterm fetus

options.rationale: Single IM dose is wrong because the regimen for neuroprotection is IV loading (4 g over 20-30 min) then maintenance infusion (1 g/hr); IM dosing does not achieve the required serum levels. Would never be the correct route (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

options.rationale: Withholding magnesium because steroids were given is wrong because corticosteroids (lung maturation) and magnesium (neuroprotection) act on different pathways and have independent benefit; they are not interchangeable. (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

options.rationale: Deferring at 29+4 is wrong because Australian guidance offers neuroprotection up to <30 weeks (with some centres extending to <32 weeks); 29+4 sits inside the window. Would be correct only at gestations beyond local cutoffs (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

explanation.summary: Term and late-preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (PROM) carries a chorioamnionitis risk that climbs with each additional hour of membrane rupture, particularly past 18 hours. From 36+0 weeks the fetal benefit of waiting for spontaneous labour does not outweigh the rising infection risk, so RANZCOG and most Australian units offer immediate induction with oxytocin or balloon. Intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for early-onset group B streptococcal disease is given to women who are GBS-positive on swab, have GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, a previous GBS-affected infant, intrapartum fever, prolonged rupture beyond 18 hours, or preterm labour with unknown GBS. Benzylpenicillin is first-line; cefazolin for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy; vancomycin or clindamycin (with susceptibility) for anaphylactoid allergy. Document time of rupture, antibiotic doses, and maternal observations contemporaneously.
key_points: PPROM 36+0 or more: plan induction rather than expectant care (RANZCOG)
Use benzylpenicillin 1.2 g IV q4h intrapartum for GBS positivity
Steroids not routinely indicated 35+0 or more in Australia
explanation.pearls: At 36+0 or later with PROM the latency benefit of expectant management is lost; immediate induction with intrapartum benzylpenicillin (3 g IV load then 1.8 g every 4 hours for GBS-positive women) cuts early-onset neonatal sepsis by about half (RANZCOG; RCH CPG).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: PPROM at or beyond 36+0 with a GBS-positive mother is managed by induction rather than expectant care to limit chorioamnionitis and neonatal early-onset GBS sepsis (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Outpatient expectant management is wrong because near-term PPROM with GBS positivity carries clear risk of chorioamnionitis and early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis, and outpatient observation prevents timely intrapartum penicillin. Would be correct only if she were GBS-negative and could tolerate close inpatient observation, not at home with GBS positivity (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Maternal Group B Streptococcus in pregnancy

options.rationale: Tocolysis plus steroids is wrong because steroids are not routinely given beyond 35 weeks and tocolysis only prolongs membrane rupture while increasing infection. Would never be correct at this gestation (RANZCOG).

Caesarean for PPROM at this gestation is wrong because PPROM is not a caesarean indication; vaginal birth after induction is the preferred route in the absence of other contraindications. Would be correct only with obstetric indications for caesarean (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Inpatient expectancy to 39+0 is wrong because prolonging ruptured membranes with GBS positivity drives chorioamnionitis and neonatal sepsis; the TERMPROM trial and RANZCOG support expediting birth. Would be correct only with reassuring clinical picture and GBS negativity, perhaps to 37 weeks, not 39 (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Cervical insufficiency is a clinical diagnosis based on a pattern of painless mid-trimester loss with progressive dilation and bulging membranes, not on any single ultrasound measurement. RANZCOG recommends history-indicated (elective) cervical cerclage at 12-14 weeks for women with three or more such losses; two losses warrant ultrasound-indicated cerclage triggered by cervical shortening below 25 mm before 24 weeks. Transvaginal McDonald cerclage is the default; transabdominal cerclage is reserved for failed transvaginal stitches or absent vaginal cervix. Vaginal progesterone is added when cervix shortens despite cerclage. Rescue (physical-exam-indicated) cerclage may be offered up to about 24 weeks if no contractions, no bleeding, and no clinical or biochemical infection.
key_points: History-indicated cerclage: 3+ prior mid-trimester losses / early PTB
Ultrasound-indicated cerclage: 1+ prior PTB and TVS cervix <25 mm before 24 weeks
Rescue cerclage: cervix dilated with intact membranes <24 weeks
explanation.pearls: Three or more painless second-trimester losses meets the RANZCOG criterion for history-indicated cerclage at 12-14 weeks; an elective McDonald stitch in this scenario approximately doubles term delivery rates compared with surveillance alone.

options.rationale: Three or more prior second-trimester losses or preterm births consistent with cervical insufficiency is the classic indication for history-indicated (elective) cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks per RANZCOG.

Vaginal progesterone alone is wrong because progesterone is indicated for asymptomatic short cervix on TVS or singleton prior preterm birth, not as a substitute for cerclage in three prior second-trimester losses. Would be correct only as adjunct, not as sole strategy in this history (RANZCOG).

Serial scans with rescue cerclage is wrong because women with three prior mid-trimester losses meet criteria for history-indicated (elective) cerclage; ultrasound-indicated cerclage is the strategy for women with one prior preterm birth where the cervix may not shorten. Would be correct only with one prior preterm birth, not three losses (RANZCOG; RCOG cerclage guideline).

Preconception transabdominal cerclage is wrong because TAC is reserved for failed transvaginal cerclage or anatomical features (very short cervix, extensive trachelectomy) precluding vaginal placement; not first-line. Would be correct after a failed vaginal cerclage in a previous pregnancy (RANZCOG; RCOG).

Cervical pessary is wrong because the evidence is mixed (PECEP positive, ProTWIN/OPPTIMUM neutral) and pessary is not first-line in Australian practice for this history. Would be correct only in research settings or specific resource-limited contexts (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: TVS cervix under 25 mm before 24 weeks identifies women at high risk of preterm birth. Vaginal progesterone (200 mg nightly) reduces preterm birth and improves neonatal outcomes; cerclage is reserved for those with prior preterm birth whose cervix shortens despite progesterone or who present with dilation.
key_points: TVS cervix <25 mm before 24 weeks: vaginal progesterone (RANZCOG)
Continue progesterone until 36 weeks
Consider US-indicated cerclage if cervix <25 mm and prior PTB
explanation.pearls: TVS is the standard cervical length method; transabdominal underestimates true length.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Use of progesterone to prevent preterm birth

options.rationale: Vaginal progesterone reduces preterm birth and perinatal morbidity in women with TVS cervix under 25 mm before 24 weeks, particularly with a prior preterm birth, per RANZCOG.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Use of progesterone to prevent preterm birth

options.rationale: IM 17OHPC is wrong because the PROLONG trial confirmed lack of efficacy and the FDA withdrew approval; vaginal progesterone has the supporting evidence (PREGNANT, OPPTIMUM, individual patient meta-analyses). Would never be correct in current Australian practice (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Use of progesterone to prevent preterm birth

options.rationale: Rescue cerclage is wrong because rescue cerclage is for advanced cervical dilation with exposed membranes; this woman has a closed short cervix. Would be correct only with dilated cervix and bulging membranes (RANZCOG).
Bedrest is wrong because trials have shown bedrest does not reduce preterm birth and increases VTE and muscle deconditioning. (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Use of progesterone to prevent preterm birth

options.rationale: qfFN testing is wrong because fFN has its strongest predictive role in symptomatic women; in an asymptomatic woman with short cervix the management trigger (progesterone) is already in place regardless of fFN. Would be correct only in symptomatic threatened preterm labour (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Threatened preterm labour in pregnancies under 34 weeks is one of the highest-volume obstetric presentations, and most women presenting do not deliver preterm. Risk stratification combines clinical assessment, transvaginal sonographic cervical length, and quantitative fetal fibronectin (qfFN) measured on a cervico-vaginal swab. qfFN must be sampled before any digital exam, before intercourse in the preceding 24 hours, and without lubricant on the speculum, otherwise the result is invalid. A qfFN under 10 ng/mL has the highest negative predictive value for birth within 7 days; a level under 50 ng/mL with a reassuring cervix length (over 25 mm on TVS) allows safe discharge home with clear safety-net advice. Levels over 200 ng/mL or shortening cervix warrant admission, corticosteroids, consideration of tocolysis to facilitate 48 hours of betamethasone, and magnesium sulfate if under 30 weeks and birth anticipated within 24 hours.
key_points: qfFN NPV for PTB within 7 days >95% when <50 ng/mL
Combine with TVS cervical length for best discrimination
Positive qfFN raises risk; manage clinically with steroids, MgSO4, tocolysis as indicated
explanation.pearls: Quantitative fetal fibronectin under 50 ng/mL combined with a TVS cervix over 25 mm has a negative predictive value over 99% for spontaneous birth within 7 days - safely discharges women presenting with threatened preterm labour (RANZCOG; QUIDS).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus
NICE NG25: Preterm labour and birth

options.rationale: qfFN below 50 ng/mL combined with a TVS cervix in the lower range still has a very high negative predictive value for birth within 7 days; admission, tocolysis, and steroids are unnecessary.
source_refs: NICE NG25: Preterm labour and birth

options.rationale: Admit, steroids and tocolysis is wrong because qfFN <50 ng/mL with a closed cervix has very high NPV for birth within 7 days; admission and steroid courses are unwarranted. Would be correct only with positive qfFN or cervical change (RANZCOG).

Magnesium sulfate is wrong because neuroprotective MgSO4 requires birth anticipated within 24 hours, which the negative fFN explicitly refutes. Would be correct only with imminent birth at <30 weeks (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Magnesium sulfate for neuroprotection of the fetus

options.rationale: Repeat fFN in 24h is wrong because management does not change for a low qfFN value with no cervical change. Would be correct only if the clinical picture changed (RANZCOG).

Emergency rescue cerclage is wrong because cerclage requires advanced cervical dilation with bulging membranes, not a closed cervix with negative fFN. Would be correct only with cervical dilation and exposed membranes (RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: ADIPS guidance supports delivery by around 40+6 in uncomplicated diet-controlled GDM. Earlier elective birth is reserved for insulin treatment, macrosomia, poor control, or other complications. Late preterm and early term iatrogenic births carry meaningful neonatal respiratory morbidity.
key_points: Diet-controlled uncomplicated GDM: birth by ~40+6 (ADIPS)
Insulin-treated GDM: consider birth 38+0 to 39+0
Complicated GDM (poor control, IUGR, hypertension): individualise earlier
explanation.pearls: Avoid elective non-medical birth before 39+0 due to neonatal respiratory morbidity.

options.rationale: ADIPS and RANZCOG support birth by around 40+6 for diet-controlled GDM with no complications; routine early term induction does not improve outcomes and increases neonatal respiratory morbidity.

Elective IOL at 37+0 is wrong because routine 37+0 induction in well-controlled diet-only GDM increases iatrogenic late preterm respiratory morbidity without improving stillbirth or shoulder dystocia outcomes; ADIPS recommends ~40+6. Would be correct only with insulin-treated GDM or comorbidities (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

Elective caesarean at 38+0 is wrong because diet-controlled GDM does not in itself indicate caesarean; macrosomia thresholds and obstetric indications drive mode of birth. Would be correct only with EFW >4500 g, prior caesarean or other indication (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

Induction at 39+0 regardless of Bishop is wrong because diet-controlled uncomplicated GDM can be managed expectantly to around 40+6 per ADIPS; routine early induction is reserved for insulin-treated or complicated disease. Would be correct only for insulin-treated GDM or other complications (ADIPS; RANZCOG).

Deferring to 41+5 is wrong because even diet-controlled GDM raises stillbirth risk beyond 41 weeks; the upper boundary in ADIPS is around 40+6. Would never be correct in GDM regardless of control (ADIPS).

explanation.summary: Term prelabour rupture of membranes occurs in around 8% of pregnancies and most women labour spontaneously within 24 hours. Shared decision-making at term PROM weighs early induction (lower chorioamnionitis and neonatal sepsis rates) against limited expectant management (higher rate of spontaneous vaginal birth). The TermPROM and subsequent Cochrane data show no perinatal mortality difference but a clear reduction in maternal and neonatal infection with immediate induction. Australian practice typically caps expectant management at 18-24 hours from rupture. GBS-positive women, women with prior GBS-affected infants, GBS bacteriuria this pregnancy, intrapartum fever, or unknown-GBS preterm rupture all receive intrapartum benzylpenicillin from the moment induction commences. Minimise digital vaginal examinations until active labour to limit ascending infection.
key_points: Either induction or expectant management for ~24 h is reasonable
GBS positivity tips management toward earlier induction with intrapartum penicillin
Document time of rupture
explanation.pearls: From 37+0 with PROM, RANZCOG accepts up to 24 hours of expectant management as a shared decision; beyond 24 hours infection risk rises sharply, and induction with concurrent intrapartum benzylpenicillin is the default for GBS-positive women.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Term PROM with GBS-positive status: RANZCOG recommends immediate induction and commencement of intrapartum GBS prophylaxis (rather than expectant management) to reduce risk of early-onset neonatal GBS sepsis. Penicillin is first-line in non-allergic women (RANZCOG term PROM; RANZCOG GBS).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Expectancy with no antibiotics unless febrile is wrong because GBS-positive PROM warrants IAP from the time of presentation; waiting for fever signals fully established chorioamnionitis. Would be correct only in GBS-negative term PROM with stable observations (RANZCOG GBS).

Home expectancy 5 days is wrong because outpatient management beyond 24h in term PROM raises chorioamnionitis risk and is incompatible with timely IV penicillin in a GBS-positive woman. Would never be correct in GBS-positive PROM (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Mandatory caesarean is wrong because vaginal birth with IAP is the standard approach in GBS-positive PROM; caesarean does not eliminate vertical transmission and adds maternal morbidity. Would be correct only for standard obstetric indications (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Erythromycin for latency is wrong because erythromycin latency therapy is for preterm PROM; at term, the goal is induction, not prolongation. Would be correct only at <34 weeks PPROM (RANZCOG; ORACLE I).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: Clinical chorioamnionitis is a clinical diagnosis based on maternal fever (38 or above) plus one or more of: maternal tachycardia (above 100), fetal tachycardia (above 160), uterine tenderness, foul or turbid amniotic fluid, or maternal leukocytosis. It complicates 1-4% of all pregnancies and up to 30% of preterm prelabour rupture of membranes managed expectantly. The diagnosis ends expectant management at any gestation because of the rising risks of maternal sepsis, neonatal sepsis, and stillbirth. Management is immediate broad-spectrum IV antibiotics (typically ampicillin or amoxicillin plus gentamicin, with metronidazole or clindamycin added if anaerobic cover needed or post-caesarean) and expedited delivery - vaginal birth where feasible. Fetal tachycardia is often the earliest objective sign and warrants vigilant observation in any woman managed expectantly with PPROM. Post-delivery, antibiotics continue until afebrile for 24-48 hours; neonatal sepsis workup is mandatory.
key_points: Triad-plus signs of chorioamnionitis = deliver (RANZCOG, eTG)
Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics started immediately on suspicion
Mode of birth depends on obstetric factors; chorioamnionitis itself is not a caesarean indication
Continue antibiotics intrapartum and postpartum until afebrile
explanation.pearls: Fetal tachycardia (FHR sustained above 160) is often the earliest objective sign of intra-amniotic infection in PPROM, preceding maternal fever by hours; clinical chorioamnionitis ends expectant management at any gestation - broad-spectrum IV antibiotics plus delivery (RANZCOG; ACOG).

sources.label: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Clinical chorioamnionitis in PPROM at 29 weeks is an indication for prompt delivery alongside IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, irrespective of gestation, per RANZCOG.
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Continued expectancy to 32 weeks is wrong because once clinical chorioamnionitis is established, prolonging pregnancy drives maternal sepsis and fetal injury (white matter injury, neonatal sepsis); delivery is the definitive treatment. Would never be correct in active chorioamnionitis (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Repeat steroids and wait 12h is wrong because steroid benefit takes hours and does not change outcome once intra-amniotic infection is overt. Would be correct only in subclinical situations (which is not this case) (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Tocolysis is wrong because tocolysis is contraindicated in chorioamnionitis: it delays definitive treatment and may mask deterioration. Would never be correct in chorioamnionitis (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

options.rationale: Amniocentesis first is wrong because the clinical diagnosis (fever, tachycardia, tender uterus, rising CRP, turbid AF) is already established; invasive testing only delays delivery. Would be correct only when subclinical infection needs confirmation and delivery is not yet planned (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Term prelabour rupture of membranes and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes

explanation.summary: After single twin demise in a monochorionic pregnancy, acute feto-fetal transfusion via placental anastomoses can cause severe anaemia in the survivor. MCA-PSV above 1.5 MoM signals fetal anaemia and warrants urgent fetal medicine assessment for in-utero transfusion. Iatrogenic preterm birth at 27 weeks rarely improves outcome and adds severe prematurity morbidity.
key_points: Surviving MC twin: ~15% risk of death, ~25% risk of neurological injury
MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM = significant risk of fetal anaemia (ISUOG)
Urgent neuroimaging (MRI) 4 to 6 weeks later if survival
Birth timing individualised; not routinely immediate
explanation.pearls: MCA-PSV is the same screening tool used in red cell alloimmunisation; same threshold.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: MCA-PSV above 1.5 MoM in the surviving twin after MC co-twin demise suggests acute fetal anaemia from feto-fetal transfusion across shared anastomoses; intrauterine transfusion may reduce neurological injury (RANZCOG, ISUOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Immediate caesarean is wrong because iatrogenic birth at 27+4 inflicts severe prematurity morbidity (RDS, IVH, NEC, ROP) and does not reverse hypoxic-ischaemic injury already sustained from the co-twin demise; intrauterine transfusion offers the chance to rescue the survivor and prolong gestation. Would be correct only after IUT fails or with further fetal deterioration (RANZCOG; ISUOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Weekly outpatient Dopplers is wrong because MCA-PSV >1.5 MoM is a time-critical red flag for fetal anaemia and requires same-day tertiary intervention, not weekly follow-up. Would never be correct with elevated MCA-PSV (RANZCOG; ISUOG).

Maternal IV heparin is wrong because clinically significant maternal coagulopathy after single twin demise is rare in the short term, especially with normal baseline coagulation. Would be correct only with documented developing coagulopathy (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

options.rationale: Cord occlusion of the survivor is wrong because the goal after MC co-twin demise is to rescue the surviving healthy twin; terminating it would be unethical and inverts the management logic. Would never be correct in this scenario (RANZCOG; ISUOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of Monochorionic Twin Pregnancy

explanation.summary: LAM provides about 98% contraceptive efficacy when all three criteria are met: exclusive or near-exclusive breastfeeding day and night, infant under 6 months, and amenorrhoea since delivery. Loss of any single criterion mandates an additional method.
key_points: Three LAM criteria: exclusive BF, <6 months, amenorrhoea
Progestogen-only pill can start from day 21 postpartum (any time if BF)
Combined hormonal contraception avoided until 6 weeks postpartum if BF (and 3 weeks if not BF, longer if VTE risk)
Postnatal IUD/IUS: usually inserted 4 to 6 weeks postpartum (immediate post-placental insertion also an option)
Etonogestrel implant: any time postpartum including day 0
explanation.pearls: If a woman wants LAM, document the three criteria explicitly and plan the bridging method for when any one fails first (usually the 6-month limit or weaning).

sources.label: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

options.rationale: LAM is reliable only while ALL three criteria are met (exclusive/near-exclusive breastfeeding, infant under 6 months, amenorrhoea). At 6 weeks she meets criteria, but planning for the transition is part of good counselling: parallel LARC or progestogen-only methods bridge the gap (FSRH; Family Planning Australia).
LAM reliable only up to 6 months, not 12; failure rate rises sharply once any criterion lapses. 12 months reliance is essentially never correct (FSRH).
Partial or mixed feeding (with formula or solids) breaks LAM criteria; reliability drops markedly. Reassurance with mixed feeding is essentially never correct (Family Planning Australia).
Return of menstruation INVALIDATES LAM; criterion is amenorrhoea since delivery, not presence of menses. LAM-with-menses is essentially never correct (Family Planning Australia).
CHC is UKMEC 4 in first 6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding (UKMEC 2 from 6 weeks to 6 months) due to VTE and supply concerns. COCP is correct >6 months postpartum or not breastfeeding (FSRH UKMEC).

explanation.summary: Postpartum VTE risk is stratified by RANZCOG/RCOG point scoring. Women with prior VTE almost always receive 6 weeks of LMWH at a weight-banded prophylactic dose; women with 4 or more transient risk factors receive 10 days; emergency caesarean alone with no other risk factors usually does not require pharmacological prophylaxis.
key_points: Weight-banded enoxaparin (typical bands): <50 kg 20 mg, 50-90 kg 40 mg, 91-130 kg 60-80 mg, 131-170 kg 80 mg twice daily considered
Duration: 10 days for transient risk; 6 weeks for prior VTE, persistent risk factors, high thrombophilia, or sustained admission
LMWH preferred over warfarin and DOACs postpartum (DOACs not used in breastfeeding women)
OHSS adds an independent high VTE risk that may warrant 6 weeks even without delivery risk factors
Hold LMWH if active bleeding or platelets <75 x10^9/L
explanation.pearls: On finals: any prior VTE = 6 weeks postpartum LMWH almost always. The decision is duration first, then dose by weight band.

sources.label: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum
RCOG GTG 37a Reducing the risk of VTE

options.rationale: CS + BMI >30 + prior provoked VTE together exceed threshold for pharmacological prophylaxis on RANZCOG scoring; mechanical alone insufficient. Mechanical alone is correct in lower-risk patients (RANZCOG VTE).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum

options.rationale: 20 mg daily is standard for <50 kg or low-risk; this woman is 108 kg and high risk, requires weight-based dosing. 20 mg daily is correct in low-weight or low-risk women (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum

options.rationale: Weight-based dose (80 mg for 91-130 kg) appropriate, but duration of only 10 days inadequate given prior VTE history. 10-day duration is correct in low-risk women without prior VTE (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum

options.rationale: She has prior provoked VTE plus emergency caesarean plus BMI greater than 30 (a high-risk profile on RANZCOG/RCOG scoring). The recommended regimen is weight-banded LMWH (80 mg daily for 91 to 130 kg) for 6 weeks postpartum (RANZCOG; KEMH; RCOG GTG 37a).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum
RCOG GTG 37a Reducing the risk of VTE

options.rationale: Warfarin compatible with breastfeeding but LMWH preferred postpartum because no INR monitoring and avoids early postpartum warfarin instability. Warfarin is correct in long-term anticoagulation with stable INR (RANZCOG).
source_refs: RANZCOG VTE in pregnancy and postpartum

explanation.summary: Postnatal contraception timing: progestogen-only methods (POP, implant) can be started any time postpartum including day 0. Cu-IUD and LNG-IUS are inserted within 48 hours of delivery or after 4 weeks. Combined hormonal contraception is generally avoided until 6 weeks postpartum if breastfeeding (and until 3 weeks if not breastfeeding, longer if VTE risk factors).
key_points: Implant: any time, WHO MEC 1 in BF women
POP: from day 21 (any time in BF women)
Cu-IUD / LNG-IUS: <48 h or >=4 weeks postpartum
COCP: avoid <3 weeks postpartum (VTE), <6 weeks if BF
LAM only reliable with exclusive BF + <6 months + amenorrhoea
explanation.pearls: Best practice is to discuss postnatal contraception antenatally and offer the implant at hospital discharge or within the first 5 days to capture women before contact is lost.

sources.label: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

options.rationale: CHC avoided in first 6 weeks postpartum breastfeeding (WHO MEC 3-4) due to theoretical effects on supply. COCP is correct >6 weeks postpartum if not breastfeeding (WHO MEC).
source_refs: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

options.rationale: Does not meet LAM criteria because only partially breastfeeding; deferral risks ovulation. LAM is correct only with exclusive breastfeeding + amenorrhoea + <6 months postpartum (FSRH).

Cu-IUD insertion within 48 hours of delivery or after 4 weeks postpartum, so feasible at 5 weeks; however requires procedure scheduling. Cu-IUD is correct option when willing to wait for insertion appointment (WHO MEC).
LNG-IUS insertion follows similar timing; requires procedure scheduling and speculum work. LNG-IUS is correct option when willing to wait for insertion (WHO MEC).

The etonogestrel implant is WHO MEC category 1 at any time postpartum in breastfeeding women, can be inserted during the postnatal consultation, has the highest typical-use efficacy of any reversible method, and avoids the VTE and lactation concerns of combined hormonal contraception in the early postpartum window (WHO MEC; FSRH; Family Planning Australia).
source_refs: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

explanation.summary: OASI (grade 3a, 3b, 3c, 4) repair: theatre with regional or general anaesthesia, end-to-end or overlap repair of the external anal sphincter with 2-0 or 3-0 PDS or polyglactin, separate IAS repair if torn, broad-spectrum IV then oral antibiotics, stool softeners for at least 10 days, and structured pelvic floor physiotherapy plus perineal clinic follow-up at 6 to 12 weeks. Counsel about mode of next delivery once symptomatic status is known.
key_points: Grades: 3a <50% EAS, 3b >50% EAS, 3c IAS torn, 4 anal mucosa torn
Repair in theatre with adequate lighting and assistance
Suture: 2-0 or 3-0 PDS for sphincters, 2-0 polyglactin for vaginal mucosa/perineal muscles
Antibiotics: cefuroxime + metronidazole IV then oral course (Therapeutic Guidelines analogous regimen)
Lactulose 10 days; physiotherapy referral; perineal clinic 6-12 weeks
explanation.pearls: Risk factors for OASI: primiparity, instrumental delivery (forceps > vacuum), prolonged second stage, macrosomia, shoulder dystocia, persistent OP. Mediolateral episiotomy reduces OASI risk in instrumental delivery.

sources.label: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.rationale: On-ward local-anaesthetic repair with no antibiotics or follow-up is wrong because OASI requires theatre repair under regional/GA with adequate lighting and exposure; broad-spectrum antibiotics, laxatives and structured follow-up (physiotherapy, perineal clinic) are mandatory. (RCOG GTG 29).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Ward repair without anaesthesia is wrong because OASI repair requires theatre-level anaesthesia for adequate visualisation and sphincter alignment; on-ward repair without anaesthesia compromises outcome. (RCOG GTG 29).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.rationale: OASI requires repair in theatre with adequate anaesthesia, regional or GA, broad-spectrum antibiotic cover, stool softeners (typically lactulose) for at least 10 days, structured pelvic floor physiotherapy referral, and follow-up in a specialist perineal clinic at 6 to 12 weeks with assessment for symptoms of incontinence (RCOG GTG 29; RANZCOG).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Theatre repair but no laxative is wrong because constipation increases dehiscence and pain; lactulose for at least 10 days is standard. Narrow staphylococcal cover alone is also inadequate - broad-spectrum cover is needed. Physiotherapy and perineal clinic are part of structured follow-up. (RCOG GTG 29).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

options.rationale: Defer repair 24h is wrong because OASI should be repaired as soon as feasible by a trained operator; delay increases infection risk. Antibiotic prophylaxis is required and laxative for at least 10 days. (RCOG GTG 29).
source_refs: RCOG GTG 29 Third- and fourth-degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome is ischaemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary following severe postpartum haemorrhage. Failure to lactate (loss of prolactin) is often the earliest feature; secondary amenorrhoea, cold intolerance, fatigue, hyponatraemia and postural hypotension follow. Workup screens each pituitary axis and includes MRI. Treat with glucocorticoid replacement first (hydrocortisone), then thyroxine, then sex steroid replacement; GH replacement is considered in symptomatic adults.
key_points: Failure to lactate is the most specific early clue
Treat cortisol before thyroxine to avoid adrenal crisis
Hyponatraemia is common (cortisol deficiency, hypothyroidism)
MRI may show empty or partially empty sella
Prolactin is typically low or undetectable (versus high in pituitary adenoma)
explanation.pearls: Any postpartum woman with prior major PPH who fails to lactate, fails to menstruate, and presents with non-specific fatigue, hypotension or cold intolerance should have a pituitary workup until proven otherwise. Hydrocortisone before levothyroxine - always.

options.rationale: Sheehan syndrome causes panhypopituitarism after pituitary ischaemic necrosis following major PPH. The investigation strategy is to assess each pituitary axis: cortisol (ACTH axis), free T4 with TSH (TSH axis - TSH may be inappropriately normal or low), LH/FSH and oestradiol (gonadotrophin axis), prolactin (lactotroph axis - typically low or undetectable), IGF-1 (GH axis), with MRI demonstrating an empty or partially empty sella (BMJ Best Practice; Endocrine Society).

TSH/T4 only with empirical thyroxine is wrong because TSH/T4 alone miss the potentially fatal cortisol deficiency; giving thyroxine before replacing glucocorticoid can precipitate adrenal crisis. Would be correct only after cortisol replacement is confirmed adequate (BMJ Best Practice).

Random cortisol and TSH is wrong because random cortisol is unreliable due to diurnal variation; 0800 morning cortisol plus the full pituitary axis screen plus imaging is required. Would never be correct as a complete workup (Endocrine Society).

24h urinary cortisol and dexamethasone suppression is wrong because these tests screen for Cushing syndrome (excess cortisol), not deficiency; the workup is in the wrong direction entirely. Would be correct only when suspecting Cushing (Endocrine Society).

Pelvic ultrasound and AMH is wrong because amenorrhoea in Sheehan is central (low LH/FSH and oestradiol), not primary ovarian failure; AMH would not establish the pituitary diagnosis. Would be correct only for ovarian reserve assessment, not pituitary workup (BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Australian Patient Blood Management Guidelines recommend: transfuse if Hb less than 70 g/L or symptomatic; IV iron if Hb 70 to 90 g/L with iron deficiency or oral iron intolerance or need for rapid response; oral iron for Hb at or above 90 g/L without urgency. Ferritin less than 30 micrograms/L confirms iron deficiency in the postpartum population.
key_points: Transfusion threshold postpartum: Hb <70 g/L or symptomatic compromise
IV iron indications: Hb 70-90 g/L with ID; oral intolerance; need for rapid response; ongoing absorption issues
Ferritin <30 micrograms/L = iron deficiency (consider <100 if inflammation)
Ferric carboxymaltose: 1000 mg single dose, infused over 15 minutes
Oral iron: alternate-day dosing improves absorption; review Hb at 4 weeks
explanation.pearls: In the postpartum setting, IV iron is increasingly the workhorse for moderate anaemia because it is faster, more reliable and avoids the constipation that compounds perineal pain and post-caesarean recovery.

sources.label: Australian Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Module 5 Obstetrics and Maternity

options.rationale: Hb 70-80 g/L in a stable postpartum woman with no ongoing bleeding does not mandate transfusion (PBM Module 5: transfusion thresholds Hb <70 g/L in stable patients). IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) corrects iron stores rapidly, supports breastfeeding and avoids transfusion risks (NBA PBM5; AMH).
source_refs: Australian Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Module 5 Obstetrics and Maternity

options.rationale: Transfuse 2 units is wrong because she is asymptomatic at rest with stable haemodynamics and no ongoing bleeding; the NBA PBM5 restrictive threshold is Hb <70 g/L in stable patients. Would be correct only with symptomatic anaemia, ongoing bleeding or Hb <70 (NBA PBM5).
source_refs: Australian Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Module 5 Obstetrics and Maternity

options.rationale: Oral ferrous sulfate TDS for 3 months is wrong because at this Hb level oral iron corrects slowly (months) and is poorly tolerated (GI side effects); IV iron is preferred for postpartum severe deficiency. Would be correct only for mild postpartum anaemia with good tolerance (NBA PBM5).
source_refs: Australian Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Module 5 Obstetrics and Maternity

options.rationale: Oral ferrous fumarate TDS no follow-up is wrong because oral iron alone for severe deficiency is suboptimal and follow-up is required to confirm correction. (NBA PBM5).
source_refs: Australian Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Module 5 Obstetrics and Maternity

options.rationale: ESA plus oral iron is wrong because ESAs are not routinely indicated in postpartum iron deficiency without renal disease; IV iron alone suffices. Would be correct only with renal-disease-associated anaemia not responding to iron (NBA PBM5; AMH).
source_refs: Australian Patient Blood Management Guidelines - Module 5 Obstetrics and Maternity

explanation.summary: Postpartum urinary retention is defined as failure to void within 6 hours of vaginal birth or post-void residual greater than 150 mL after attempted void. Risk factors include epidural, prolonged second stage, instrumental delivery, OASI, episiotomy, and large infant. Management is indwelling catheter for 24 to 48 hours then trial of void with bladder scans.
key_points: Catheterise within 6 hours of vaginal birth if no spontaneous void
Bladder volume >500-700 mL: indwelling catheter 24-48 h preferred over single in-out
TWOC after 24-48 h with pre- and post-void scans
PVR >150 mL: re-catheterise and reassess
Risk factors: epidural, instrumental, prolonged labour, OASI, big baby
explanation.pearls: Detrusor overdistension can cause permanent voiding dysfunction. Document time and volume of every void in the first 24 hours postpartum, and act on the first failed attempt rather than waiting.

options.rationale: Encourage more fluids and re-scan in 4 hours is wrong because 720 mL after 11 hours of failed voiding meets retention criteria requiring drainage; continued conservative measures risk detrusor overdistension and long-term voiding dysfunction. Would be correct only with smaller residual volume and short time since last void (KEMH; RCOG).

Single in-out catheter then discharge is wrong because single drainage without a structured plan risks recurrent retention; indwelling catheter for 24-48h plus structured TWOC is needed when residual >500-700 mL. Would be correct only with residual <500 mL and good spontaneous voiding (KEMH).

Urgent urology cystoscopy is wrong because postpartum urinary retention is typically transient and managed by obstetric teams with catheterisation and TWOC; urology referral is not first-line. Would be correct only with persistent retention after multiple failed TWOCs or suspected structural pathology (RCOG).
IV furosemide is wrong because furosemide treats fluid overload not retention; it would worsen the problem by increasing bladder volume further. Would never be correct in retention (KEMH).

Bladder volume greater than 500 to 700 mL with failed voiding after vaginal birth defines covert/overt postpartum urinary retention. Management is indwelling catheterisation for 24 to 48 hours to allow detrusor recovery, followed by a structured trial of void with pre- and post-void scans; persistent residual volumes greater than 150 mL prompt repeat catheterisation and further investigation (KEMH; RCOG; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Postpartum hypertension management after preeclampsia: continue and adjust antihypertensives, monitor BP for at least 6 weeks postpartum, wean methyldopa (depression risk), and use labetalol, nifedipine, enalapril or captopril as preferred agents in breastfeeding. Preeclampsia can present de novo up to 6 weeks postpartum.
key_points: Wean methyldopa postpartum (depression risk)
Labetalol, nifedipine CR, enalapril, captopril all compatible with BF
Avoid atenolol in BF (neonatal beta-blockade)
Treat BP >=150/100 mmHg sustained; aim BP <140/90 mmHg postpartum
Monitor BP and proteinuria up to 6 weeks; postpartum review at 6 weeks plus 6 to 12 months for CVD risk
explanation.pearls: Postnatal new-onset headache plus elevated BP within 6 weeks of delivery is preeclampsia or eclampsia until proven otherwise. Always screen mood in postpartum hypertensive women - methyldopa is a hidden contributor.

options.rationale: Increase methyldopa is wrong because methyldopa is associated with postpartum depression and sedation and is typically weaned in the puerperium rather than uptitrated; SOMANZ prefers other agents postpartum. Would never be correct as escalation strategy (SOMANZ).

SOMANZ recommends weaning methyldopa postpartum (depression risk, no clear postpartum benefit), continuing or uptitrating labetalol and adding a calcium channel blocker such as nifedipine controlled-release as a second agent; all three are compatible with breastfeeding (SOMANZ; AMH).

Atenolol is wrong because atenolol concentrates in breast milk and can cause neonatal bradycardia, hypotension and hypoglycaemia; it is avoided in breastfeeding. Would be correct only outside breastfeeding (AMH).

Enalapril replacing labetalol immediately is wrong because while enalapril is breastfeeding-compatible, SOMANZ prefers stepwise change with labetalol or nifedipine as first-line postpartum and methyldopa weaning pending. Would be correct only after stepwise titration of preferred agents (SOMANZ).

Stop all antihypertensives at >5 days postpartum is wrong because BP characteristically peaks at days 3-6 postpartum and pre-eclampsia can present or worsen up to 6 weeks postpartum; treatment continues while BP remains >=150/100. Would be correct only with sustained BP normalisation (SOMANZ).

explanation.summary: Failure to establish lactation has several distinct causes: delayed lactogenesis II (most common, transient), retained placental fragments (progesterone continues to inhibit prolactin), Sheehan syndrome (low prolactin after major PPH), insufficient glandular tissue (tubular, asymmetric, widely spaced breasts), prior breast surgery, severe stress, and PCOS. Investigation is targeted: prolactin and pituitary axis first, plus pelvic USS for retained products if any third-stage concern.
key_points: Lactogenesis II is the copious milk production phase that normally begins at day 2 to 5 postpartum
Retained placental tissue continues progesterone production and inhibits lactogenesis II
IGT clinical features: tubular, widely spaced, asymmetric breasts; minimal antenatal growth
Sheehan presents with failure to lactate as an early sign
Galactagogues (domperidone, metoclopramide) only after diagnostic workup
explanation.pearls: If you cannot tick off latch, positioning, frequency, and infant transfer as adequate, fix those first. If they are adequate and supply remains poor, investigate the mother.

sources.label: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

options.rationale: Infant tongue-tie assessment is wrong because optimal latch and positioning and a normal infant suck have already been confirmed by lactation consultant assessment; a primary infant-side cause is unlikely. Would be correct only with suspected suck problems (ABA).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply
