options.rationale: Maternal FBC and ferritin only is wrong because anaemia may contribute to fatigue but rarely causes complete failure of lactogenesis II; targeted prolactin and pituitary axis testing is needed. Would be correct only as adjunct to the targeted workup (ABA).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

options.rationale: Pelvic ultrasound only is wrong because while pelvic USS helps exclude retained products, it is most useful in combination with prolactin and wider pituitary workup; alone it misses pituitary, glandular and endocrine causes. Would be correct only as part of comprehensive workup (ABA).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

options.rationale: Failure to establish lactation despite optimal latch and positioning prompts investigation for hypoprolactinaemia (Sheehan), retained products causing persistent progesterone elevation, primary insufficient glandular tissue (suggested here by tubular, widely spaced, asymmetric breasts) and significant stress. Serum prolactin is the targeted first investigation, with concurrent screening of the pituitary axis to exclude Sheehan especially in any woman with peripartum bleeding or retained tissue (ABA; LactMed; BMJ Best Practice).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

options.rationale: Empirical domperidone without investigation is wrong because galactagogues should follow characterisation of the underlying cause; empirical treatment risks missing Sheehan and retained products which need specific management. Would be correct only after underlying cause is established and primary low supply is confirmed (ABA; AMH).
source_refs: Australian Breastfeeding Association - Low milk supply

explanation.summary: Postpartum thyroiditis is a destructive lymphocytic thyroiditis presenting 1 to 12 months postpartum, classically biphasic: thyrotoxic phase (1 to 4 months postpartum, lasting weeks to months) followed by a hypothyroid phase (4 to 8 months postpartum, also transient). Most resolve to euthyroidism; approximately 20% develop permanent hypothyroidism. Anti-TPO antibodies are usually positive. Treat the thyrotoxic phase with a beta-blocker only, and the hypothyroid phase with levothyroxine if symptomatic.
key_points: Biphasic course: thyrotoxic (months 1 to 4) then hypothyroid (months 4 to 8)
Anti-TPO positive in approximately 70 to 80%
Distinguish from Graves: TRAb negative, reduced uptake on RAIU (low Doppler flow on USS as proxy in breastfeeding)
Treat thyrotoxic phase with beta-blocker; treat hypothyroid phase with thyroxine if symptomatic
20% develop permanent hypothyroidism; annual TFT screening thereafter
explanation.pearls: If TRAb is positive, think Graves disease (which can also present postpartum). If TRAb is negative and anti-TPO is high in a postpartum woman, think postpartum thyroiditis. Doppler ultrasound is a useful surrogate for radioiodine uptake in lactating women.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: Carbimazole is wrong because postpartum thyroiditis causes thyrotoxicosis by destructive release of preformed hormone, not new synthesis; antithyroid drugs (carbimazole, PTU) are ineffective. Would be correct only in Graves or other synthesis-mediated thyrotoxicosis (BMJ Best Practice; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: Radioiodine ablation is wrong because radioiodine is for Graves disease or toxic nodular disease, not transient destructive thyroiditis; postpartum thyroiditis typically resolves spontaneously. Would never be correct here (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: The thyrotoxic phase of postpartum thyroiditis is destructive (reduced vascularity, anti-TPO positive, TRAb negative) and treated symptomatically with a beta-blocker such as propranolol while monitoring TFTs every 6 to 8 weeks. Spontaneous resolution into euthyroidism or progression to a hypothyroid phase typically follows; permanent hypothyroidism occurs in approximately 20% at 1 year (BMJ Best Practice; Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: Levothyroxine is wrong because she is currently thyrotoxic (TSH <0.01, fT4 32); levothyroxine would worsen her state. Would be correct only in the subsequent hypothyroid phase or permanent hypothyroidism (Endocrine Society).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Thyroid Disease and Pregnancy 2017

options.rationale: Lugol iodine plus dexamethasone for thyroid storm is wrong because thyroid storm requires severe features (high fever, marked tachycardia, altered consciousness, organ dysfunction) which are absent; her thyrotoxicosis is mild-to-moderate. Would be correct only with established thyroid storm (BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Hyperprolactinaemia in a patient on a dopamine-blocking antipsychotic should be presumed iatrogenic until proven otherwise, since drug effect is far more common than pituitary adenoma in this group. Confirm with a fasting morning prolactin and exclude pregnancy, primary hypothyroidism, renal failure and chest wall stimulation. Antipsychotic-induced prolactin typically sits between 500 and 2000 mIU/L; levels above 5000 mIU/L raise concern for a macroadenoma and warrant pituitary MRI even on therapy. Management is shared with psychiatry - switch to aripiprazole or quetiapine where clinically appropriate, then recheck after 4-6 weeks. Dopamine agonists like cabergoline are second-line because they can destabilise psychosis. Persistent hypogonadism risks bone loss, so DXA and consideration of HRT are part of long-term care.
key_points: Common secondary causes: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, dopamine antagonists, oestrogens, opioids, renal failure, chest wall stimulation
Prolactin >5000 mIU/L strongly suggests prolactinoma
Macroprolactin screen if asymptomatic and isolated lab finding
MRI pituitary if confirmed persistent elevation with secondary causes excluded
explanation.pearls: Risperidone and amisulpride drive the largest prolactin elevations among second-generation antipsychotics; aripiprazole is partial-agonist at D2 and is usually prolactin-neutral or prolactin-lowering, making it the preferred substitute (eTG Psychotropic; AMH).

options.rationale: Urgent MRI first is wrong because when a known dopamine antagonist (risperidone) is the strongly suspected cause, identifying and managing the drug effect should precede imaging; pituitary MRI is reserved for sustained unexplained hyperprolactinaemia off the offending drug. Would be correct only after switching to a prolactin-sparing agent confirms persistence of hyperprolactinaemia (Endocrine Society 2011).

Risperidone is a strong dopamine D2 antagonist and a common cause of pharmacological hyperprolactinaemia. The first step is collaborative medication review with the prescribing psychiatrist; switching to a prolactin-sparing agent (aripiprazole) and re-measuring before imaging avoids unnecessary MRI and identifies the cause (Endocrine Society 2011; eTG Endocrinology).

Empirical cabergoline is wrong because dopamine agonists can precipitate or worsen psychosis in patients with schizophrenia and are not first-line when a drug cause is likely; the cause needs addressing before the laboratory abnormality is treated. Would be correct only for prolactinoma confirmed on imaging in stable patients (Endocrine Society 2011).

Macroprolactin screen is wrong because macroprolactin testing is for asymptomatic hyperprolactinaemia; this woman is clinically symptomatic (amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, low libido), confirming biologically active prolactin. Would be correct only in asymptomatic elevation (Endocrine Society 2011).

Abrupt risperidone cessation is wrong because stopping antipsychotic without psychiatric input risks relapse and self-harm; switches require shared decision-making with the prescribing team. Would never be correct unilaterally (Endocrine Society 2011).

explanation.summary: OHSS severity is classified mild/moderate/severe/critical. Moderate OHSS adds sonographic ascites to mild features. Severe OHSS requires clinical ascites with haematocrit >0.45, WCC >15, hypoalbuminaemia and oliguria. Critical adds tense ascites, ARDS, VTE or renal failure (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).
key_points: Risk factors: young age, low BMI, PCOS, high antral follicle count, high AMH, >20 oocytes retrieved
Prevention: GnRH antagonist protocol + GnRH agonist trigger + freeze-all embryos
Severe/critical OHSS = admission, VTE prophylaxis, fluid balance, paracentesis if tense
Most cases resolve by next menses; symptoms can be prolonged if pregnancy occurs
explanation.pearls: OHSS adds an independent high VTE risk; thromboprophylaxis is mandatory in admitted moderate-to-severe disease.

options.rationale: Moderate OHSS labelling is wrong because the haematocrit >=0.45, rising creatinine, oliguria, hypoalbuminaemia and ascites above the umbilicus push her into the severe category; outpatient management would miss thromboembolic and renal complications. Would be correct only with mild ascites and no biochemical derangement (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).

Haematocrit 0.48, oliguria, creatinine rise, hypoalbuminaemia, ascites above the umbilicus and pleural effusion meet severe OHSS criteria. Management is admission for IV fluids, prophylactic LMWH (high VTE risk), strict input/output and paracentesis for symptomatic tense ascites (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).

Critical OHSS labelling is wrong because critical OHSS requires anuria, ARDS, thromboembolism or multiorgan failure; she has oliguria not anuria and normal oxygenation. Would be correct only at the critical end of the spectrum, not now (RANZCOG OHSS).
Large-volume saline boluses is wrong because aggressive crystalloid worsens third-spacing and ascites in OHSS. Would be correct in haemorrhagic shock, not OHSS (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).

Withholding thromboprophylaxis is wrong because OHSS is markedly hypercoagulable (raised oestrogen, haemoconcentration, immobility) and early LMWH is recommended. Would never be correct in severe OHSS (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE).

explanation.summary: For unexplained infertility in a woman under 36 with normal investigations and short duration, expectant management with timed intercourse is appropriate. Stimulated IUI is considered if pregnancy has not occurred after a further 6 months, and IVF is offered for prolonged unexplained infertility, age >=36, or after failed IUI cycles (RANZCOG; NICE CG156).
key_points: Investigate at 12 months if female <35; at 6 months if female >=35; earlier if known cause
IUI is first ART step for mild male factor or ovulatory disorder responsive to mild stimulation; offers little benefit in unexplained infertility with normal semen
IVF first-line if: bilateral tubal disease, severe male factor, failed IUI, age >=40, advanced endometriosis
Single embryo transfer minimises multiple pregnancy risk
explanation.pearls: The female partner's age is the single strongest predictor of ART outcome; don't delay referral past 35.

options.rationale: Another 12 months of timed intercourse is wrong because women >=35 with infertility >=6-12 months warrant referral now; spending another year erodes cumulative live-birth probability, especially with low AMH. Would be correct only in women under 35 still inside the 12-month diagnostic window (RANZCOG; NICE CG156).
At 38 with AMH 6 pmol/L and AFC 6 (low ovarian reserve), IVF gives the highest cycle live-birth chance and allows aneuploidy management; IUI is less effective in this context (NICE CG156; RANZCOG).

Three IUI cycles is wrong because IUI offers minimal incremental benefit over expectant management in unexplained infertility with low ovarian reserve at 38, and cycles spent on IUI reduce her usable IVF window. Would be correct only for mild male factor or cervical factor infertility with adequate reserve and younger age (NICE CG156).

Clomifene alone is wrong because she is already ovulating; clomifene targets anovulation and does not address her age-related and reserve-related decline. Would be correct only in WHO-II anovulation (e.g. PCOS) (NICE CG156).

Donor oocyte IVF as first line is wrong because at 38 with AMH 6, autologous IVF still has reasonable cumulative live-birth probability; donor oocytes are reserved for very low reserve plus repeated autologous failure or POI. Would be correct only after failed autologous IVF or POI (RANZCOG; NICE).

explanation.summary: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after 12 months in women <35 (or 6 months in women >=35) of regular unprotected intercourse. Workup is parallel in both partners: semen analysis (WHO 2021 criteria), ovulation assessment (mid-luteal progesterone), ovarian reserve (AMH + AFC), TSH and prolactin, and tubal patency assessment by HyCoSy or HSG (RANZCOG; NICE CG156; ASRM).
key_points: Earlier workup if known anovulation, prior pelvic surgery, chemo, endometriosis, varicocele, cryptorchidism
Semen analysis: 2 samples, 4 weeks apart, after 2 to 7 days abstinence
AMH and AFC predict response to ovarian stimulation, NOT spontaneous conception
Day-2 to day-5 FSH and oestradiol are an alternative ovarian reserve marker
explanation.pearls: 30 to 40% of infertility has a male factor component; never defer semen analysis.

options.rationale: Reassure and review in 4 months is wrong because infertility is defined as 12 months in women <35 or 6 months in women >=35; this 36-year-old has crossed that threshold and ovarian reserve declines steeply through this age band. Would be correct only in a woman <35 within the 12-month window (RANZCOG; NICE CG156; ASRM).

At >=35 years, investigation is recommended after 6 months of unprotected intercourse; investigation is parallel in both partners and includes semen analysis (WHO 2021), ovulation assessment, ovarian reserve (AMH + AFC), thyroid, prolactin and tubal patency assessment by HyCoSy or HSG (RANZCOG; NICE CG156; ASRM).

AMH and ultrasound only, deferring semen analysis, is wrong because male factor accounts for 30-40% of infertility and semen analysis is the single most informative test; deferring delays diagnosis. Would never be correct in initial workup (RANZCOG; ASRM).

Immediate IVF without baseline tests is wrong because baseline tests identify treatable causes (anovulation, tubal blockage, male factor) and guide stimulation protocol choice; IVF without a semen analysis can miss severe male factor needing ICSI. Would be correct only when baseline workup has been completed and IVF chosen (RANZCOG; NICE CG156).

Diagnostic laparoscopy first is wrong because laparoscopy is not first-line workup; non-invasive tests (semen analysis, hormones, HyCoSy/HSG) come first. Would be correct only with strong suspicion of endometriosis or adhesive disease after non-invasive workup (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Ovarian reserve testing in subfertility uses anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle count (AFC) as the primary measures, with day-3 FSH and oestradiol as adjuncts. Low values (AMH under 7 pmol/L, AFC under 5-7 follicles) predict poor response to controlled ovarian stimulation in IVF, lower oocyte yields per cycle, and may warrant higher gonadotrophin doses, dual stimulation (DuoStim), oocyte accumulation strategies across multiple cycles, or earlier consideration of donor oocytes. High values (AMH over 35 pmol/L, AFC over 24) predict ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome risk and lower the gonadotrophin starting dose. POSEIDON poor-responder classification stratifies women into four groups based on age (under or over 35) and ovarian reserve, guiding personalised stimulation protocols. Critically, AMH and AFC do not predict per-oocyte live birth rate, spontaneous conception likelihood, or absolute time to menopause - many women with low AMH conceive naturally, and the markers should not be used to discourage attempts at natural conception.
key_points: Day-3 FSH >10 IU/L with oestradiol <200 pmol/L = diminished reserve; high E2 can mask FSH
AMH <7 pmol/L = low reserve; >35 pmol/L = high (PCOS-like) with OHSS risk
AFC <7 (total both ovaries) = poor responder
POSEIDON criteria integrate age + reserve markers + prior cycle response
explanation.pearls: AMH and antral follicle count are the best validated predictors of ovarian response to controlled ovarian stimulation, but neither reliably predicts spontaneous conception, time to menopause, or live birth rate per oocyte. Low AMH counsels for IVF strategy, not against trying naturally (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

options.rationale: AMH and AFC are the best validated markers of ovarian response to controlled ovarian stimulation in IVF (low values predict poor response and high values predict OHSS risk); they do NOT reliably predict natural conception probability, time to menopause, or live-birth rate per oocyte (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

Saying AMH <5 confirms POI is wrong because POI requires amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea PLUS FSH >25 IU/L on two readings 4 weeks apart in a woman <40; AMH alone does not diagnose POI. Would be correct only after biochemical and clinical POI criteria are met (ESHRE POI Guideline; AMS).
High FSH predicting high yield is wrong because elevated day-3 FSH reflects reduced reserve and predicts poor response to stimulation; the relationship is inverse. (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

AMH predicting years to menopause is wrong because AMH correlates with biological ovarian age at a population level but cannot reliably predict an individual's menopause timing; clinical predictors must be integrated. Would be correct only as population-level prediction, not individual counselling (ESHRE POI Guideline; SREI).

AFC >4 excluding POSEIDON poor-responder is wrong because POSEIDON integrates age, AMH, AFC and previous stimulation response; AFC of 5 with AMH 4 can still fall into poor-prognosis categories. Would never single-handedly exclude POSEIDON classification (ESHRE POSEIDON).

explanation.summary: On day-3 cycle bloods, a high oestradiol (>250 to 290 pmol/L) suppresses FSH via negative feedback and can mask diminished ovarian reserve. AMH (not cycle-dependent) and AFC are more reliable in this setting; both low here, indicating diminished reserve and warranting prompt referral (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).
key_points: Day-3 FSH must be interpreted alongside oestradiol
High oestradiol with apparently normal FSH = uninterpretable; reserve still may be low
AMH is the most reliable single ovarian reserve marker; not cycle-dependent
AFC adds prognostic information and should be measured early follicular
explanation.pearls: A 'normal' day-3 FSH with high oestradiol can be falsely reassuring.

options.rationale: Saying normal day-3 FSH excludes diminished reserve is wrong because high day-3 oestradiol (>250-290 pmol/L) suppresses FSH by negative feedback and falsely normalises the level; FSH cannot be interpreted in isolation. Would be correct only with confirmed low/normal day-3 oestradiol (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

Day-3 oestradiol >250 pmol/L suppresses FSH and renders the FSH uninterpretable; the AMH (6 pmol/L, low) and AFC (7, low) both indicate diminished ovarian reserve and should drive counselling and ART planning (ESHRE POSEIDON; RANZCOG).

LH:FSH ratio confirming PCOS is wrong because LH:FSH ratios were dropped from PCOS diagnostic criteria; PCOS is diagnosed by Rotterdam criteria (oligo/anovulation, hyperandrogenism, polycystic ovaries on ultrasound or raised AMH). Would never confirm PCOS alone (2023 International PCOS Guideline).

Confirming POI is wrong because POI requires FSH >25 IU/L on two readings 4 weeks apart plus menstrual disturbance in a woman <40; low AMH/AFC alone is diminished reserve, not POI. Would be correct only with biochemical and menstrual POI criteria met (ESHRE POI Guideline; AMS).

Repeat day-3 bloods without changing strategy is wrong because the high oestradiol is the interpretive problem; AMH (cycle-independent) and AFC are the appropriate markers regardless of cycle day. Would be correct only after timing or technique is corrected (ESHRE POSEIDON).

explanation.summary: At PCOS diagnosis, the 2023 international guideline recommends a baseline 75 g OGTT, fasting lipid panel and BP measurement, with repeat OGTT every 1 to 3 years based on risk factors. Fasting insulin and HOMA-IR are not recommended for clinical use (2023 International PCOS Guideline; Jean Hailes).
key_points: OGTT preferred over HbA1c or fasting glucose for IGT detection in PCOS
Lipid screening recommended at diagnosis
BP, weight and waist circumference monitored yearly
Increased background risk of T2DM, GDM, dyslipidaemia, OSA, NAFLD, endometrial cancer
explanation.pearls: PCOS confers a 4-fold lifetime risk of T2DM independent of BMI; OGTT is the preferred screen.

options.rationale: The 2023 international PCOS guideline recommends a 75 g OGTT (preferred over fasting glucose or HbA1c due to higher sensitivity in PCOS), a fasting lipid panel and blood pressure measurement at diagnosis, with repeat OGTT every 1 to 3 years based on risk factors (2023 International PCOS Guideline; Jean Hailes).

Fasting glucose plus HbA1c alone is wrong because both have lower sensitivity than the 75 g OGTT for detecting impaired glucose tolerance in PCOS, where post-load hyperglycaemia is the dominant abnormality; the 2023 PCOS guideline explicitly prefers OGTT. Would be correct only when OGTT is impractical and an initial low-yield screen is accepted (2023 International PCOS Guideline).

Annual fasting insulin is wrong because the international guideline does not recommend fasting insulin or HOMA-IR for clinical use due to assay variability and lack of management impact; OGTT and lipid screening are the recommended tools. Would be correct only in research settings (2023 International PCOS Guideline).

Cardiac MRI plus stress testing is wrong because PCOS diagnosis does not warrant imaging-based cardiac assessment; risk stratification uses traditional calculators with intensified screening intervals. Would be correct only with symptoms or risk-calculator-driven indication for ischaemia testing (2023 International PCOS Guideline; NHMRC CV risk).

Liver biopsy is wrong because metabolic screening at PCOS diagnosis uses non-invasive markers (LFTs, FIB-4, ultrasound) for NAFLD when suspected; biopsy is reserved for staging significant fibrosis. Would never be correct at initial diagnosis (2023 International PCOS Guideline).

explanation.summary: After first-line COCP plus NSAID failure in suspected endometriosis, second-line medical options include progestogen-only therapy (LNG-IUS, dienogest, DMPA, etonogestrel implant) or a 3 to 6 month course of GnRH analogue with add-back HRT. Laparoscopic excision is offered when medical therapy fails, when fertility is impaired, or when deep infiltrating disease is suspected (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).
key_points: Endometriomas: laparoscopic cystectomy improves pain but may reduce ovarian reserve; weigh against fertility plans
GnRH analogues require add-back HRT if used >6 months to protect bone density
MRI for surgical planning of deep infiltrating endometriosis
Opioids are not recommended for chronic pelvic pain
explanation.pearls: Laparoscopic excision is preferred over ablation for deep infiltrating endometriosis.

options.rationale: If first-line continuous COCP plus NSAID fails, second-line options include progestogen-only therapy (LNG-IUS, dienogest, DMPA) or a short course of GnRH analogue with add-back HRT to control symptoms and reduce vasomotor and bone-density side effects; this is preferable to surgery in a woman who declines it (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

Hysterectomy with BSO is wrong because definitive surgery in a 28-year-old with endometriosis requires completed childbearing and severe refractory symptoms after thorough medical and conservative surgical management; she has not yet had second-line therapy. Would be correct only after exhausting medical and conservative surgical options in a woman who has completed her family (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

Tranexamic acid is wrong because it targets heavy menstrual bleeding rather than endometriosis-associated pain, and continuous COCP suppresses cyclical bleeding anyway. Would be correct only for HMB, not endometriosis pain (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

Empirical IVF is wrong because IVF is for endometriosis-associated infertility (or advanced disease with planned pregnancy), not for pain management in a woman not currently planning conception. Would be correct only when fertility is the goal (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022; RANZCOG).

Long-acting opioids are wrong because chronic opioid use in endometriosis pain causes dependence, hyperalgesia and no disease-modifying effect; hormonal treatment or laparoscopic excision targets the disease instead. Would be correct only as short-term peri-operative analgesia, never chronic (ESHRE Endometriosis 2022).

explanation.summary: The FIGO leiomyoma classification categorises fibroids by location: type 0 (pedunculated intracavitary), type 1 (less than 50% intramural extension), type 2 (50% or more intramural), type 3 (intramural abutting endometrium), type 4 (intramural), type 5 (subserosal more than 50% intramural), type 6 (subserosal less than 50% intramural), type 7 (subserosal pedunculated), type 8 (parasitic, broad ligament, cervical). Submucosal fibroids (types 0-2) distort the endometrial cavity, reduce implantation and pregnancy rates, and cause heavy menstrual bleeding. Hysteroscopic myomectomy is the fertility-sparing intervention of choice and combines treatment of HMB and improvement of fertility. Type 0 and small type 1 fibroids resect in a single procedure; type 2 fibroids often need a staged second-look hysteroscopy at 6-8 weeks. LNG-IUS requires an undistorted cavity and is therefore inappropriate when significant submucosal disease is present. Uterine artery embolisation and hysterectomy are reserved for women who do not desire fertility. Pregnancy is usually delayed 3-6 months post-resection.
key_points: FIGO 0 to 1 fibroids almost always removable hysteroscopically
FIGO 2 fibroids >=50% intramural may need staged resection
Laparoscopic or open myomectomy for intramural or subserosal causing symptoms in fertility-seeking women
Risk of caesarean delivery after deep myometrial myomectomy due to scar integrity
explanation.pearls: FIGO type 0-2 (submucosal) fibroids distort the endometrial cavity and reduce implantation rates; hysteroscopic myomectomy improves both fertility and heavy menstrual bleeding, with a 30-50% pregnancy rate within 12 months. Type 2 fibroids may need a second-look hysteroscopy at 6-8 weeks (RANZCOG; AAGL).

options.rationale: FIGO 0-2 submucosal fibroids distorting the cavity reduce fertility and cause HMB; hysteroscopic myomectomy is the fertility-sparing intervention of choice per RANZCOG: Fibroids and AAGL Fibroids guidance.

LNG-IUS is wrong because cavity-distorting submucosal fibroids contraindicate Mirena placement (high expulsion, reduced efficacy) and the LNG-IUS is contraceptive rather than fertility-enhancing in a woman trying to conceive. Would be correct only for HMB without cavity distortion and without conception plans (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

UAE is wrong because uterine artery embolisation is not recommended for women who wish to conceive due to reduced ovarian reserve from non-target embolisation, raised placental complication risk and uncertain fertility outcome. Would be correct only for women with completed family or those declining surgery (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

Hysterectomy is definitive for HMB and fibroid bulk but ends fertility; would be correct if the patient had completed childbearing, but this patient is actively trying to conceive per RANZCOG: Fibroids and NICE NG88.

Long-term GnRH analogue is wrong because GnRH analogues induce hypogonadism and suppress ovulation; they are short-term (3-6 month) pre-operative or bridging agents and are not a fertility-preserving long-term solution. Would be correct only as pre-operative shrinkage before myomectomy (RANZCOG; NICE NG88).

explanation.summary: POI confers significantly increased risk of osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and cognitive decline. Physiological-dose HRT (oestradiol with progestogen if uterus present) until at least the average age of natural menopause (around 51) is the cornerstone of management. HRT is NOT contraceptive; spontaneous pregnancy occurs in ~5 to 10% (ESHRE POI Guideline 2024; AMS POI; Endocrine Society).
key_points: Diagnosis: amenorrhoea/oligomenorrhoea >=4 months + FSH >25 IU/L on 2 readings 4+ weeks apart in woman <40
Workup: karyotype, FMR1 premutation, adrenal (21-OH) and thyroid antibodies, baseline DXA
HRT options: oral or transdermal oestradiol + cyclical progestogen or LNG-IUS
Counselling: HRT is not contraceptive; spontaneous pregnancy ~5 to 10%; donor oocyte IVF main fertility pathway
explanation.pearls: Discuss contraception separately - HRT is not contraceptive.

options.rationale: POI confers significantly increased risk of osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease and cognitive decline; physiological-dose HRT (oestradiol with progestogen if uterus present) until at least age 51 reduces these risks and treats vasomotor and genitourinary symptoms (ESHRE POI Guideline 2024; AMS POI; Endocrine Society).

Bisphosphonate first-line is wrong because POI is fundamentally an oestrogen-deficiency state; physiological HRT addresses bone, cardiovascular, vasomotor and genitourinary needs simultaneously, while bisphosphonates only target bone. Would be correct only when HRT is contraindicated or established osteoporosis fails to respond (AMS POI; ESHRE POI Guideline 2024).

Calling COCP equivalent to HRT lifelong is wrong because while COCP is an acceptable alternative (especially when contraception is needed - spontaneous ovulation can occur in POI), physiological HRT generally provides better bone protection; both should continue at least to age 51 rather than truly lifelong. Would be correct only with the COCP-HRT equivalence overstated and the lifelong claim modified (ESHRE POI Guideline 2024; AMS POI).

Defer HRT 6 months is wrong because delay in oestrogen replacement accelerates bone loss, cardiovascular risk and vasomotor/urogenital symptoms; POI is not managed like natural menopause, where watchful waiting might be acceptable. (ESHRE POI Guideline 2024; AMS POI).

Topical vaginal oestrogen alone is wrong because vaginal oestrogen treats genitourinary symptoms only with negligible systemic absorption; it provides no bone or cardiovascular protection. Would be correct only as adjunct to systemic HRT for persistent vulvovaginal symptoms (AMS POI).

explanation.summary: Hypertension >=160/100 (uncontrolled or with vascular disease) is UKMEC category 4 for combined hormonal contraception. Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, LNG-IUS) are UKMEC 1 to 2 and are appropriate alternatives. DMPA carries a UKMEC 3 rating at this BP level due to vascular and lipid effects (FSRH UKMEC 2016).
key_points: BP 140-159/90-99: COCP is UKMEC 3; progestogen-only methods UKMEC 1-2
BP >=160/100: COCP is UKMEC 4; progestogen-only methods UKMEC 1-2; DMPA UKMEC 3
Hypertension with established vascular disease: COCP UKMEC 4
Hypertension is the single most common cardiovascular risk encountered in contraception
explanation.pearls: UKMEC 4 means 'unacceptable health risk' - the method must not be used.

options.rationale: Continuing COCP is wrong because systolic >=160 or diastolic >=100 is UKMEC category 4 (unacceptable risk) for combined hormonal contraception; waiting 3 months exposes her to stroke/MI risk. Would never be correct at UKMEC 4 levels (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

Hypertension >=160/100 is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception, contraindicating COCP. Progestogen-only methods (POP, implant, LNG-IUS) are UKMEC 1 to 2 in hypertension; DMPA is UKMEC 2 in BP 140-159/90-99 and UKMEC 3 in BP >=160/100 due to its slight adverse lipid and vascular effects (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

Switching to patch or ring is wrong because UKMEC categorises all combined hormonal methods (pill, patch, ring) the same in hypertension; the route does not modify oestrogen-driven vascular risk at this BP. (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

Adding antihypertensive and lower-dose COCP is wrong because FSRH guidance is to avoid combined methods if BP is uncontrolled or vascular disease is present; treated hypertension is still UKMEC 3 with adequate control and UKMEC 4 if uncontrolled. Would be correct only when BP is well-controlled in low-risk younger women (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

Tubal ligation as the only option is wrong because progestogen-only LARC methods (implant, LNG-IUS) are highly effective, reversible and UKMEC 1-2 in hypertension; offering sterilisation only is reductive. Would be correct only when she explicitly declines reversible methods (FSRH UKMEC 2016; RANZCOG: Contraception).

explanation.summary: Letrozole is first-line ovulation induction in PCOS, achieving higher live birth rates and lower multiple pregnancy rates than clomifene (PPCOS II trial). Metformin is an adjunct (particularly with BMI >25 or impaired glucose tolerance). Gonadotrophin injection and laparoscopic ovarian drilling are second-line (2023 International PCOS Guideline; ASRM; RANZCOG).
key_points: Letrozole: 2.5 mg daily day 2-6; titrate to 5 mg then 7.5 mg if anovulatory
Monitor first cycle with ovulation tracking (LH urine or follicular USS)
Lifestyle intervention foundational - aim for 5 to 10% weight reduction in BMI >25
Refer to fertility specialist if anovulatory after 3 to 6 ovulatory cycles or age >=35
explanation.pearls: Letrozole is teratogenic if taken during early pregnancy; use only in early follicular phase and confirm non-pregnancy.

options.rationale: The 2023 international PCOS guideline and ASRM both recommend letrozole as first-line ovulation induction in PCOS for anovulatory infertility; letrozole achieves higher ovulation, pregnancy and live birth rates than clomifene with lower multiple pregnancy risk (2023 International PCOS Guideline; ASRM; RANZCOG).

Clomifene is wrong because PPCOS II and subsequent meta-analyses showed letrozole achieves higher ovulation, pregnancy and live birth rates with lower multiple pregnancy risk; clomifene is now second-line where letrozole is unavailable or fails. Would be correct only if letrozole is contraindicated or inaccessible (2023 International PCOS Guideline; ASRM).

Metformin monotherapy is wrong because it gives lower ovulation, pregnancy and live birth rates than letrozole; it is an adjunct (particularly in BMI >25 or IGT) rather than primary ovulation induction. Would be correct only as adjunct to letrozole or clomifene (2023 International PCOS Guideline; ASRM).

Injectable gonadotrophins are wrong because they are second-line after oral failure due to higher cost, OHSS risk, multiple-pregnancy risk and need for daily follicular monitoring. Would be correct only after letrozole/clomifene resistance (2023 International PCOS Guideline; RANZCOG).

Laparoscopic ovarian drilling is wrong because it is reserved for women with clomifene/letrozole resistance, particularly when laparoscopy is already indicated for another reason; first-line surgical treatment in treatment-naive PCOS would skip the evidence-based oral therapy. Would be correct only as second-line after oral failure (2023 International PCOS Guideline; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Dopamine agonists (cabergoline preferred) are first-line for prolactinomas, including macroprolactinomas with chiasmal compression; the majority show tumour shrinkage and visual recovery within weeks to months. Transsphenoidal surgery is reserved for medical failure, intolerance, apoplexy or progressive visual loss despite treatment (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011; eTG: Endocrinology).
key_points: Cabergoline 0.25 mg twice weekly, titrate to prolactin response; monitor for impulse control disorder and (high cumulative dose) cardiac valve effects
Repeat MRI at 3 to 6 months to assess shrinkage; visual fields at similar interval
Pre-pregnancy planning: bromocriptine has more safety data than cabergoline in early pregnancy
Pituitary apoplexy = emergency: glucocorticoid replacement + neurosurgical referral
explanation.pearls: Don't add an SSRI or antipsychotic to a patient with new amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea without first checking prolactin and considering prolactinoma.

options.rationale: Dopamine agonists (cabergoline preferred over bromocriptine for efficacy and tolerability) are first-line for macroprolactinomas including those with visual field deficits; tumour shrinkage and visual recovery occur in the majority within weeks to months. Surgery is reserved for failure of medical therapy or apoplexy (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011; eTG: Endocrinology).

Urgent transsphenoidal surgery is wrong because prolactinomas, unlike other pituitary adenomas, are exquisitely sensitive to medical therapy; dopamine agonists shrink the tumour and restore vision in most cases within weeks. Would be correct only with failed/intolerant dopamine agonist therapy, pituitary apoplexy or rapidly progressive visual loss not responding to medical therapy (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011).

External beam radiotherapy is wrong because radiotherapy is third-line after failed surgery or for residual aggressive disease; slow onset and risk of hypopituitarism make it unsuitable for treatment-naive prolactinoma. Would be correct only in refractory or aggressive prolactinoma after surgery (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011).

Observation is wrong because a macroadenoma with visual field defect requires active treatment; chiasmal compression untreated causes permanent visual loss, and dopamine agonists are highly effective. Would be correct only for asymptomatic microprolactinomas with no compressive features (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011).

COCP alone is wrong because it treats symptomatic amenorrhoea without addressing the tumour or visual compromise, and can mask prolactin monitoring. Would be correct only for microprolactinomas with stable imaging where contraception/menstrual regulation is the priority (Endocrine Society Hyperprolactinaemia 2011).

explanation.summary: Severe/critical OHSS with haemoconcentration, oliguria, tense ascites and respiratory compromise requires admission, judicious IV crystalloid (albumin if albumin <30 g/L), VTE prophylaxis (OHSS confers independent high VTE risk), strict fluid balance and paracentesis for tense ascites or respiratory/renal compromise. Diuretics are contraindicated until intravascular volume is restored (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE OHSS).
key_points: Critical OHSS thresholds: Hct >0.55, WCC >25, tense ascites, ARDS, VTE, hepatorenal dysfunction, anuria
Severe OHSS thresholds: Hct >0.45, WCC >15, clinical ascites, oliguria, hypoalbuminaemia <35 g/L
VTE prophylaxis: enoxaparin throughout admission and at least until clinical resolution; longer if pregnancy ensues
Continued worsening if pregnancy occurs (HCG-driven) - persistent symptoms warrant beta-hCG check
explanation.pearls: OHSS is one of the few conditions where IV albumin is routinely used; diuretics are explicitly contraindicated until intravascular volume is restored.

options.rationale: Severe/critical OHSS with haemoconcentration (Hct >0.50), WCC >20, oliguria, tense ascites and respiratory compromise requires admission, IV crystalloid (with albumin in severe hypoalbuminaemia), VTE prophylaxis (high independent VTE risk in OHSS), strict fluid balance and paracentesis to relieve tense ascites/respiratory compromise/renal dysfunction (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE OHSS).

Discharge home is wrong because haemoconcentration, oliguria, tense ascites and respiratory compromise meet severe OHSS criteria that mandate inpatient IV management and close monitoring; outpatient management risks VTE, renal failure and rapid deterioration. Would be correct only for mild OHSS with adequate oral intake (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE OHSS).

Furosemide infusion is wrong because diuretics in an intravascularly depleted, third-spaced state worsen haemoconcentration and renal dysfunction; volume replacement must precede any diuretic consideration. Would be correct only after intravascular volume is restored and pulmonary oedema persists, not first-line in OHSS (RANZCOG OHSS; ESHRE OHSS).

Laparotomy with oophorectomy is wrong because hyperstimulated ovaries are friable and bleed readily; surgery is reserved for torsion, rupture with significant haemorrhage or ectopic pregnancy. Would be correct only for surgical complications, not for severe OHSS itself (RANZCOG OHSS).

Broad-spectrum antibiotics and antivirals are wrong because the elevated WCC in OHSS reflects the inflammatory state rather than infection; empirical antibiotics are not indicated without clinical evidence of infection. Would be correct only when superimposed infection is clinically suspected (RANZCOG OHSS).

explanation.summary: Contraception choice in women with current or past breast cancer is governed by the UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC), adopted by Australian practice. Current breast cancer (within 5 years of diagnosis) is UKMEC 4 (absolute contraindication) for all hormonal contraception, including combined oral contraceptive pill, progestogen-only pill, depot medroxyprogesterone acetate, etonogestrel implant, and levonorgestrel intrauterine system - despite the LNG-IUS often being framed as 'local action'. Past breast cancer with 5 years free of disease is UKMEC 3 for hormonal methods (theoretical risk outweighs benefit). The copper intrauterine device is UKMEC 1 in all phases and is the preferred long-acting reversible option. Female sterilisation by tubal ligation or salpingectomy is the highest-efficacy permanent option. Male partner vasectomy is equally effective and lower-morbidity. Barrier methods are UKMEC 1 but have higher typical-use failure rates and are reserved for women who decline the above.
key_points: Current breast cancer (any subtype, any time on treatment): UKMEC 4 for all hormonal methods
Past breast cancer (>5 years remission): UKMEC 3 for hormonal methods
Copper IUD: UKMEC 1 in current and past breast cancer
Tamoxifen is teratogenic - contraception is mandatory throughout treatment and for 2 months after
explanation.pearls: Current breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for ALL hormonal contraception including LNG-IUS - the 'local action' framing of the levonorgestrel IUD does not change the categorisation. Copper IUD (UKMEC 1) or female sterilisation are the appropriate highly-effective options (UKMEC 2016; RANZCOG).

options.rationale: Current and past breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for ALL hormonal contraception (combined and progestogen-only). The copper IUD is UKMEC 1 and is the recommended highly effective reversible option in a woman with breast cancer who has completed her family; female sterilisation is also acceptable (FSRH UKMEC 2016; RANZCOG: Contraception).

LNG-IUS is wrong because current breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for the LNG-IUS; despite local progestogen action, systemic exposure means it is contraindicated in current/recent breast cancer (UKMEC 3 only when remission is >5 years). Would be correct only after >5 years' disease-free remission and only as UKMEC 3 (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

COCP is wrong because current/recent breast cancer is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception due to oestrogen-driven recurrence risk; absolute contraindication. Would never be correct in current/recent breast cancer (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

Etonogestrel implant is wrong because UKMEC 4 applies to all progestogen-only methods (implant, POP, DMPA, LNG-IUS) in current breast cancer; the systemic progestogen exposure is unacceptable. Would never be correct in current breast cancer (FSRH UKMEC 2016).
DMPA is wrong because depot progestogen is UKMEC 4 in current breast cancer; all hormonal methods are contraindicated. Would never be correct in current breast cancer (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

explanation.summary: Contraception choice in systemic lupus erythematosus integrates disease activity, organ involvement, and antiphospholipid antibody status (anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-GP1, lupus anticoagulant). Active disease or positive aPL antibodies makes combined hormonal contraception UKMEC 4 (absolute contraindication) because oestrogen significantly increases the thrombotic risk that aPL antibodies already confer. Progestogen-only methods are generally safer: the LNG-IUS (UKMEC 1-2 depending on aPL status) is the preferred LARC, with the copper IUD (UKMEC 1) the alternative if hormone-free is desired. DMPA is UKMEC 3 due to small VTE association and effect on lipids and bone density. Progestogen-only pill and etonogestrel implant are UKMEC 3 in active disease. Pregnancy planning should occur with rheumatology in stable disease, with hydroxychloroquine continued, and aspirin and low molecular weight heparin added for aPL-positive women through pregnancy and 6 weeks postpartum. Folate supplementation, vaccination review, and counselling about flare risk in early pregnancy are part of pre-conception care.
key_points: Triple-positive antiphospholipid profile carries highest thrombosis risk
Stable SLE without antiphospholipid antibodies: COCP UKMEC 2
Pregnancy planning in antiphospholipid syndrome requires multidisciplinary management with aspirin +/- LMWH
Hydroxychloroquine is safe in pregnancy and reduces lupus flares and obstetric APS complications
explanation.pearls: In SLE, positive (or unknown) antiphospholipid antibodies make combined hormonal contraception UKMEC 4 (absolute contraindication) because of synergistic VTE and arterial thrombosis risk. LNG-IUS (UKMEC 1-2) and copper IUD (UKMEC 1) are first-line LARC (FSRH UKMEC 2016; EULAR Lupus).

options.rationale: COCP is wrong because SLE with positive (or unknown) antiphospholipid antibodies is UKMEC 4 for all combined hormonal contraception due to substantially elevated VTE and arterial thrombosis risk; lowering the oestrogen dose does not change the category. Would never be correct with APL positive (FSRH UKMEC 2016; EULAR Lupus).

In SLE with positive antiphospholipid antibodies, the LNG-IUS is UKMEC 1 to 2: highly effective, no systemic oestrogen, minimal interaction with hydroxychloroquine, low VTE risk, and acceptable in a woman who has completed her family. The Cu-IUD (UKMEC 1) is also acceptable but the LNG-IUS additionally reduces menstrual blood loss (relevant if anticoagulation is initiated later) (FSRH UKMEC 2016; EULAR Lupus).

Combined ring is wrong because UKMEC 4 applies to all combined methods regardless of route in APL-positive SLE; route does not modify thrombotic risk. Would never be correct in this group (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

DMPA is wrong because it is UKMEC 3 in APL-positive SLE (adverse lipid profile and small but increased VTE association), so an IUD is preferred. Would be correct only when LARC IUDs are not feasible and benefits are judged to outweigh risks (FSRH UKMEC 2016; EULAR Lupus).

Condoms alone is wrong because typical-use failure ~13%/year is inadequate when she has completed her family and seeks reliable contraception; effective LARC is available and appropriate. Would be correct only when she explicitly preferred barrier methods after counselling (FSRH UKMEC 2016; RANZCOG: Contraception).

explanation.summary: After malabsorptive bariatric procedures (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, biliopancreatic diversion), oral hormonal contraception has reduced and unreliable absorption. LARCs that bypass the gut (LNG-IUS, Cu-IUD, etonogestrel implant, DMPA injection) are preferred. Restrictive procedures (sleeve gastrectomy, gastric band) do not impair absorption to the same degree. Pregnancy should be delayed 12 to 24 months post-bariatric surgery (FSRH UKMEC 2016; ASMBS/ACOG Bariatric Pregnancy; RANZCOG).
key_points: Malabsorptive procedures (RYGB, BPD): avoid oral hormonal contraception
Restrictive procedures (sleeve, band): oral methods acceptable if absorbed
Rapid return of fertility post-weight loss; high unintended pregnancy risk
Multidisciplinary pre-conception planning: micronutrient repletion, optimised glycaemia, mental health
explanation.pearls: After Roux-en-Y, treat oral hormonal contraception as you would an enzyme-inducing medication - assume unreliable absorption.

options.rationale: After malabsorptive bariatric procedures (Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, biliopancreatic diversion), oral hormonal contraceptive absorption is unreliable; LARCs that bypass the gut (LNG-IUS, Cu-IUD, etonogestrel implant) are preferred. The COCP also carries elevated VTE risk in the post-operative period and may be UKMEC 3 to 4 with persistent obesity and other risk factors; pregnancy should be delayed 12 to 24 months post-bariatric surgery (FSRH UKMEC 2016; ASMBS/ACOG; RANZCOG).

COCP after RYGB is wrong because the malabsorptive bypass impairs absorption of oral hormonal contraception, making efficacy unreliable regardless of condom backup; FSRH advises against oral methods after malabsorptive bariatric surgery. Would be correct only after restrictive procedures (sleeve gastrectomy, band) where absorption is preserved (FSRH UKMEC 2016; ASMBS/ACOG Bariatric Pregnancy).

POP is wrong because, like the COCP, POP absorption is impaired after Roux-en-Y; the narrow timing window worsens the reliability problem. Would be correct only after restrictive procedures (FSRH UKMEC 2016).

Fertility awareness is wrong because typical-use failure ~24%/year is incompatible with the need for reliable contraception, and post-bariatric menstrual irregularity makes cycle tracking unreliable. Would be correct only as personal preference after counselling about high failure rates (Therapeutic Guidelines: Contraception).

Immediate pregnancy attempts is wrong because ASMBS/ACOG and RANZCOG recommend deferring pregnancy 12-24 months post-bariatric surgery to allow weight stabilisation, micronutrient optimisation (B12, iron, folate, vitamin D) and reduce SGA, prematurity and nutritional deficiency in the fetus. Would be correct only after the 12-24 month interval and nutritional optimisation (ASMBS/ACOG Bariatric Pregnancy; RANZCOG).

explanation.summary: Bacterial vaginosis is diagnosed clinically by Amsel criteria (3 of 4: thin grey-white discharge, pH > 4.5, positive whiff with KOH, clue cells) or by Nugent score >= 7 on Gram stain. First-line treatment is oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5-7 days.
key_points: Amsel: 3 of 4 (discharge, pH > 4.5, whiff, clue cells)
Nugent score >= 7 confirms BV on Gram stain
Candida: itch, curdy, pH < 4.5, pseudohyphae
Trichomonas: frothy yellow-green, strawberry cervix, motile
Lactobacillus loss is the unifying pathophysiology of BV
explanation.pearls: A positive whiff test plus clue cells is virtually pathognomonic. BV is not classified as an STI but is associated with sexual activity and increases HIV/STI acquisition risk.

sources.label: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

options.rationale: Repeating the same 7-day metronidazole alone is wrong because recurrent BV (>=3 episodes/year) needs re-induction PLUS suppressive maintenance therapy; standard courses alone have high recurrence rates due to residual biofilm. Would be correct only for a first or non-recurrent BV episode (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

options.rationale: Recurrent BV in Australia is managed with re-induction (oral or intravaginal metronidazole) followed by intravaginal metronidazole or clindamycin twice weekly as suppression for several months to reduce recurrence (Australasian STI Guidelines; eTG).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

options.rationale: Reassurance is wrong because all four Amsel criteria are met (homogeneous discharge, pH >4.5, positive whiff test, clue cells); symptomatic BV warrants treatment. Would be correct only with normal discharge and no Amsel criteria met (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

options.rationale: Empirical partner treatment is wrong because routine treatment of male partners is not currently standard in Australian guidelines (though emerging evidence is evolving the picture); suppressive therapy for the index woman is the established next step. Would be correct only within research protocols or jurisdictions adopting recent partner-treatment data (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Bacterial vaginosis

options.rationale: IUD removal is wrong because the copper IUD has not been clearly established as a cause of recurrent BV and removal sacrifices effective contraception; suppressive vaginal therapy should be tried first. Would be correct only after suppressive therapy fails with strong temporal IUD association (Family Planning Australia).

explanation.summary: Patient-applied first-line options for external anogenital warts are imiquimod 5% cream three nights per week up to 16 weeks, or podophyllotoxin 0.5% solution. Clinician-applied options include cryotherapy, TCA and surgical removal. Counsel about HPV vaccination (Gardasil 9 covers HPV 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, 58) regardless of past exposure.
key_points: Imiquimod 5%: 3 nights/week, wash off after 6-10 h, up to 16 weeks
Podophyllotoxin 0.5%: BD x 3 days then 4 days off, up to 4 cycles; avoid in pregnancy
Cryotherapy / TCA / excision are clinician-applied
HPV vaccine still recommended after warts diagnosis
Recurrence common; warts are not cancer-causing types (6/11)
explanation.pearls: HPV 6 and 11 cause 90% of anogenital warts and are not oncogenic. Cervical screening continues per national program; warts diagnosis does not change screening intervals.

sources.label: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts
CDC STI Treatment Guidelines - Anogenital warts

options.rationale: Podophyllotoxin is wrong because it is contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenicity (antimitotic activity); self-application is doubly inappropriate when she is pregnant. Would be correct only outside pregnancy (Australasian STI Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

options.rationale: Imiquimod is wrong because imiquimod has limited pregnancy safety data and is not recommended in pregnancy; the immunomodulatory mechanism creates additional uncertainty. Would be correct only outside pregnancy (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

options.rationale: Cryotherapy is safe in pregnancy and is the preferred first-line treatment for anogenital warts in pregnant women in Australian guidelines; trichloroacetic acid is an alternative. Self-applied options are contraindicated (Australasian STI Guidelines; eTG).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

options.rationale: Watch and wait is wrong because anogenital warts may proliferate dramatically during pregnancy and obstruct the birth canal at term; antenatal treatment reduces burden at delivery rather than waiting for postpartum regression. Would be correct only for very small isolated lesions in late pregnancy (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

options.rationale: Elective caesarean for HPV is wrong because caesarean is not indicated solely for HPV transmission risk; vaginal delivery is acceptable unless warts physically obstruct the birth canal. Would be correct only with mechanical obstruction at term (Australasian STI Guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Anogenital warts

explanation.summary: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis complicating PID, classically due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae, producing RUQ pain with characteristic 'violin-string' adhesions between liver capsule and abdominal wall at laparoscopy. Mild transaminitis is common; biliary imaging is normal. Treatment is the same as for PID (ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole for 14 days).
key_points: Fitz-Hugh-Curtis = chlamydial/gonococcal perihepatitis
RUQ pain + PID + normal biliary tree
Violin-string adhesions on laparoscopy (classical)
Treat as PID (no different regimen)
Other PID complications: TOA, infertility, chronic pelvic pain, 6-10x ectopic risk
explanation.pearls: Suspect Fitz-Hugh-Curtis in any sexually active young woman with RUQ pain and pelvic findings, even when LFTs are only mildly deranged. It is a clinical and supportive imaging diagnosis - laparoscopy is rarely performed.

options.rationale: Viral hepatitis A is wrong because acute HAV would produce more dramatic transaminitis (often >1000 U/L) and prodromal/systemic features but would not explain CMT, mucopurulent cervicitis, positive chlamydia NAAT or pleuritic RUQ pain; the constellation of PID plus RUQ pain points to perihepatitis. Would be correct only with isolated severe transaminitis and HAV serology positive (BMJ Best Practice).

Acute cholecystitis is wrong because ultrasound shows no stones, wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid, and Murphy's sign is negative; the combination essentially excludes cholecystitis. Would be correct with characteristic ultrasound findings and positive Murphy's sign (BMJ Best Practice).

Tubo-ovarian abscess is wrong because pelvic ultrasound shows no TOA (trace free fluid is non-specific) and TOAs typically cause severe pelvic, not primarily RUQ, pain. Would be correct only with an imaged abscess and corresponding clinical picture (Therapeutic Guidelines).
Ruptured ectopic is wrong because serum beta-hCG <5 IU/L excludes pregnancy and therefore ectopic; this is a definitive exclusion. Would never be correct with a negative beta-hCG (RANZCOG).

Fitz-Hugh-Curtis is perihepatitis from haematogenous or transperitoneal spread of chlamydia (or gonorrhoea) complicating PID. RUQ pain with mild transaminitis, normal biliary imaging and concurrent PID with positive chlamydia NAAT fits the classical picture (ASHM; BMJ Best Practice).

explanation.summary: Women on antiretroviral therapy with a viral load below 50 copies/mL near term can have a planned vaginal birth, and intrapartum IV zidovudine is not required. When the low-risk criteria are met (sustained suppression on at least two consecutive tests at least 4 weeks apart, term birth), the perinatal guideline recommends 2 weeks of neonatal zidovudine rather than 4. ASHM advises that formula feeding is the safest choice; if a woman with sustained suppression chooses to breastfeed, she is supported through shared decision-making with specialist monitoring. Planned caesarean at 38-39 weeks is reserved for a raised or unknown viral load near term, with IV zidovudine intrapartum and consideration of neonatal combination prophylaxis.
key_points: VL < 50 at 36 weeks: vaginal birth, no IV zidovudine
Low-risk infant (sustained suppression, term): neonatal zidovudine for 2 weeks
VL 50-1000: individualised; consider CS at 38-39 weeks
VL > 1000 or unknown: pre-labour CS at 38-39 weeks + IV zidovudine + neonatal combination prophylaxis
Avoid invasive monitoring (FSE, FBS) if possible during labour
Formula feeding is the safest choice; breastfeeding by choice is supported through shared decision-making (ASHM 2021)
explanation.pearls: Vertical transmission risk falls to < 1% (and approaches 0.1%) when maternal viral load is suppressed throughout pregnancy. The biggest modifiable factor is maternal adherence, not mode of delivery.

sources.label: Australian HIV guidelines: perinatal (DHHS with Australian commentary, 2023)

options.rationale: Intrapartum IV zidovudine is not needed when the viral load is below 50 copies/mL near term, and 6 weeks of neonatal zidovudine is longer than the low-risk course. The current perinatal guideline recommends 2 weeks rather than 4 when the low-risk criteria are met; longer courses are for infants who do not meet them. (Source: Australian HIV guidelines: perinatal (DHHS with Australian commentary, 2023); ASHM HIV in pregnancy guidelines)
source_refs: Australian HIV guidelines: perinatal (DHHS with Australian commentary, 2023)

options.rationale: A viral load below 50 copies/mL near term removes the indication for caesarean and intrapartum IV zidovudine, and vaginal birth is preferred with suppression. Would be correct only with a viral load of 50 copies/mL or more near term. (Source: ASHM HIV in pregnancy guidelines; RANZCOG HIV in pregnancy)

Caesarean is reserved for an unsuppressed viral load and triple-drug PEP for higher-risk infants. ASHM advises that formula feeding is the safest choice and that clinicians should not actively recommend breastfeeding; a woman who chooses to breastfeed with sustained suppression is supported through shared decision-making, not advised to do so by default. (Source: ASHM HIV in pregnancy guidelines; ASHM HIV infant feeding guidance 2021)

With three consecutive viral loads below 50 copies/mL and a planned term birth she meets the low-risk criteria. Vaginal birth is recommended, intrapartum IV zidovudine is not required, and the perinatal guideline now recommends 2 weeks of neonatal zidovudine rather than 4. Formula feeding is the safest choice per ASHM. (Source: Australian HIV guidelines: perinatal (DHHS with Australian commentary, 2023); ASHM HIV in pregnancy guidelines; ASHM HIV infant feeding guidance 2021)
source_refs: Australian HIV guidelines: perinatal (DHHS with Australian commentary, 2023)

options.rationale: Intrapartum IV zidovudine is reserved for an unsuppressed or unknown viral load, and single-dose neonatal nevirapine is not the Australian regimen; a low-risk infant receives 2 weeks of oral zidovudine. (Source: ASHM HIV in pregnancy guidelines; Australian HIV guidelines: perinatal (DHHS with Australian commentary, 2023))
source_refs: Australian HIV guidelines: perinatal (DHHS with Australian commentary, 2023)

explanation.summary: Non-occupational HIV PEP for a high-risk exposure (condomless receptive anal/vaginal sex with a source with HIV who is not virally suppressed, within 72 hours) is TDF 300 mg + FTC 200 mg + dolutegravir 50 mg daily for 28 days. Baseline tests: HIV Ag/Ab, syphilis, HBV, HCV, beta-hCG, renal function. Follow-up HIV tests at 6 weeks and 3 months (4th gen). Counsel on adherence, side effects, and condom use during follow-up.
key_points: Window: < 72 hours, ideally < 24 hours
Regimen: TDF/FTC + dolutegravir (or raltegravir) x 28 days
Baseline: HIV, syphilis, HBV, HCV, beta-hCG, U&E
Follow-up: HIV Ag/Ab at 6 weeks and 3 months
If source has confirmed undetectable VL, PEP may not be needed (U=U)
explanation.pearls: U=U (Undetectable = Untransmittable): a source with confirmed sustained viral load < 200 copies/mL transmits HIV through sex effectively at zero risk - in those cases, PEP is not required.

options.rationale: Single-dose tenofovir is wrong because PEP requires a 28-day course of combination antiretrovirals; single-dose or monotherapy approaches do not prevent HIV acquisition. Would never be correct as PEP (ASHM PEP guidelines).

Dual NRTI PEP is wrong because Australian guidance now recommends three-drug PEP (TDF/FTC plus dolutegravir or raltegravir) for high-risk exposures; dual NRTI-only PEP is outdated. Would be correct only under older guidelines, not current practice (ASHM).

TAF/FTC/rilpivirine 7 days is wrong because PEP duration is 28 days (not 7) and rilpivirine is not a standard third agent due to drug interactions and resistance considerations. Would never be a recommended PEP regimen (ASHM).

Australian PEP for a high-risk exposure (condomless receptive vaginal intercourse with a source person with HIV not on effective treatment, within 72 hours) is TDF/FTC plus dolutegravir for 28 days, with HIV testing at baseline, 6 weeks, and 3 months post-exposure (ASHM Australian PEP guidelines).

Defer PEP until source viral load is known is wrong because PEP efficacy falls rapidly with time and must start within 72 hours (ideally <24); waiting for source results risks missing the treatment window. Would be correct only if exposure were truly low risk and pending data could rapidly redirect care (ASHM).

explanation.summary: Cisgender women eligible for PrEP receive daily oral TDF 300 mg + FTC 200 mg. Baseline workup: HIV Ag/Ab, HBV serology, HCV antibody, syphilis EIA, gonorrhoea/chlamydia NAAT (multi-site), renal function, beta-hCG. Quarterly: HIV test, STI screen, adherence and side-effect review. Renal function 6-monthly. On-demand (2+1+1) dosing only for cisgender MSM with predictable infrequent exposures. PrEP can be continued in pregnancy if substantial risk persists.
key_points: Daily TDF/FTC for cisgender women (no on-demand)
MSM may use daily or on-demand (2+1+1)
Baseline: HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, GC/CT, renal, beta-hCG
Monitoring: HIV + STI every 3 months; renal every 6 months
HBV must be screened pre-PrEP (rebound on cessation)
explanation.pearls: Exclude acute HIV before initiation: ask about fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, sore throat in the past 6 weeks. Acute HIV may have a still-negative Ag/Ab and starting PrEP could select for resistance.

options.rationale: Deferring PrEP 4 weeks is wrong because a single recent negative HIV test plus absence of acute HIV symptoms is sufficient to start PrEP; deferring prolongs an unnecessary exposure window. Would be correct only if there are symptoms suggestive of acute seroconversion (ASHM PrEP guidelines).

On-demand (2+1+1) PrEP is wrong because on-demand dosing is only recommended for cisgender MSM with infrequent exposures; cisgender women require daily PrEP due to slower tissue drug levels in cervicovaginal tissue. Would be correct only for selected MSM, not for cisgender women (ASHM).

Daily oral TDF/FTC is the recommended PrEP regimen for cisgender women at substantial risk. Baseline workup includes HIV Ag/Ab, HBV serology, HCV antibody, syphilis serology, gonorrhoea/chlamydia NAAT, renal function and beta-hCG. Quarterly monitoring includes HIV testing and STI screen; renal function 6-monthly (ASHM PrEP guidelines).
Defer PrEP because partner is detectable is wrong because a partner with detectable viral load is exactly the indication for PrEP; PrEP is strongly indicated, not contraindicated. (ASHM).
Dolutegravir monotherapy is wrong because dolutegravir is not a PrEP agent; PrEP uses TDF/FTC (daily or, for selected MSM, on-demand). (ASHM).

explanation.summary: Acute presentation within 72 hours of sexual assault requires concurrent medical and forensic priorities: forensic examination with chain of custody by a trained examiner regardless of reporting intent; emergency contraception (levonorgestrel up to 96 hours, ulipristal up to 120 hours, or copper IUD up to 5 days); STI baseline tests and prophylaxis (ceftriaxone 500 mg IM, azithromycin 1 g or doxycycline 100 mg BD for 7 days, metronidazole 2 g single dose); HIV PEP eligibility assessment for source with HIV or unknown source with high-risk features; hepatitis B vaccination and HBIG where indicated; safety planning; mental health support and follow-up at 2 weeks, 6 weeks, and 3 months.
key_points: Forensic kit window: 72 hours (some up to 7 days for specific samples)
EC: levonorgestrel < 96 h, ulipristal < 120 h, Cu-IUD < 5 days
STI prophylaxis: ceftriaxone + azithromycin/doxycycline + metronidazole
HIV PEP: assess within 72 h; high-risk sources warrant PEP
HBV: vaccinate if unvaccinated; HBIG if source HBsAg-positive
Forensic exam offered regardless of reporting intent
explanation.pearls: Documentation matters - use trained examiners (FAMU/SARC), follow chain-of-custody, photograph injuries, store kit per jurisdiction protocol. Mental-health and safety planning are not afterthoughts; ongoing risk of further violence is high in the first weeks.

sources.label: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Sexual assault

options.rationale: Defer forensic examination until daylight is wrong because forensic evidence degrades within the <72-hour window; delaying loses DNA, secretions and trace evidence regardless of patient distress (a trained sexual assault examiner is best placed to balance comfort with timeliness). (RANZCOG; Australasian Sexual Health Alliance).

Forensic-only first is wrong because medical priorities (EC within 120 hours, STI prophylaxis, HIV PEP within 72 hours, HBV cover, safety planning) cannot be deferred to await kit processing; they run in parallel with forensic care. (RANZCOG).

Linking forensic exam to police reporting is wrong because forensic examination should be offered regardless of reporting intent, with anonymous kit storage available to preserve future options; mandating reporting acts as a barrier to disclosure. Would never be correct under Australian best practice (RANZCOG; Australasian Sexual Health Alliance).

Showered as contraindication is wrong because showering reduces but does not eliminate forensic yield; trace DNA and other evidence can still be recovered, and discharging without addressing EC, STI prophylaxis, HIV PEP, HBV cover and safety is unsafe. (RANZCOG).

Acute sexual assault management within 72 hours requires concurrent attention to medical priorities (EC within 120 hours, STI prophylaxis, HIV PEP assessment within 72 hours, HBV protection, mental health support and safety planning) and forensic priorities (kit collection with chain of custody by a trained examiner), regardless of whether the patient has decided to report (RANZCOG; ASHM; Australasian Sexual Health Alliance). Full care includes: forensic examination by trained examiner with documented chain of custody; LNG or UPA or copper IUD for emergency contraception; ceftriaxone IM plus azithromycin or doxycycline plus metronidazole for empirical STI prophylaxis; HIV PEP if eligible; hepatitis B vaccination (and HBIG if indicated); safety planning, counselling and follow-up.
source_refs: Australasian STI Management Guidelines - Sexual assault

explanation.summary: Trichomoniasis in non-pregnant adults is treated with oral metronidazole 2 g single dose, or 400 mg BD for 7 days (alternative for those at higher risk of treatment failure such as HIV). In pregnancy, treatment is still recommended (oral metronidazole 400 mg BD for 5-7 days). Always treat sexual partners empirically. Test of cure not routine but re-test for reinfection at 3 months.
key_points: First-line: metronidazole 2 g PO stat OR 400 mg BD x 7 d
Strawberry cervix (colpitis macularis) in 2-5% but pathognomonic when present
Motile flagellated protozoa on wet mount confirms; NAAT most sensitive
Partner notification and empirical treatment essential
Pregnancy: treat with oral metronidazole; avoid topical preparations
explanation.pearls: Avoid alcohol during and for 24 hours after metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction). HIV co-infection increases treatment failure risk; consider 7-day BD regimen in that group.

options.rationale: Single-dose metronidazole 2 g is first-line for trichomoniasis in adults, including breastfeeding women, with brief interruption of breastfeeding (12-24 hours) and discarding milk during peak levels to minimise infant exposure. Partner treatment is essential to prevent reinfection (Australasian STI Guidelines; eTG).

Intravaginal metronidazole gel is wrong because topical metronidazole achieves <50% cure for trichomoniasis (parasites in urethra, glands, etc. not reached); systemic therapy is required and partners must be treated to prevent ping-pong reinfection. Would never be correct for trichomonas (Australasian STI Guidelines).

Tinidazole with continued breastfeeding is wrong because tinidazole has a longer half-life requiring an approximately 3-day breastfeeding pause; metronidazole 2 g single dose with a 12-24h pause is preferred in breastfeeding. Would be correct only outside breastfeeding (Australasian STI Guidelines).
Permanently cease breastfeeding is wrong because a brief 12-24h pause is sufficient to clear peak metronidazole levels; permanent cessation is unnecessary and harmful. (Australasian STI Guidelines).

Doxycycline to her only is wrong because doxycycline has no activity against Trichomonas vaginalis and is contraindicated in breastfeeding due to enamel staining; treating her alone also leaves partners to reinfect. Would never be correct for trichomoniasis (eTG; ASHM).
